On this topic, MGen Laroche said he was never questioned by the NIS on the possibility detainees were being abused post transfer.Footnote 894 Nor was he ever questioned by a member of the military police about his decision to transfer the individual interviewed on November 5, 2007.Footnote 895 MGen Laroche said, with obvious emotion in his voice, while no one questioned him afterwards about his decision to transfer this individual, “any individual who is tortured is one individual too many […] it is always unfortunate, regardless of what happens.”Footnote 896

12.3.4.2 BGen Juneau

BGen Juneau was MGen Laroche’s deputy commander and a colonel while in theatre in Afghanistan at the time of this complaint. He has served over 27 years in the CF, much of that time in combat units, infantry in particular. He arrived in the Afghanistan theatre on July 25, 2007 and took responsibility as deputy commander on August 1st. He finished his tour in Afghanistan on May 15, 2008.Footnote 897

Much of BGen Juneau’s testimony covered similar territory to that of MGen Laroche. The focus in this section is therefore on the new information that BGen Juneau provided in testimony.

Prior to his deployment, BGen Juneau had no particular information about the detainee issue, other than “the same thing as most people might have seen when they watched the news on television, in newspaper articles, et cetera.” BGen Juneau received no briefings on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, although he was aware of the issue, “as most people were, because it was an issue that was very public at that time.”Footnote 898 As for the Graeme Smith articles, he did not read them, but knew the detainee controversy related to things said in the media about allegations of mistreatment of detainees. BGen Juneau also did not read any of the international reports, from DFAIT, the US State Department or elsewhere, nor were briefings provided. Although he did not view AIHRC reports, he knew the AIHRC was available to the Afghan government to ensure detainees were treated properly.Footnote 899 He indicated that if General Laroche had read certain of those reports, he had done so of his own accord because these were not documents that were circulated at headquarters for everyone to read.Footnote 900

BGen Juneau was aware a complaint had been filed with the MPCC several months before he went to Afghanistan, but did not know the details of the complaint. It appears, though, he was referring to the Attaran complaint, and not the February 21, 2007 complaint dealing with the legality of the detainee transfers and the MP role therein.Footnote 901

BGen Juneau had some contact with the military police prior to deploying, during parts of the training with respect to detainees. In particular, he met Maj Zybala and some other members of his team.Footnote 902

BGen Juneau knew during his time in theatre that something related to detainees was happening at the Federal Court. He understood there was a possibility the transfers might be stopped. He therefore spoke with legal experts about the Federal Court process to understand whether there would be complications during the mission. BGen Juneau did not recall having discussed the Federal Court or the MPCC complaint with the TFPM.Footnote 903

BGen Juneau understood the second arrangement was signed in May 2007 because there was “a need for a system that was a little more robust, where there was – that created conditions for having better confidence that detainees who were transferred by Canadian troops to the Afghan authorities would be treated according to the rules.” He referred to this as the “maturing process” for the transfer regime, and knew the chief improvement to be the right to visit detainees, unannounced, and to do private interviews. Interestingly, he was not aware that transfers had been suspended in May 2007.Footnote 904

In terms of transition from ROTO 3 to 4, he spoke with his predecessor, Deputy Commander Mike Cessford, about detainee issues, and based on that discussion, he believed there were significant improvements in the situation and there were no major concerns at the point when they took over the mission. BGen Juneau could not recall any such discussions with either Major Hudson or Major Zybala.Footnote 905 Like MGen Laroche, he was not provided with reports on the site visits that pre-dated his time in theatre.Footnote 906

BGen Juneau’s particular duties with respect to detainees required him to provide a level of supervision to ensure all was done in accordance with the procedures in place and the issue had visibility at the senior level within headquarters. BGen Juneau was to pay particular attention to the detainee issue.Footnote 907

BGen Juneau explained the TFPM’s office was at TFHQ, not next to his, but in another building. BGen Juneau had access to the TFPM as much as he wanted, and vice versa. The whole of headquarters was located within a compound 200 metres by 200. The Provost Marshal also had a work area outside headquarters, near the detainee facilities. The NIS commander in theatre was not located at the headquarters compound, and the deputy commander was not actually sure of his work location.Footnote 908

Process-wise, BGen Juneau said an advisor such as the Provost Marshal would normally go through the deputy commander before going to General Laroche. This was the case 95% of the time. For detainee issues, he described the role of the TFPM as ending at transfer:

[…] ses responsabilités commençaient au point de capture et puis se terminaient au point de soit libération ou de transfert aux autorités afghanes. Donc c’est sur cette partie‑là du processus vraiment que portait une grande partie de son attention.

[unofficial translation][...] his responsibilities started at the point of capture and ended at the point of either release or transfer to the Afghan authorities. So it was really on that part of the process that a lot of his attention was focused.Footnote 909

Like MGen Laroche, BGen Juneau’s evidence was unclear when he was asked whether the TFPM was involved with discussions about what was happening after transfer:

Il était impliqué dans certaines discussions qu’on avait. Puis il faisait partie du groupe, de l’équipe dont je parlais tantôt qui traitait du dossier des détenus. Il faisait partie de cette équipe‑là mais vraiment, l’ensemble de ses responsabilités directes au jour le jour était ce que je viens de décrire.

[unofficial translation] He was involved in certain discussions we had. And he was part of the group, of the team I was talking about, that handled the detainees issue. He was part of that team, but really, all of his day to day direct responsibilities were what I have described.Footnote 910

The team he spoke of was a reference to the same committee or advisory group on detainee issues that MGen Laroche had mentioned. BGen Juneau clarified the composition of the committee as an intelligence officer, legal advisors, the TFPM, the detainee officer, the POLAD and others as needed. He explained, though, once the committee came up with a recommendation for or against transfer, he was usually the one to take that recommendation to the Commander personally.Footnote 911

The committee did sit down physically, without the Commander, to make decisions related to transfer, medical issues, etc., but he did not recall conveying information during these meetings to the TFPM about post-transfer mistreatment. He also did not know whether the TFPM had access to the site visit reports. BGen Juneau himself received paper copies from the POLAD.Footnote 912 The committee was called together ad hoc, depending on the nature of the problem being analyzed at that particular point in time. As such, it was quite possible the Provost Marshal would not be there for aspects of the decision-making process that did not relate to his direct mandate:

La nature du comité était composée de façon ad hoc, c’est‑à‑dire dépendamment de la nature du problème qu’on analysait à ce moment‑là, j’appelais dans mon bureau ou dans une autre salle les gens que j’avais besoin de consulter pour le problème qu’on était en train d’analyser. Donc dans certains cas, l’officier de détenus était là. La plupart du temps, il était là parce qu’encore une fois, dans sa fonction de teneur de livres, j’aimais qu’il soit au courant de pas mal ce qui se passait. De temps à autre on appelait le Provost Marshal, de temps à autre on appelait l’officier d’intelligence, le POLAD, “ aviseur “ légal, encore une fois, dépendamment de la nature dont ce qu’on analysait.

[unofficial translation] The nature of the committee was composed ad hoc, that is, depending on the nature of the problem being analyzed at that point, I called people into my office or into another room that I needed to consult for the problem we were analyzing. So in some cases, the detainee officer was there. Most of the time, he was there because, once again, in his job as bookkeeper, I liked him to be aware of pretty much everything that was going on. From time to time we called on the Provost Marshal, from time to time we called on the intelligence officer, the POLAD, the legal advisor, once again, depending on the nature of what we were analyzing.Footnote 913

Moreover, he said the analysis of the risk of torture was not something that was discussed in that committee per se. It was discussed with certain individuals – the legal advisors on some occasions and the POLAD on others, but not within the committee.Footnote 914

BGen Juneau was asked about the distribution of the Commander’s Directive and Supplementary Directive issued by LGen (ret’d) Gauthier, and said Maj Zybala would not likely have gone through such a document in detail. He did say they were “probably distributed fairly widely within headquarters.”Footnote 915

Like MGen Laroche, he did not recall receiving any reports about detainees resisting or objecting to transfer.Footnote 916

BGen Juneau could say, with greater certainty, the TFPM was involved in discussions about post-transfer issues when they were thinking of stopping transfers:

Le grand prévôt a été impliqué dans des discussions relativement aux conditions que subissaient les détenus une fois transférés aux autorités afghanes, quand on a commencé à envisager de stopper le transfert où est‑ce que le niveau de risque commençait à augmenter. Et puis on commençait à avoir certaines préoccupations parce qu’en bout de ligne, si on les transférait pas, il fallait les garder.

[unofficial translation] The Provost Marshal was involved in discussions relating to the conditions the detainees were subject to once they were transferred to the Afghan authorities, when there started to be thoughts of stopping the transfer when the level of risk started to increase. And there started to be some concerns because at the end of the day, if they weren’t transferred, we had to keep them.Footnote 917

The concern for the TFPM, of course, was that his work would multiply because he would have to keep detainees for longer. The TFPM was asked whether, if necessary, he was prepared and capable of keeping detainees for longer.Footnote 918 BGen Juneau said it was probable that in those meetings with the TFPM present they spoke about why the transfers needed to be stopped, but he could not recall whether words to that effect were being used.Footnote 919 Thus, again, the evidence is uncertain as to what information and discussions the TFPM was privy to during committee meetings on the topic of detainees.

BGen Juneau did not involve the Provost Marshal in the production of his draft letter to the CEFCOM Commander, entitled in part “Points to Pass on to the Comd CEFCOM [...]”Footnote 920 This was the document dated November 4 or 5, 2007 that indicated, inter alia, the TFHQ was not currently receiving any additional information from any source other than DFAIT C4 traffic, that a risk assessment matrix was being developed for the transfer process, and that the frequency of DFAIT reporting was of concern because no reports had been received since September 27, 2007. The memo indicated notwithstanding these and other deficiencies, transfers could continue, but the light was “amber” and concern at the TFHQ was “mounting and approaching the point where the Comd will soon have to seriously consider temporarily halting transfers until the DFAIT/PRT monitoring and reporting situation improves.”Footnote 921

BGen Juneau gave direction to his staff to prepare this document. The CEFCOM Commander had asked him to provide the TFHQ assessment of the situation. He was given a few days to prepare it, but the TFPM did not assist and was not consulted. Instead, it was the Acting Chief of Staff and the legal advisors who were involved. The TFPM may have been involved with other discussions, but not the preparation of this document per se.Footnote 922 BGen Juneau explained again the TFPM’s involvement as follows:

Il était impliqué dans les discussions dans le sens que, comme je l’ai expliqué précédemment, si on considérait arrêter le transfert, il fallait lui demander bon, qu’est‑ce que ça veut dire pour lui parce que ça se traduisait en termes concrets. Il y aurait plus de détenus à garder dans la facilité de transfert, à KAF, pour une période plus longtemps. Est‑ce qu’il pouvait le faire physiquement? Est‑ce qu’il avait les capacités de le faire? Est‑ce que les installations le permettaient? Dans ce sens‑là, il était impliqué dans les discussions.

[unofficial translation] He was involved in the discussion in the sense that, as I explained earlier, if stopping the transfer was being considered, he had to be asked, well, what does that mean for him, because that translated into concrete terms. There would be more detainees to keep in the transfer facility, at KAF, for a longer time. Could he do that physically? Did he have the capacity to do it? [...] In that sense, he was involved in the discussions.Footnote 923

The Provost Marshal seemed not to have been present during discussions of risk assessment:

De ce que je peux me souvenir, il n’était pas présent pendant les quelques réunions qu’on a eues pour préparer ce dossier‑là et pour préparer une analyse du risque et dire: O.K., voici où on est rendu. Est‑ce que c’est un risque réel ou est‑ce qu’on est capable de vivre avec la situation présente? Le grand prévôt, d’après mes souvenirs, ne faisait pas partie de ces discussions‑là.

[unofficial translation] From what I can recall, he wasn’t present during the few meetings we had to prepare that issue and to prepare a risk analysis and say: Okay, this is where we are. Is this a real risk or are we capable of living with the present situation? The Provost Marshal, to my recollection, was not part of those discussions.Footnote 924

Similarly, BGen Juneau recalled sharing the November 5th site visit report with his Acting Chief of Staff and his legal advisors, but did not know if the Provost Marshal received it.Footnote 925 BGen Juneau was also not aware whether the TFPM was consulted with respect to the steps deemed necessary before resuming transfers to the NDS. He said during that timeframe the Provost Marshal had his hands full dealing with the surplus of detainees being held at a transfer facility not meant to hold detainees long term.Footnote 926

Once transfers stopped in November 2007, BGen Juneau said the Provost Marshal came to him to discuss detainees because the transfer facility was starting to fill to capacity, creating a problem. During those discussions, though, he did not recall discussing the results of site visits.Footnote 927 BGen Juneau knew that the POLAD’s distribution list for the site visits was “relatively limited”, but said if the TFPM had asked him, he would “probably have shown him a copy”.Footnote 928 He did think the Provost Marshal was aware of the reason why transfers had been stopped, but was not certain.Footnote 929

Maj Zybala left Afghanistan in February 2008. BGen Juneau was asked whether the same type of decision making committee existed when Maj Gribble was in theatre from late February 2008 onwards. It appears the committee did not meet often, if at all, and Maj Gribble’s involvement was almost nonexistent:

De ce que je me rappelle, le dossier des détenus, à partir du mois de ‑‑ au moment où est‑ce qu’on a recommencé les transferts au mois de février, s’était stabilisé beaucoup et puis il n’y avait pas eu de nécessité de réunir le comité en question très souvent. Je ne me rappelle pas d’une occasion où est‑ce qu’on aurait réuni le comité dans le dernier trois mois ou deux, trois mois de mon séjour là‑bas.

[unofficial translation] From what I recall, the detainees issue, starting in – starting when we began transferring again in February, stabilized a lot and there was no need to have the committee in question meet very often. I don’t recall an occasion when the committee met in the last three months or two, three months of my time there.Footnote 930

BGen Juneau’s interaction with Maj Gribble was infrequent. BGen Juneau did not know if Maj Gribble received the site visit reports.Footnote 931

After being shown the risk assessment matrix, BGen Juneau explained the people who saw this analysis were the Commander, the detainee officer, and the intelligence officer.Footnote 932 BGen Juneau’s evidence was not clear whether the risk assessment matrix and the Commander’s Review went together to people such as the TFPM. Ultimately, it appeared, from BGen Juneau’s evidence, the risk assessment matrix did not go to the TFPM.Footnote 933

The MP Technical Directive was shown to BGen Juneau, in particular the portions calling for investigation by the military police of allegations of violations of international law. He was asked whether he saw or experienced any tension stemming from the fact the TFPM was part of headquarters, but also responsible in some way for ensuring the investigation of such allegations? BGen Juneau’s answer was an unequivocal “no”. He understood the MP function, and expected, if they saw something they thought needed investigation, they could do so, free from intervention from the chain of command in place. For example, he had no thought the TFPM should be excluded when discussions occurred about possibly stopping transfers in late October 2007, nor was there ever discussion with Maj Zybala about the idea he might have to investigate aspects of the transfer decisions.Footnote 934

BGen Juneau’s contact with the NIS in theatre was very limited – he had one or two meetings with them related to troops killed in combat.Footnote 935

12.3.5 ROTO 3 – DFAIT in Afghanistan

The Commission also explored the information environment for DFAIT personnel in Afghanistan, and the extent to which, if at all, DFAIT information about detainee treatment made its way to the military police.

The only witness to have provided information about the information environment in Afghanistan prior to and during ROTO 3, from a DFAIT perspective, was Mr. Richard Colvin, who has been with Foreign Affairs since April 1994, and had overseas assignments in Sri Lanka, Russia, the Palestinian Territories, and Afghanistan. At the time of his testimony, he was the Deputy Head of the Intelligence Liaison Office at the Canadian Embassy in Washington.Footnote 936 His service in Afghanistan spanned from late April 2006 to October 2007, during all or parts of ROTOs 1 to 4. His first role in Afghanistan was as the senior DFAIT representative at the Provincial Reconstruction Team (PRT) headquarters in Kandahar City. From there, he became the head of the political section and chargé d’affaires at the Canadian embassy in Kabul.Footnote 937

As political director, Mr. Colvin was the senior DFAIT officer at the PRT. Indeed, at the time, he was the only DFAIT officer. The PRT was the whole of government vehicle for Kandahar, which meant every government department represented in Kandahar had officials or staff there. The intent was to mobilize all the different aspects of Canadian government power in the interests of stabilization and reconstruction in Afghanistan. Mr. Colvin’s work involved, in his own words:

[...] a lot of engaging with Afghans, with local officials, with the governor, with provincial council members, with representatives of non-governmental organizations, with internationals, for example, from the United Nations, with poppy eradication officials. We talked to the military, talked to the police, and tried to build a picture of what was happening in Kandahar.Footnote 938

Mr. Colvin testified information about the collective risk to detainees came to him very quickly after his arrival in Afghanistan. He considered the source “very credible”.Footnote 939

While at the PRT, he issued two reports about detainees that he deemed important.Footnote 940 It was his evidence that the second report, in particular, conveyed “not just a risk, but the fact of mistreatment” of Canadian-transferred detainees.Footnote 941 The first report was dated May 26, 2006, and entitled: “KANDH0029 – Detainees: ICRC concerns over notification by Cdn forces”. The report’s summary indicates that: “Because of inadequate information collection and occasional reporting delays, the [blank due to redactions] ICRC office is losing track of some Afghan detainees. [...] ICRC is “very much taken aback” by the lack of cooperation from Cdn military in theatre.” The response to this email indicates the TFPM at the time, Major James A. Fraser, was the national point of contact on detainee issues in theatre.Footnote 942 As such, his first email dealt with issues related to timely and effective notification to the ICRC, for the ICRC’s own tracking and visitation purposes.

The second report was the one in which Mr. Colvin felt he had conveyed that Canadian-transferred detainees were being mistreated. The most important portions of the document were heavily redacted by the Government, making it very difficult for the Commission to formulate its own judgment on just what the report conveyed. It was sent on June 2, 2006 over the C4 network, and was titled: “KANDH0032 – Kandahar prison and Afghan detainees”. Mr. Colvin explained that over the period in question – May 2006 – he was able to get good information from credible sources about the way in which detainees transferred by the Canadian Forces were being treated post transfer. Mr. Colvin advised the Commission that the source had conveyed that Canada was not meeting its international obligations with respect to transfer, but indicated the basis for this concern was partially hidden behind the national security redactions found at paras 20–23 of his report.Footnote 943 Mr. Colvin attempted, as best he could, to explain how that message was conveyed by him:

  • Thank you. Now, Mr. Colvin, we were looking at your 0032 email, and, similar to what I said about your first email, I didn’t see any reference to torture or risk of torture in this email.
  • The issue of torture, risk of torture is in the section, paragraphs 20 to 23, but the words that are used, as I mentioned in the email, are code. So the words used do not mean exactly what, on the surface, they mean but are standing in for something else. So in this case, unsatisfactory conditions, unsavoury conditions, all kinds of things are going on. My understanding at the time and my understanding today is that these are references to abuse, mistreatment, torture.

    I mean, there’s a question of, you know, what is abuse versus mistreatment versus torture, and that’s obviously an issue that I am not really qualified to pass, but they all fit into a category of improper treatment, and that’s what this section deals with.

    In the context of the particular source or sources, the information we got was, by necessity, presented in a cautious fashion. And so I flag in this message that these words are being given in a cautious fashion, in code, and that there is more of the same ilk, which, for reasons which I can’t get into, can’t be told more directly.

    So I am alerting the readership that these words are standing in for words which might would, in my view, include torture.
  • Okay. Now, would you allow for the possibility that perhaps outside of the DFAIT circle, for example, within the CF command elements, they may not appreciate or understand that these terms are code for something else?
  • There is, you know, an assumption when you write these things that you are writing for a reasonably sophisticated audience, but I agree with you. I felt at the time there might be a risk of misunderstanding, and that was actually, maybe less for the content as for the amount of material on the prison.

    So this is why I added this emphasis in the summary that the important material has to do with and then I summarize what my understanding of the concern was, but it is the overall treatment of detainees that is the concern,

    […]

    and so there is no confusion and they think, well, it is maybe detainees generally or some other people’s detainees or detainees in a specific province, I specify it is our detainees.

    So it is not saying what exactly is happening to the detainees. I didn’t have that level of knowledge, but the knowledge I did have spoke to the fact, the understanding, the assessment from very credible source or sources that our detainees were being subject to improper treatment, were being badly treated, mistreated, abused, without the knowledge of the techniques or specificity.

    You know, to say that this rises to a level of torture would be a step for which I didn’t have that detail, but I did have an awareness that there were problems with treatment, mistreatment.

    And in the context of Afghanistan, the context of Kandahar, the context of other aspects that we were aware of, for example, behaviour of the Governor of Kandahar, it was clear that, in an Afghan context, this isn’t some sort of mild treatment, or inadequate food or the beds aren’t soft enough. This would be a severe problem, a clear problem of how our detainees are being treated.Footnote 944

Mr. Colvin had feedback from Pamela Isfeld that the ROTO 1 TFPM, Maj Fraser, was told about this message, and had commented.Footnote 945 Although, Maj Fraser was the TFPM for ROTO 1, while Maj Hudson, the first TFPM subject in chronological order, was not in theatre until approximately eight months later.

Mr. Colvin stated that he intended these reports to make their way to the military police. The reports were sent out over the DFAIT C4 network. Access to this network was limited, and he knew the Provost Marshal in theatre did not have a C4 connection.Footnote 946 However, Mr. Colvin thought there were two ways MPs could have received the reports he sent out over the C4 network. The first possibility was via the CEFCOM J9 and others at CEFCOM who were on his distribution lists. He thought the “CEFCOM J9 would then be in contact with their people in the field, including, on an issue such as this, the military police.”Footnote 947 Mr. Colvin certainly understood the TFPM was to be the point of contact for the ICRC to raise any issues it had.Footnote 948

The other way he thought his C4 information would get to the MPs was via Pamela Isfeld at KAF. She was the political advisor to the Task Force Commander at KAF, who was BGen David Fraser at the time that Mr. Colvin would have been sending these initial reports (May/June 2006). Ms. Isfeld was on Mr. Colvin’s distribution list for these first two reports. Mr. Colvin understood that she would maintain contact with numerous individuals at KAF, and this was his evidence on her contact with the Provost Marshal at KAF:

And so in the case of messages on detainees, she would physically print up the message, and then walk over with it to the Provost Marshal, in this case, discuss it with him, and then come back and report back to me.Footnote 949

It is important to note that even if the information in these two reports (KANDH0029 and KANDH0032) made its way into the hands, or the knowledge base, of the TFPM, it does not follow the TFPM or other MPs in theatre during ROTO 3 knew about these messages. Indeed, it is likely they did not, given how dated the messages were, having been drafted approximately eight months prior to Maj Hudson’s arrival in theatre for ROTO 3.

In August of 2006, Mr. Colvin moved to Kabul to take up his position there. He was responsible for all Canadian policy files, and any issues he judged important to Canada, especially as it related to the engagement in Kandahar. This continued to include the detainee issue.Footnote 950 From Kabul, he sent other reports involving detainees, one of which related to ISAF having trouble making contact with Canada and getting information on detainees. The other message, though heavily redacted, included information about treatment of detainees.Footnote 951 Mr. Colvin also authored portions of the DFAIT country report for Afghanistan for 2006.Footnote 952

Mr. Colvin was also present, with Ms. Duschner, at the inter-agency meeting on March 9, 2007, where he informed everyone present that the NDS tortures people, and if Canada did not want its detainees tortured, then they should not send them to the NDS. Mr. Colvin’s own recounting of the meeting was very similar to the description already provided in the CEFCOM section above.Footnote 953

Mr. Colvin’s early C4 messages were broadly distributed. However, they all pre-dated the timeframe for this complaint, and it is likely that they would not have been seen by someone such as Maj Hudson. During the timeframe for this complaint, that is, from May 2007 onwards, the site visit reports from DFAIT visits to transferred detainees were the most important DFAIT documents on post-transfer treatment of detainees. Once those site visit reports began to be produced during ROTOs 3 and 4, however, Mr. Colvin found himself more or less out of the loop in terms of knowing their distribution. With the passage of time, he was no longer copied on those reports:

  • [...] To your knowledge, were such reports provided to the Canadian Forces by DFAIT?
  • That’s a hard one for me to answer, because especially as time went on, I, myself, began not to be copied on these reports.”

    So the distribution list was reduced to a very few people and I wasn’t always privy to these reports, myself. So it is hard for me to say what happened to them and who they went to.Footnote 954

Indeed, he was aware the distribution of the site visit reports was being seriously curtailed:

So I was certainly aware at the time that the distribution was being extremely curtailed, which seems to contradict somewhat the intention of the SOPs that these reports be shared with all appropriate officials, including obviously particularly the Task Force Commander in Kandahar, officials of the military police, provost marshals of whichever kind, officials who would need to be informed of what was happening to our detainees based on the monitoring reports.

And it seemed to me at the time that these reports were really being seen by a very small number of people, mostly very senior people in Ottawa, who were jealously guarding them to the point where instructions began to be written into these reports not for forward distribution, just in case someone felt the urge to share them.

[...]

So the information was not being shared in a form I think envisaged by the SOPs.Footnote 955

Mr. Colvin also agreed the military police were not on that limited distribution list for the site visit reports, with, perhaps, the exception that the report could be distributed to them within or via CEFCOM:

“[...] the distribution specifies in most cases exactly which individuals should get them. That is not really done for CEFCOM J9. So according to this, CEFCOM J9 in its entirety is the recipient, and, depending on how they define that, that CEFCOM J9, I mean, it could extend right down into Kandahar. In fact, that would be my expectation. These were sort of vertically structured, if you like, and so the people in the field under this distribution could still have got the message. That would depend on how you interpret CEFCOM J9, but there is no restrictions spelling out who exactly in CEFCOM J9 should get it.”Footnote 956

Mr. Colvin agreed the military police were dependent on someone from the limited distribution list giving them the site visit reports.Footnote 957

Mr. Colvin was part of the team that conducted the June 5 & 6, 2007 site visit to the Kabul detention facility, during which three of the four detainees interviewed said they had been whipped with cables, shocked with electricity and/or otherwise “hurt” while in NDS custody in Kandahar.Footnote 958 This report has already been described in detail. Mr. Colvin found the accounts of abuse to be “highly credible”.Footnote 959 He was not, however, responsible for the distribution of this report, once created.

For the purposes of this complaint, i.e., in terms of MP access to DFAIT information about post-transfer treatment of detainees, Mr. Colvin had no further, significant involvement with the detainee question during the remainder of his time in Afghanistan.

12.3.6 ROTOs 4 & 5 – DFAIT in Afghanistan

The Commission heard from three DFAIT witnesses who had information to provide about post-transfer treatment of detainees in Afghanistan during ROTOs 4 & 5, that is, from August 2007 onwards. They were Eelco (Ed) Jager, the policy advisor to MGen Laroche, John Davison, the political director for DFAIT at the PRT, and Nicholas Gosselin, a policy officer in the area of human rights and the individual chiefly responsible for conducting site visits commencing November 5, 2007.

12.3.6.1 Ed Jager, POLAD

Mr. Jager arrived in Afghanistan in late July 2007, and spent ten months as General Laroche’s policy advisor (POLAD). He left the Afghanistan theatre in May 2008, on the same flight as General Laroche.Footnote 960 Mr. Jager described his role as the “juncture between the general DFAIT structure and the military in Afghanistan.” As policy advisor he was to “help the General understand the political environment in which he was operating.”Footnote 961 Located at TFHQ, he was a staff of one, but tied into the DFAIT hierarchy via the Head of Mission in Kabul and the Afghanistan department in Ottawa (bearing the acronym FTAG).Footnote 962

Mr. Jager was stationed at KAF, had a close working relationship with the military personnel there, and had occasion to work with the military police. Mr. Jager was asked about the decision making committee for detainee transfers referred to by Generals Laroche and Juneau in their testimony, and whether he knew the TFPM to be on it. Mr. Jager did not view it as a committee, per se, and could not recall Maj Zybala ever being present at a meeting where detainees were discussed:

I don’t remember there being a committee as such. I believe that there was a group of us that the General and the Deputy Commander consulted from time to time.

  • Did that include the Task Force Provost Marshal, Major Zybala?
  • I don’t have a specific memory of him being with us at any particular time.

    [...]

    I can remember seeing Major Zybala at various omnibus meetings. Specific meetings dealing with detainees at which he was present, I have no memory of.Footnote 963

Mr. Jager also could not remember if he ever advised the Task Force Commander on issues such as risk to detainees post transfer, although he admitted that it may have been a topic that was discussed that he simply did not recall.Footnote 964 Mr. Jager said he did not provide advice to the Task Force Commander on whether to transfer, and the associated risks.Footnote 965

Mr. Jager was responsible for reading the supplementary transfer arrangement agreement to detainees just prior to their transfer to the NDS, with the assistance of an interpreter. That was his first and last interaction with the detainees. He was not at all involved with the post-transfer monitoring process.Footnote 966 He described the physical transfer process – the portion that he viewed – as follows:

[...] The transfer would take place within the confines of the transfer facility on Kandahar Air Field. That transfer facility was completely managed and run by the military police. Unless I happen to run into someone who identified himself as something else, I would have assumed that every single person I met was an MP at some level.Footnote 967

Mr. Jager’s evidence seemed to indicate the military police were present when he read the supplementary transfer arrangement out to the detainees:

  • When you encountered a member of the NDS in the context of an anticipated transfer of a prisoner, that would happen at the transfer facility with MPs present?
  • That is correct.Footnote 968

Elsewhere he said “[t]o the best of his knowledge, yes, at all times there was always an MP at some level present, simply because I don’t think I would feel comfortable in the room with the detainees by myself.”Footnote 969 The NDS was not present when he read the arrangement out to the detainees.Footnote 970

He recalled detainees occasionally professed their innocence upon learning of their transfer to the NDS, but he heard no complaints about what might happen to them after transfer in terms of mistreatment. Mr. Jager did not recall any complaints from detainees about their inability to pay their way out of NDS custody: “No, no one ever expressed that to me or, if they did, it wasn’t translated that way to me.” Mr. Jager also did not witness any physical resistance to transfer throughout all the transfers he did.Footnote 971

The POLAD was the gatekeeper of the site visit reports coming in over the DFAIT C4 network in KAF. Indeed, he received all the monitoring reports between July 20, 2007 and May 14, 2008. These were secret reports Mr. Jager provided to those on his distribution list, which included, to his recollection, Col Juneau, the Chief of Staff, Chief of Staff (National), the detainee officer and the legal advisor. To the best of his knowledge, the TFPM was not on that list.Footnote 972

Like other witnesses with access to the site visit reports, Mr. Jager was asked whether he would have provided the reports to the military police if asked. Mr. Jager’s answer was somewhat equivocal, although he agreed there was no prohibition on it per se: “I mean, that never happened so I can’t imagine how I would have reacted at that time. Looking back at it three years ago, no one had ever told me not to give it to them.” In his view, though, his client was the Task Force Commander, not the military at large or the MPs, so he would have provided information to the military police if the Task Force Commander had asked him to do so.Footnote 973

Mr. Jager did not think he received or viewed the site visit reports from visits that occurred prior to his arrival in Afghanistan, nor did he brief MGen Laroche on those site visits.Footnote 974

Mr. Jager said he could not remember if there were discussions about the post-transfer monitoring, and with whom.Footnote 975 Mr. Jager did recall there was concern during the period preceding November 5, 2007 about the frequency of site visits, but could not say the TFPM was present during some of those discussions.Footnote 976 Mr. Jager could not recall one way or the other whether the Ouimet article in late October 2007 resulted in a meeting involving Generals Laroche and Juneau, the detainee officer, the TFPM, himself and perhaps others, as suggested by the two Generals. He simply had no recollection of such a meeting.Footnote 977

Mr. Jager did say certain of the site visit reports generated direct and immediate discussion, such as the one he received on November 5, 2007, which he read, and brought immediately to Col Juneau. Mr. Jager said he would not have alerted the military police when he received that report. Mr. Jager said there were a number of meetings that took place through that period, with various groups of people present. The legal advisor, Deputy Commander Juneau and the Chief of Staff National largely handled the issue of the November 5th report “with a minimum of input from me.”Footnote 978 Mr. Jager understood as well the TFPM had no input into a decision making process he described as sensitive and subject to need to know principles:

It is my understanding the Provost Marshal had no input into the decision making process. They were responsible for implementing it, but it was the General and his staff who made the decisions and they kept it – this was a very sensitive matter and they kept it on the basis of who needed to know.Footnote 979

12.3.6.2 John Davison, PRT Political Director

Mr. Davison was the political director on the Provincial Reconstruction Team in Kandahar. Mr. Davison first arrived in June 2007 for a temporary duty assignment, and formally assumed his position in August. He left Afghanistan in June 2008. He described his duties as follows:

The political director was in charge of the DFAIT component within the Provincial Reconstruction Team. There were, ultimately, five of us in that unit, and we were responsible for all aspects of Canada’s relations in Kandahar province with regards to support for the police forces, the development of the police forces in Kandahar province, for the justice system in Kandahar province, for just general reporting on what was going on in Kandahar. [...] and also, as you are aware, we were also responsible for follow up interviews with Canadian transfer detainees.Footnote 980

He received torture awareness training before going to Afghanistan, first, by taking a course given by an expert and, second, by way of a briefing session with the unit within DFAIT responsible for Afghanistan. At that briefing session, standard operating procedures and the “rules of the game” for detainee interviews were discussed.Footnote 981

Monitoring would be only one aspect of his responsibilities in Afghanistan. Mr. Davison also represented the DFAIT perspective to people from DND and CSC, attended numerous meetings on the workings of the PRT, and had other responsibilities mentioned previously. Mr. Davison explained nobody dealt exclusively with monitoring until Nicholas Gosselin arrived in Afghanistan.Footnote 982

Mr. Davison interacted with the military police situated at the PRT, but in a limited way: “The only interaction with the Military Police was in the sort of twice a week meeting that we had, so whoever was representing the Military Police would attend this sort of group meeting with all units of the PRT represented. But I had no other interaction aside from that.”Footnote 983

Mr. Davison accompanied his predecessor on a site visit in June 2007, and conducted site visits in early September: “[...] sometime probably in [the] beginning of September, I was asked to make sure to start the – start up the visits again.”Footnote 984 Mr. Davison went on two site visits in September, where he received allegations of mistreatment from two detainees. These would appear to be the two allegations that led to a Tiger Team investigation, as discussed in the evidence of MGen Laroche (KANDH 0074 and KANDH 0082).Footnote 985 The details of these allegations of abuse have been discussed elsewhere in this Report. At no point did Mr. Davison raise a concern with his superiors or with the military police about the fact transfers continued after he received these reports of abuse and mistreatment.Footnote 986 Mr. Davison said he did not see it as his duty to assess credibility when conducting a site visit or composing a report.Footnote 987

After the September visits, Mr. Davison went on his first leave at the start of October. Upon returning from his leave later that month, he scheduled a site visit with Mr. Gosselin as soon as practicable.Footnote 988 From what the Commission could discern, therefore, it appears Mr. Davison and/or Mr. Gosselin were present for all site visits that occurred during the first part of ROTO 4 (from August 2007 to November 5, 2007). The November 5, 2007 site visit was Mr. Gosselin’s first.

Mr. Davison had no input into the distribution list for the site visit reports that went out over the C4 system. This was established for him and others doing visits. To his knowledge, no military police members were on that distribution list, nor did the MPs accompany him during the site visits.Footnote 989 Mr. Davison gave the following perspective on whether the military police in Afghanistan would know about the results of his site visits:

The truth is that there were, I am sure the Military Police, by and large, didn’t even know I existed there. They had no reason to. Their contact on the detainee file was in KAF with the POLAD, Ed Jager, and not with me going out to actually conduct the interviews. You know, we reported, it went to KAF, and, as far as I know, Ed circulated those reports through the military, at least the senior chain of command. Whether the Military Police were on that sort of circulation, I don’t know.Footnote 990

Not only were Mr. Davison`s links to the military police limited in the manner described, but he also never interacted directly with the Task Force Commander while in Afghanistan.Footnote 991

When transfers recommenced in early March 2008, Mr. Davison suggested the site visits were occurring very frequently, at an approximate rate of once per week. From that point on, until he left Afghanistan, he could not recall any further allegations of abuse.Footnote 992 The visits in that timeframe did not always involve face-to-face, private interviews with Canadian-transferred detainees. It depended on time constraints and other factors:

It was all subject to time too. I mean, it could take up to 30 minutes to interview one detainee, that’s using a translator, so everything was kind of double the length of time. It might be, you know, versus a conversation, a shared conversation in one language. So time was the real problem for us, but we could normally do up to two interviews, and then we were beginning to push the time limit with which our Canadian Forces escort were comfortable with us being in one place at one time.

  • Were you able to have personal contact or interviews with all of the transferred detainees given those time constraints?
  • No, we sampled [...]

    [...]
  • So you saw every individual but couldn’t necessarily interview them?
  • That’s correct.Footnote 993
12.3.6.3 Nicholas Gosselin, Policy Officer, Human Rights

Mr. Gosselin started at the PRT in November 2007 as a policy officer in the area of human rights. Previously, he had been with DFAIT as a senior labour relations officer. Mr. Gosselin’s job included working with the various local institutions in Afghanistan on human rights issues (capacity building), but his primary task was to do the monitoring visits. The latter amounted to 80% of his responsibilities while in theatre. Mr. Gosselin reported to Mr. Davison, and was, essentially, assuming a newly created position upon his arrival.Footnote 994 Mr. Gosselin conducted site visits until his time in Afghanistan ended in August 2008.Footnote 995

Like Mr. Davison, he was given special training on human rights and torture awareness to prepare him for his monitoring work. The course on torture awareness was specifically developed for consular officers around the world, whose job it is to monitor the situation in various prisons and penal institutions. Mr. Gosselin also took a course with NATO to prepare for the environment at the PRT.Footnote 996 Prior to going to Afghanistan, he familiarized himself with the general human rights situation using newspaper articles and reports published by the UN, AIHRC and the US State Department. Mr. Gosselin had not viewed the DFAIT country reports for Afghanistan.Footnote 997

Unlike many witnesses interviewed by the Commission, it appears Mr. Gosselin read some of the site visit reports that had been created prior to his arrival in Afghanistan.Footnote 998

Mr. Gosselin recalled meeting certain MPs in person at the PRT, and at the detention centre at KAF where he went in the beginning to familiarize himself with the transfer process. Mr. Gosselin never had occasion to discuss detainee treatment post transfer with the MPs he met.Footnote 999

In the beginning, Mr. Davison would accompany him regularly for the visits. On some occasions, a person from CSC would join them.Footnote 1000 The military police were never with him.Footnote 1001

Upon returning from a visit, he described how there was a predefined format in which he had to report his conclusions, and a set distribution list for those reports. The list of recipients included the POLAD at TFHQ (for onward distribution to the Commander and the detainee officer), the embassy, DFAIT Afghanistan HQ in Ottawa, PCO, PSEPC, and a list of acronyms within DND with which he was not familiar. The political director would review his report before it was sent out to this list.Footnote 1002 Mr. Gosselin felt he could not add anyone to the distribution list for the site visit reports, describing it as a very “rigid process”.Footnote 1003

Mr. Gosselin was of course present during the November 5, 2007 visit. Mr. Gosselin said the frequency of visits increased significantly as a result, occurring practically every other day until December.Footnote 1004 Over the course of his time in Afghanistan, he suggested visits occurred, on average, at a frequency of twice per week.Footnote 1005 To his knowledge, no further stoppages of transfers occurred after November 5, 2007.Footnote 1006

Following his November 5, 2007 visit, Mr. Gosselin said he received five more allegations of mistreatment from interviewed detainees prior to going on leave in December. As mentioned, this number was larger than the figures provided in some of the DFAIT materials before the Commission. Mr. Gosselin recounted having reported on various forms of abuse at least six times during interviews up to the date of his leave.Footnote 1007

In late February 2008, he went on a series of capacity-building visits,Footnote 1008 before visits to individual detainees began to occur again. Mr. Gosselin was accompanied on several of these visits by representatives from CSC and the RCMP:

  • Je ne peux pas me souvenir exactement de quand ça a commencé, mais le point différent ici c’est qu’il y avait des agents de la GRC qui nous ont accompagnés dans certaines visites.

    Ce n’était pas nécessairement une nouvelle pratique, mais c’est que dans les analyses de projets de reconstruction dont on a parlé tout à l’heure, on a identifié qu’il y avait une opportunité de travailler avec les autorités NDS et de Sarpoza sur les techniques d’entrevue puis d’interrogation.

    Donc ces policiers‑là étaient responsables de cette dimension‑là.

    [unofficial translation] I can’t recall exactly when it started, but the difference here is that RCMP agents accompanied us on some of the visits.

    It was not necessarily a new procedure, but in the analyses of reconstruction projects we talked about earlier, we identified an opportunity to work with NDS authorities and with Sarpoza on interview techniques, as well as on interrogation techniques.

    So those police officers were responsible for that aspect.Footnote 1009

The police officers involved in these reconstruction and training efforts were from CIVPOL, a contingent of police officers assigned to the PRT. They were Canadians, but not military police.Footnote 1010

As Mr. Davison explained, sometimes the interviews of transferred detainees in 2008 amounted to little more than a visual assessment:

Il n’y avait pas de raison en particulier, autre que possiblement le climat de sécurité qui ne permettait pas de prendre le temps de faire ces visites‑là, ou encore qu’il y avait d’autres activités qui étaient prévues à l’horaire puis qui devaient être faites.

Je ne peux pas vous donner une raison précise là, mais au minimum à chacune de ces visites‑là, on s’assurait de voir chacun des détenus transférés par le Canada.

[unofficial translation] There was no particular reason other than possibly a security issue that did not allow taking time for those types of visits, or perhaps there were other activities scheduled at that time that needed to be attended to. [...] However, during each of the visits, we at least made sure we saw every one of the detainees that were transferred by Canada.Footnote 1011

Sometimes, interviews did not occur because the individual detainee had already been tried within the Afghan system.Footnote 1012 There is also evidence that for periods of time there were simply no detainees to interview.Footnote 1013

During the entire 2008 timeframe within which he conducted site visits, Mr. Gosselin never again had the opportunity to discuss these visits with members of the military police. Mr. Gosselin did have a discussion once with someone from the NIS, but believed it had to do with a completely separate matter not related to detainees.Footnote 1014

XIII. CFNIS Investigations

On February 1, 2010 the Commission received a voluminous disclosure package of CFNIS investigations into Afghan detainee issues. Most of the investigations in this package related to incidents which pre-date the complaint in this inquiry, and largely relate to allegations of abuse of detainees by members of the CF rather than post-transfer abuse allegations. None of these investigations dealt with the legality of the commanders’ transfer orders.Footnote 1015

A review of these investigations is appropriate nonetheless as they were relied upon by both Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore and LCol (ret’d) Garrick in answer to the allegations in the complaint.Footnote 1016 In addition, the examinations of NIS witnesses (including LCol (ret’d) Garrick) concerning some of these investigations was instructive with respect to the issue of NIS methodologies, resources and prioritization of investigative files. For ease of reference, the investigations are referred to by their General Occurrence (GO) file numbers.

13.1 General Occurrences

13.1.1 GO 2007–2598Footnote 1017 – Operation Camel Spider

Operation Camel Spider was the NIS investigation into the facts underlying allegations brought to this Commission by Dr. Amir Attaran concerning the treatment of three injured detainees who passed through CF custody in Kandahar during ROTO 1. The Commission’s final report is an exhibit in this inquiryFootnote 1018 and the facts underlying that allegation are thoroughly canvassed in that report and elsewhere in this Report. Dr. Attaran contended MPs: (i) failed to investigate the cause of injuries to the three detainees; (ii) failed to treat humanely the three injured detainees while they were in MP custody; (iii) failed to exercise due diligence in safeguarding evidence by transferring the detainees prior to a forensic medical examination; and (iv) failed to seize and inventory the personal effects of at least one of the three detainees.Footnote 1019

The NIS investigation of CF treatment of these detainees was known as “Operation Camel Spider”. The Case Manager was RCMP Inspector George Gfellner, who had previously been seconded from the RCMP to the NIS and was assigned to this investigation, WO Steeve Chamberland was the lead NIS investigator. The NIS was ordered by the CFPM to investigate whether any of the three detainees suffered mistreatment or abuse while in CF custody, whether they were given proper medical care, and whether the military police ought to have investigated the cause of the detainees’ injuries.Footnote 1020

By all accounts, the investigation of these allegations was extensive and resource intensive. Inspector Gfellner went so far as to try to locate and interview the detainees themselves.Footnote 1021

None of the subject matter of 2007–2598 dealt with the legality of the orders to transfer detainees or the issue of post-transfer detainee abuse. In the course of this investigation other allegations concerning detainees began to arise, and the NIS did not have the resources to pursue those allegations while conducting the Camel Spider investigation. These other investigations were eventually compiled into Operation Centipede.Footnote 1022

13.1.2 GO 2008–6259Footnote 1023 – Investigation into Allegations of Extended Detention

This investigation was initiated after MPCC personnel alerted the NIS to the fact that during the period of time in late April and early May 2007 a detainee or detainees were held without transfer or release for considerably longer than the 96 hour time period prescribed in the governing TSO.Footnote 1024 This information was conveyed to the NIS in March, 2008 and the GO was initiated by the CFNIS Pacific Region branch on March 12, 2008 when they received the initial information from CFNIS HQ.

The focus of this investigation was on the conduct of the MPs who were the custodians of the detainee(s) in question. The investigation included formal interviews of Sgt Utton and Capt Worsfold (the actual custodians) concerning the facts surrounding the extended detention, the conditions, and the efforts made to ensure humane treatment of the detainee(s). There was contact with the TFPM Maj Hudson and the CEFCOM PM Maj Laflamme concerning the circumstances, but this resulted in no relevant evidence. LCdr Siepka, who was legal adviser to MGen (ret’d) Grant when these detainees were held under his command, was consulted but offered only a reference to the governing TSO and the suggestion that MGen (ret’d) Grant be contacted. WO Chamberland and Inspector Gfellner were spoken to regarding detainee handling issues in general. Further discussions and interviews were held with the MPCC investigator who had initiated the matter.

Sgt Utton testified before the Commission about the circumstances and said the detainee(s) were left in extremely hot conditions in a facility not designed at that time to hold a person for so long. Sgt Utton was obviously very concerned for the mental and physical well-being of the detainee(s). The MPs brought in a swamp cooler, and took numerous other steps to help assuage the heat which was apparently somewhere in the range of 140 degrees Fahrenheit.Footnote 1025 Nevertheless, the order remained in place that the detainee(s) could not be released. Sgt Utton and her commander Capt Worsfold both believed the transfers had ceased due to court proceedings in relation to the Amnesty complaint about mistreatment of the detainees by the CF.

Although MGen (ret’d) Grant’s legal counsel suggested that MGen (ret’d) Grant or the CEFCOM J3 could clarify the issue whether the TSO was followed or not, MGen (ret’d) Grant does not appear to have been consulted by the NIS. The Commission is aware, from MGen (ret’d) Grant’s testimony, that transfers had been suspended due to concerns about allegations of post-transfer abuse and the monitoring provisions that were to take effect following the implementation of the May 3, 2007 transfer arrangement.

It is noteworthy the NIS investigators recognized that to get to the root of the investigation “it is essential to determine the time line regarding the passage of information between the KAF MP Chain of Command and the TFA Cdr, so that it can be precisely determined who made what decisions and when”.Footnote 1026 Once it was determined the MP company had registered its concerns with the Chain of Command about holding the detainee(s), and the decision to neither transfer nor release the detainee(s) rested with the TFA Cdr, the investigation was concluded and the matter referred to CEFCOM:

[...]It shall be noted that this matter was simply a concern brought forward to the CFNIS Chain of Command by the MPCC and that there was no specific allegation or complaint regarding the conduct of MP members. With respect to the fact that the TSO was not followed, it is suggested that the CEFCOM Comd review this issue.

Through discussions with Inspector Gfellner and review of information to date, it seems clear that as there is no complaint specific to the MP role or complaint from the detainee or outside agencies; the situation is an issue revolving around the decision to suspend Detainee transfers and not requiring CFNIS investigation at this time. Investigation into this matter is concluded.Footnote 1027

13.1.3 GO 2008–3134Footnote 1028 – ROTO 4 Human Dimensions Operations (HDO) Survey

A confidential survey of CF personnel during ROTO 4 disclosed that a small number of CF personnel might have witnessed abuse of detainees and/or non-combatants by members of the CF.Footnote 1029 The Operational Chain of Command conducted an internal investigation when the results of this survey became known. The MP do not appear to have been notified until after the Operations Branch investigation. On February 1, 2008 the CFPM requested the NIS conduct an expedited investigation while potential witnesses were still in theatre and accessible. The CFPM pledged to provide necessary personnel, and asked the NIS to “[a]dvise me if you encounter resistance that will result in delay”.Footnote 1030

It is apparent a significant amount of effort and resources were expended on this investigation as the publicly available portion of the GO file disclosed to the Commission comprises three full binder volumes, about half of the disclosed NIS investigations.

It should be stressed the incidence of reported abuse was very small – eight persons (1.2% of those polled) reported witnessing one instance of physical abuse of a detainee or non-combatant, and six persons (1% of those polled) reported witnessing this type of incident more than once There is nothing in the Commission’s record indicating whether there could be overlap in reporting, i.e., more than one person reporting the same incident, such that the actual number of separate incidents could be even lower.Footnote 1031 It is clear that both the Chain of Command and CFPM took even this level of reported abuse seriously, as remedial measures were proposed by the former, and extensive investigations ordered by the CFPM.

The investigation disclosed five particular allegations. It was concluded in March 2009 with two allegations being substantiated and pursued (both in relation to one CF member), one allegation being reviewed in theatre, and two found not to involve abuse against detainees or non-combatants.Footnote 1032 None of the allegations related to post-transfer abuse or legality of transfer orders.

13.1.4 GO 2008–6906Footnote 1033 – Operation Centipede

Operation Centipede was a GO generated on March 19, 2008:

  1. OP CENTIPEDE was created in order to investigate numerous incidents related to the alleged abuse of CF detainees in Afghanistan. All allegations were placed under one investigative umbrella in order to direct an order of priority based on the severity of the offences and to be able to seek out any possible event-to-event linkages. The mandate was a full time task force utilizing Major Case Management principles to determine if any CF personnel acted illegally or improperly regarding the handling or treatment of Afghan detainees that were in the custody of the CF.
  2. From this, eight different General Occurrence (GO) reports were created and investigators assigned accordingly. This particular GO was used as an administrative file in order to properly manage the files.Footnote 1034

The alleged abuse being investigated in Operation Centipede was said to have occurred at the hands of the Afghan authorities, not the CF. The investigation was limited to the issue whether any member of the CF was potentially implicated in any service or criminal offence in this context.

Maj Bolduc was in charge of Operation Centipede and LCol (ret’d) Garrick was his Commanding Officer when the matter commenced. LCol Sansterre was the commanding officer at the conclusion of OP CENTIPEDE and signed off on the completion of the investigation.Footnote 1035 The allegations in question related to incidents from 2006 and reports in the Globe and Mail in March and April 2007, as well as an affidavit of Col Noonan dated May 1, 2007. All of the allegations pre-date the specific time period of this inquiry.

Between March and June 2008 the investigators sought TSOs, MP policies, CF doctrine and technical directives, and guidance from CF legal counsel concerning the obligations of members of the CF when they become aware of allegations or witness post-transfer abuse of detainees by Afghan authorities. The relevant documentation was obtained from the investigators in Operation Camel Spider. There were claims of solicitor-client privilege and confidentiality made by legal counsel over the issue of legal guidance, and some exchanges between the CFPM and senior legal counsel to attempt to clarify that it was information being sought, not disclosure of legal advice which had been given. Ultimately, in one particular investigation, questions about the obligations of CF members witnessing abuse were answered by LCol Irwin.

The GO’s initiated within Operation Centipede were numbers 2008–6912, 2008–6913, 2008–6917, 2008–6918, 2008–6919, 2008–6920, 2008–6921 and 2008-23231. The order of priority was determined by first priority being whether the allegation involved an MP member, then whether Canadian soldiers had neglected their duties, then any other kind of allegationFootnote 1036. A brief description of each investigation is warranted.

13.1.5 GO 2008–6912Footnote 1037 – Investigation into Allegations of Possible Summary Execution, ROTO 1

This allegation pre-dated Operation Centipede as a distinct investigation, under GO 2007–7482, but the substance of the investigation occurred between March and May 2008. Significant portions of the GO are redacted but the essence of the allegation can be discerned. An MP at the PRT MP company during ROTO 1 reportedly believed a prisoner who had been seen in the custody of the ANA or ANP was subsequently summarily executed. The particular MP came to this conclusion on the basis of hearing a rumour that human remains had been found in a ditch near the PRT and he felt it could be the same prisoner as he had seen earlier.

The MP who reported this incident was suffering from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and had difficulty speaking with NIS investigators. The existence of the human remains was not confirmed, much less the identity of them, and it was confirmed that the prisoner in question was never in CF custody in any event. As a result, the NIS concluded the investigation since it was lacking evidence and beyond the scope of their investigative jurisdiction in any event.

This investigation was formally concluded by Maj Bolduc by letter dated June 4, 2008.

13.1.6 GO 2008–6913Footnote 1038 – Investigation into Allegations of Assault by ANA

This allegation was also previously opened under GO 2007–5564.Footnote 1039

A corporal who had served in Afghanistan during ROTO 1 in 2006 had seen an ANA convoy with a Taliban prisoner restrained in the rear of one vehicle. The prisoner was cross-checked in the head with an RPG barrel, apparently without justification. No further abuse was alleged.

On March 5, 2007 the corporal emailed photographs of a prisoner in the custody of the ANA to the MP, with a brief explanation of what he had seen. He was interviewed by the NIS on March 8, 2007 and indicated upon seeing media reports about abuse of prisoners he felt duty bound to come forward with what he knew, and he felt he should have reported what he had seen to the chain of command. The prisoner had never been in the custody of the CF.

On March 16, 2007, Col Gleeson at JAG sent a letter to the Globe and Mail in response to detainee abuse issues which had recently been reported. Later that day, the corporal sent copies of the photographs and an email to Col Gleeson with a copy to the MP.

On July 18, 2007 the investigation was placed on hold temporarily “as Detainee Files have been prioritized with the Task Force concentrating on one investigation at this time”.Footnote 1040

In May of 2008, there were further interviews of the corporal and another CF soldier. The conclusion was that the detainee was never in CF custody, nor did the detainee have significant marks or bruising, nor were any threats made to the detainee. Elements of Maj Bolduc’s closing letter of July 11, 2008 are redacted, but the conclusion was that there was nothing beyond speculation to justify any further investigation.Footnote 1041

13.1.7 GO 2008–6917Footnote 1042 – Investigation into Allegations of Summary Executions – ROTO 2

A CF medical doctor reported a CF patient being treated for PTSD who claimed that CF detainees who were transferred to the ANA or ANP were taken out of sight and shot. He alleged this was well-known to himself, his colleagues and the chain of command. The patient was suffering from PTSD and in the doctor’s opinion he may have exaggerated his allegation or even made it up. The doctor felt he may have been telling the truth.

Investigation including interviews of the platoon commander during June and July, 2008 revealed no evidence to confirm any particulars of detainee transfers and executions, and it appears the patient was in theatre at a time when his unit encountered no detainees being captured or transferred. The patient ultimately did not wish to discuss the allegations with the NIS.

As part of this investigation, the NIS sought to obtain the TSOs and other materials or directives which would shed light on the obligations of a CF member who might witness actual or suspected abuse of a detainee at the hands of persons other than a Canadian. After enquiring of CEFCOM legal counsel, they were referred to LCol Irwin, who was the CEFCOM COS at the time.Footnote 1043 It is puzzling to the Commission that the NIS’s attempts to gain insight into the legal terrain were rebuffed by CF lawyers, and that they were referred for that information to a senior officer in the chain of command rather than a legal officer.

LCol Irwin’s information reiterated the CF commitment to living up to the standards of the Geneva Conventions; however, he could not say whether there was any written direction on what to do in the circumstances of a CF member witnessing abuse of detainees by Afghan personnel. He stated he would expect the CF member to report such an incident to the chain of command, but whether there would be any legal authority to intervene in case of abuse outside the scope of CF jurisdiction was not clear to him. LCol Irwin also indicated CF commanders’ expectations emphasized the conduct of CF members, not the conduct of others. He would hope a CF member would intervene to prevent abuse if they were able to – “the emphasis was placed on can I act, not must I act”.

LCol Irwin did recognize a distinction in CF obligations when handing someone over believing they would get hurt, as opposed to reacting to abuse after the fact.Footnote 1044

This investigation was concluded by Maj Bolduc by letter dated July 16, 2008. The investigation was closed due to a lack of credible evidence supporting the allegations.Footnote 1045

13.1.8 GO 2008–6918Footnote 1046 – Col Noonan Affidavit

The Globe and Mail published an article on May 4, 2007 which described an incident of post-transfer abuse derived from the Federal Court affidavit of Col Noonan dated May 1, 2007. According to the initial description in the GO, a prisoner who was transferred was abused and “CF persons observed it and took no action. Why did Chain of Command not report this to MP?”Footnote 1047

The article relates the fact a detainee was abused, but in fact describes an opposition critic who said the government knew about the abuse and did nothing. In the article, the description of the abuse and CF response is substantially the same as is related in Col Noonan’s affidavit.

The abuse of detainees was described in two paragraphs of his affidavit and consisted of a threat by the ANA to execute one detainee if he was transferred, and the retrieval of another detainee from the local ANP because the CF had learned this detainee was beaten. This second detainee was then transferred to a provincial branch of the ANP rather than the local branch.

The file was initiated on July 10, 2008, assigned to Operation Centipede, and review and analysis of the affidavit took place in January 2009. There were no other steps in the investigation but for the review of the newspaper article and affidavit.

Having reviewed the affidavit, the NIS concluded CF personnel took appropriate action with the detainees, and had no jurisdiction over the Afghan officials in question. As a result the investigation was concluded.Footnote 1048

13.1.9 GO 2008–6919Footnote 1049 – Investigation into Tactical Questioning

The Army Provost Marshal was advised on April 30, 2007 of concerns raised by an army captain who was involved in tactical questioning. An email chain describing the incident was forwarded to Operation Camel Spider and was reviewed by the PM. The investigation was placed into Operation Centipede, and not investigated until January 2009 due to resource constraints caused by prioritizing another unrelated high profile investigation.Footnote 1050

The investigation involved review of the email chain disclosing the events and an interview with the recipient of the email from the captain on February 20, 2009. The investigating NIS officer did not interview the captain from whom the information originated, but did read his further commentary in an email thread.

The CF captain was relating third-hand information from other CF personnel involved in tactical questioning at the invitation of the ANSF. During this questioning, CF members noticed signs of injury and forced labour on the detainee, and while particulars are redacted, the Captain indicated the ANSF “don’t necessarily follow our policies on detainee handling if you know what I mean.” The CF questioner was uncomfortable assisting in the circumstances, but was also aware of the importance of assisting the ANSF as part of Canada’s mission in Afghanistan.Footnote 1051 There was no suggestion the detainee in question was ever in CF custody, although this was not confirmed either way by the NIS investigator.Footnote 1052 Concerns were expressed in the complaint the chain of command knew or ought to have known about potential for abuse during tactical questioning.

On March 3, 2009 the NIS concluded its investigation into this matter. While portions of the concluding remarks are redacted, it appears remedial actions were taken by the chain of command to address the concerns raised in the email thread. Additionally, the NIS noted the detainees had not been in the custody of the CF. It was determined, based upon this evidence, that no service or criminal offence had occurred.

13.1.10 GO 2008–6920 and 6921Footnote 1053 – Investigation into Globe and Mail Reports of Abuse

Articles in the Globe and Mail dated March 9, 2007 and April 23, 2007 reported CF transferred detainees had been or would be abused by Afghan authorities after transfer. The March 9 articleFootnote 1054 was authored by Professor Attaran and described an incident in the summer of 2006 where CBC reporters allegedly observed CF personnel preparing to transfer a detainee. The Afghan security personnel threatened to kill the detainee once turned over to them. The CF personnel hesitated but then turned over the detainee after the cameras were off.

The April 23, 2007 article reported interviews by Globe and Mail reporter Graeme Smith with a number of CF transferred detainees who alleged they were abused by Afghan personnel following transfer. Names and particulars of these people were contained in the article. One of the persons said CF personnel had encouraged him to provide useful information to avoid further abuse. The worst of the abuse was alleged to have occurred at the hands of the NDS and included allegations of beatings, sleep deprivation, whipping with electrical cables, electric shocks, hanging by the ankles for extended periods of time, suffocation and exposure to cold.

The investigation into these matters was formalized in Operation Centipede on July 10, 2008. The investigation, such as it was, concluded on November 19, 2008. It is clear the NIS investigation consisted of nothing beyond reading the articles in question. No attempt was made to obtain the CBC video, to confirm (or not) the allegations outlined by Prof Attaran, or to interview Graeme Smith, let alone interview the detainees themselves. The NIS was unaware the CEFCOM PM LCol Boot had conducted, at LGen (ret’d) Gauthier’s request, a point-by-point review of the Globe and Mail article and had confirmed certain elements such as the identity of some of the detainees as CF transferees. Not a single external source of information was considered or reviewed in these investigations.

The Access to Information “Details of Release” sheet for GO 2008–6920 indicates nothing in this investigation was withheld from the Commission or redacted. There appears to be nothing withheld in GO 2008–6921, although in both instances it is difficult to conclude the file is complete since the articles themselves are not included in the GO and there is no “Details of Release” sheet for GO 2008–6921.

The concluding remarks for these investigations are identical; it thus appears to the Commission the two matters were not given independent consideration.

The Concluding Remarks are reproduced in full:

  1. This report was initially created to investigate the allegations that Afghans that had been capture [sic] by CG personnel were being abused. These allegations stemmed from two reports in the “Globe and Mail” dated 9 Mar 07 and 23 Apr 07. In brief, these reports relate that prisoners, specifically those who have captured by [sic] Canadian Forces and then later transferred to Afghan authorities, have been abused, tortured and even summarily executed by the Afghan powers that be. At that time and especially in consideration that Operation Centipede had been recently formed to investigate similar complaints; it was decided that the aforementioned news paper articles would be followed up on with the intention that an investigation(s) would ensue to determine if any service or criminal offences had been committed by CF personnel. However, since these early articles, the media has been inundated with countless reports of a similar nature. Paradoxically, many of these articles report that none of the aforementioned maltreatment was inflicted by Canadians, in fact most of the alleged captives have praised the Canadian soldiers on their civility, good manners and the relatively comfortable detention centre located at KAF. Since then, the Government of Canada (GOC) has taken notice and has discussed these reports in great fact. Subsequently the GOC, including the CF and DND have taken action on many levels throughout its various parliamentary affairs in high level national and international menus [sic].
  2. Although these newspaper journalists are reporting that they have interviewed former Afghan captives or at least received information concerning their treatment at the hands of the Afghans, considering the general rules of evidence, the inadmissibility of statements as they pertain to hearsay information, and the lack of any other credible evidence, there is no satisfactory justification to continue this investigation. Likewise, even if these reports were somehow deemed to be credible, the allegations of ill-treatment are directed against the Afghan authorities.
