This alone excludes our jurisdictional interests and the mandate of the CFNIS. As such, there is no satisfactory justification to proceed with an investigation that focuses on the actions of the Afghan authorities and their handling of prisoners.
  3. Upon reflection, it seems to be obvious that there will be additional reports in the far reaching future that will address the manner in which Afghan authorities handle their Afghan captives. To that end, any pending media reports/articles concerning the treatment of Afghan prisoners by Afghan authorities which are void of any direct accusations of criminal wrongdoings of CF members, will not be investigated by this office. This file is concluded.Footnote 1055
13.1.11 GO 2008-23231Footnote 1056 – Investigation into Disclosure during MP Training

Although the particulars are redacted, this was an allegation of detainee abuse related by a Warrant Officer (WO) to a group of MP trainees during a lecture at the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy. The investigation was opened on August 21, 2008 and interviews of the WO and some of the lecture attendees occurred shortly thereafter.

The WO was interviewed and indicated his information came from a discussion he had in June 2007 with a returning member of the CF, whose identity he could not recall. The member had said he witnessed abuse of a detainee in the hands of Afghan authorities, but the WO indicated, to his knowledge, the detainee was never in CF custody. The witness to the abuse indicated he had tried to intervene and had related the incident to the chain of command. The WO did not confirm that this occurred.

The lecture attendees’ accounts were substantially similar to those of the WO. There were no apparent attempts by the NIS to identify who the direct witness to the incident might be although the WO knew his rank, knew he was a returning member of the RCR, and had encountered him during pre-deployment training at CFB Wainwright.

The NIS investigation was concluded on November 3, 2008. The conclusion was that there was no evidence to corroborate the allegations, and there was no evidence of CF involvement or wrongdoing. The NIS concluded the allegation was a culmination of several stories, some of which had already been investigated in Operation Centipede, and there was no separate new allegation to be investigated.

13.2 Delays, Investigative Procedures, Resources and Priorities for NIS Investigations

The Commission recognizes resource limitations were a very serious issue for the NIS during the period of these investigations. Operation Camel Spider and a major fraud investigation occupied a tremendous amount of NIS resources in 2007.Footnote 1057 The HDO Survey investigation was also very resource intensive during the time period. Operation Centipede was initiated by Maj Bolduc in order to clear the backlog of detainee-related matters which had arisen incidentally during the Camel Spider investigation.

In addition to the resource pressure caused by other major investigations, NIS personnel in Afghanistan were faced with the extremely difficult and stressful tasks of investigating CF use of force in combat, forensic investigations concerning CF members who were killed in action, and the difficult task of repatriation of those members, as well as other investigations which did not relate in any way to detainee issues. That being said, it is difficult to reconcile the senior MP and operational commands’ views about the “mission critical” nature of detainee abuse issues with the level of priority and attention that was given to some of these investigations.

Operation Centipede was placed lower in priority to Maj Bolduc’s existing investigations when he first proposed it. This is why the GOs were opened in March 2008 despite the allegations stemming from 2006–2007 and coming to light during the Camel Spider investigation. NIS personnel acknowledged it is preferable from a policing perspective to investigate matters in a more timely fashion to prevent the loss of potential evidence through the passage of time,Footnote 1058 yet the combination of priorities and resource issues meant these investigations were essentially on the back burner for over a year in some instances.

The Commission is also of the view that some of the investigations received short shrift or were half-hearted at best. Several of the investigations involved little more than a review of the complaint and its paper trail, without any attempt to verify whether detainee abuse was or was not occurring and whether any CF personnel, including commanders, were aware of it. There was a paper review of the Globe and Mail article allegations, without any attempt to speak to the author or the detainees, to obtain confirmatory records from CEFCOM, or otherwise test the veracity of these shocking and serious allegations. As noted above, one NIS report concluded by bluntly stating that any other media reports of detainee mistreatment which did not include CF members would not be investigated.

This apparent laxity and closed-mindedness is indeed troubling from a policing perspective and appears to be inconsistent with NIS commanders’ own view of proper investigations. Maj Bolduc acknowledged that determining whether an allegedly abused detainee had been in CF custody was a key piece of information in determining whether to move an investigation into abuse forward,Footnote 1059 yet on these two files there was no attempt to obtain this information despite it being readily available at CEFCOM. In the Commission’s view, one cannot expect to obtain further information without asking questions or making inquiries. The allegations were not followed up in part because the newspaper article was said to be “hearsay”, but no attempt was made to obtain original evidence. LCol Sansterre was at something of a loss to explain the basis upon which the hearsay nature of information would rule out the investigative pursuit of further information.Footnote 1060 The Commission is well aware that often investigations are initiated and moved forward on the basis of hearsay and untested or uncorroborated evidence –this is consistent with normal police practice. LCol (ret’d) Garrick and Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore acknowledged this, and both indicated they expected a more thorough investigation to follow upon these allegations.Footnote 1061

It appears to the Commission the main focus of MP concern was CF abuse of detainees, and the significance of post-transfer abuse (and the implications with respect to transfer orders leading to or subsequent to allegations of abuse) was not at the forefront of MP’s concerns.

Perhaps this was because of a tendency to conflate the issue of jurisdiction over charges and relevance to an investigation. Maj Bolduc, the case manager, described Afghan abuse of Afghan detainees as outside the scope of MP jurisdiction, and LCol Sansterre expressed similar views.Footnote 1062 However, as LCol Sansterre noted, the fact abuse was committed by persons outside NIS jurisdiction does not mean that facts cannot be solicited from sources outside NIS charging jurisdiction,Footnote 1063 and it does not preclude the prospect that CF personnel could bear some legal culpability for that abuse in certain circumstances.

It appears to the Commission the real significance of post-transfer abuse with respect to the issue of the legality of transfer orders really did not register with the CO of CFNIS until June 12, 2008 when the issue was articulated in writing by the Complainants in this matter.Footnote 1064 At that point, more than a year had passed since the allegations in OP CENTIPEDE had occurred. Both Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore and LCol (ret’d) Garrick indicated they expected any evidence relating to the issue of the legality of transfer orders to be substantively addressed in the course of the investigations in Operation Centipede. However, it is clear this issue was not probed during that investigation.

XIV. The Analysis of Professors Forcese and Sassoli Relating to Legal Allegations in the Complaint

The foundation of the “failure to investigate” complaint is an allegation that “crimes” were committed by members of the CF in ordering the transfer of detainees to the custody of the Afghan National Directorate of Security despite compelling first hand reports of previous CF detainees being tortured by those authorities. AIC/BCCLA contend there is no reasonable explanation why the Task Force Commander did not halt transfers much sooner than November 5, 2007, when earlier reports of torture were disclosed to Canadian officials. In short, AIC/BCCLA submit that officers in the chain of command ignored much evidence pointing to a substantial risk of torture, thus showing a disregard for the lives and safety of the detainees.

The legal basis on which the allegation of “crimes” exists is said by AIC/BCCLA to reside in certain provisions of the Criminal Code, the NDA, the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act, and the Geneva Conventions Act. AIC/BCCLA submit these Acts create a number of offences that would apply to members of the CF who ordered the transfer of detainees when they knew or ought to have known a substantial risk of torture existed.

The jurisdiction of this Commission does not extend to making findings of criminal or possible criminal liability against military commanders, and nothing in this Report is to be construed as making such findings or even suggesting such liability exists. However, the underlying legal allegations in the complaint necessarily have to be examined as part of the inquiry into whether a duty to investigate was triggered. As counsel for seven of the subjects acknowledged in written submissions, among the issues the Commission must address is: “What, if any, were the offences known to law which could have been investigated…”Footnote 1065

The alleged duty to investigate in this case arises from the Complainants’ allegation that certain offences were committed by commanders in relation to the transfer of detainees. It is therefore necessary to consider whether there are offences that potentially could arise out of detainee transfer orders, as the Complainants allege. If no offences exist under the law that are even potentially applicable to the nature of the complaint, then it is difficult to see how a duty could arise on the part of the MP to investigate, and how they could be faulted for a failure to investigate. To put the matter another way, if there is no offence known to law that could be applicable to orders to transfer detainees, then there would be no act or omission by CF commanders that the MP should reasonably be expected to investigate. The Commission therefore considered it necessary to its investigation to understand the potential scope and application of the various legal enactments cited by AIC/BCCLA in their complaint.

To assist the Commission in this regard, two experts were retained (Professor Craig Forcese of the University of Ottawa, and Professor Marco Sassoli of the University of Geneva, Switzerland) to provide a report analyzing whether and how the international and domestic legal instruments cited by AIC/BCCLA could be relevant to the circumstances set out in the complaint. They were instructed not to draw any conclusions as to the actual validity of any of the Complainants’ allegations, and did not do so. For the purpose of framing their analysis they hypothesized certain facts, without opining or concluding whether any of these facts were true.

The reports of Professors Sassoli and Forcese were distributed to the parties, and marked as exhibits.Footnote 1066 These experts appeared together as a witness panel on May 6, 2010, to present their reports and to answer questions from the parties.

It is clear from the evidence the CF chain of command was aware of its responsibilities and directed that detainees were not to be transferred into situations where a substantial risk of torture was known, or reasonably ought to be known, to exist. On June 18, 2007, LGen (ret’d) Gauthier, the Canadian Expeditionary Forces Command (CEFCOM) Commander, issued a clear direction to the Task Force Commander, BGen Laroche (as he then was), which stated:

24. The chain of command bears the potential liability should we become aware of torture or mistreatment following the transfer of detainees to Afghan authorities. It is for this reason that I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that the follow up of transferred detainees is sufficiently robust. I expect a proactive engagement with DFAIT at all levels, but particularly at your level, to ensure monitoring occurs and reporting and analysis is provided. The monitoring, reporting and analysis must be sufficient to enable command decisions regarding continuation of transfers. You are to engage with me directly should a concern arise.Footnote 1067

On September 12, 2007, LGen (ret’d) Gauthier issued an Amplifying Guidance on Detainees Reference: Chain of Command Obligations With Respect to Post-Transfer Follow-Up to the Task Force Commander, that stated:

2. The chain of command bears potential legal liability should we transfer a detainee into Afghan custody when we know, or can be reasonably expected to know, that substantial grounds exist for believing that the detainee faces a real risk of subsequent abuse or mistreatment. It is for this reason that I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that all relevant information regarding the treatment of detainees while in Afghan custody is actively sought and considered.Footnote 1068

On November 25, 2007, when the Task Force Commander (BGen Laroche) suspended transfers, he gave as reasons:

5. With the arrival of DFAIT/PRT C4 of 5 November 2007 and details of the latest abuse allegation (allegations which, in the circumstances therein described, have an air [of] believability), I am forced to conclude that, if required to make a transfer decision at this time, I would not be able to approve the transfer on the basis that the legal test upon which such decisions must be based cannot be satisfied, having due regard to all the information and lack of information at my disposal.Footnote 1069

MGen Laroche said he recognized that transfer decisions were subject to a legal test, which he described in his letter as follows:

The discretion to authorize a detainee transfer may only be exercised where there are not substantial grounds for believing that there is a “real risk” that a detainee would face subsequent abuse or mistreatment if transferred to the NDS.Footnote 1070

MGen (ret’d) Grant (the Task Force Commander during the last three months of ROTO 2 and all of ROTO 3) testified on September 22, 2010:

  • At the first paragraphFootnote 1071 it says:

    “The discretion to authorize a detainee transfer may only be exercised where there are not substantial grounds for believing that there is a real risk that a detainee would face subsequent abuse or mistreatment if transferred to the NDS.”

    Is that, in summary, the test you were applying as far as you understood it?
  • In summary, yes.Footnote 1072

It is clear from the above directions of the CEFCOM Commander, and the evidence given by Task Force Commanders, the CF chain of command was very alive to the prospect of legal liability in relation to post-transfer abuse of detainees. The direction and amplifying guidance issued by the CEFCOM Commander sets out an expected standard of conduct in relation to transfer decisions. This acknowledgment of potential liability existed despite the diplomatic assurances given by the Government of Afghanistan, or the fact the responsibility for conducting post-transfer monitoring of detainees lay outside the CF under the May 3, 2007 Supplementary Arrangement.

Professors Forcese and Sassoli presented a very thorough analysis of the potential liabilities that could be imposed on individuals and states where military commanders authorized the transfer of detainees where they knew, or ought to have known, a substantial risk of torture existed. As noted, their analysis was based on assumed facts. The actual applicability of the various domestic and international legal instruments would depend on the facts that are actually found to exist.

For his part, Professor Forcese opined that, depending on the facts disclosed by an investigation, a number of possible offences could come into play. Professor Forcese refers to these as offences that might be “plausibly invoked” depending on the circumstances. These include: aiding and abetting torture contrary to section 6 of the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act and (more doubtfully) section 269.1 of the Criminal Code; criminal negligence under section 219 of the Criminal Code; disgraceful conduct and/or acting in a cruel or disgraceful manner contrary to sections 92 and 93 of the NDA; negligent performance of a military duty contrary to section 124 of the NDA; and conduct to the prejudice of good order and discipline, contrary to section 129 of the NDA.

Of doubtful applicability, in the view of Professor Forcese, was the offence of violating Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, and certain concepts under the Crimes Against Humanity and War Crimes Act.

With respect to placing reliance on diplomatic assurances, Professor Forcese advised the Commission:

Diplomatic assurances are controversial – they amount to a supplemental promise by a state to not do something (torture) that the state is already prohibited from doing. For this and other reasons, there often may be strong reasons to doubt their utility. At any rate, it is doubtful that such an assurance could continue to relieve a transferring state’s Torture Convention obligations where evidence emerges that the receiving state has not honoured the assurance.Footnote 1073

[…]

Mr. Forcese: The whole purpose of a lot of these documents that we are now seeing in international practice, including things like the transfer arrangement, is to vitiate that substantial grounds for believing; that is, you get an undertaking from the other state, which goes by the parlance of diplomatic assurance, saying they’re not going to torture. That then reduces or eliminates, arguably at least, the substantial grounds for believing. Now this is a very controversial subject in public international law, because a lot of people say that, What’s the virtue of an additional piece of paper from a state that already violates international law by torturing? But, anyway, I will leave it there.Footnote 1074

[…]

Ms. Cheung: So if there is evidence that assurances in the May 2007 transfer arrangement were not strictly honoured by the Afghan government, then you would agree with me that such assurances should be given little weight in the substantial risk assessment?

Mr. Forcese: That would be my view, yes.Footnote 1075

In terms of the offence of criminal negligence under section 219 of the Criminal Code, Professor Forcese stated:

While the jurisprudence is less than crystal clear, the test for the mental element of this offence is likely a “modified objective test”. Thus, it focuses on whether a “reasonable person in the accused’s position would have been aware of the risks arising from the conduct”, but “where the accused raises a reasonable doubt whether a reasonable person in his or her position would have been aware of the risks arising from the conduct, the premise for finding objective fault is no longer sound […]”Footnote 1076

In the opinion of Professor Forcese:

[…] it seems reasonable that the appropriate standard is the one set down in the rules governing CF activities in relation to detainees: as described, e.g., by the Technical Arrangement between Canada and Afghanistan, “detainees would be afforded the same treatment as Prisoners of War. Detainees would be transferred to Afghan authorities in a manner consistent with international law and subject to negotiated assurances regarding their treatment and transfer. A marked and substantial departure from this standard would, therefore, be the gravamen of the offence […]

[…] a sustained pattern of transferring to Afghan authorities where there was a substantial risk that those transfers would result in torture could plausibly be invoked as such a marked and substantial departure […]Footnote 1077

In terms of negligent performance of a military duty contrary to section 124 of the NDA, Professor Forcese stated:

The Queen’s Regulations and Orders provide that “[t]he word ‘negligently’ in section 124 of the NDA signifies that the accused either did something or omitted to do something in a manner which would not have been adopted by a reasonably capable and careful person in his position in the Service under similar circumstances” and that the offence “should not be invoked in ordinary cases of carelessness but only where the nature of the military duty, or the circumstances in which it is being performed, is such as to impose upon the individual a need to take special care in its performance”. The Court Martial Appeal Court has approved this approach, and has held that “[t]he impugned act or omission of the accused must constitute a marked departure from the expected standard of conduct in the performance of a military duty, as distinguished from a general duty of care”. This standard appears less demanding than the requirement of a marked and substantial departure from the reasonable norm at issue with criminal negligence under the Criminal Code […]Footnote 1078

In terms of the offence of conduct prejudicial to good order and discipline, contained in section 129 of the NDA, Professor Forcese stated:

As noted above, the TSOs that apply to Operation Athena all specify that detainees will be treated to the standard required for prisoners of war as defined by GCIII. […] A violation of all and any of these orders at least arguably meets the Code of Service Discipline’s definition of conduct prejudicial to good order and discipline. It is difficult to see how transfers ordered with knowledge of the probability of torture would meet the standards of GCIII or international law.Footnote 1079

Professor Sassoli’s report focused on the applicability of the Geneva Conventions, international criminal law, international human rights law and international customary rules to CF commanders who ordered detainees in Afghanistan to be transferred to Afghan authorities. In general terms, it was his view that the transfer of detainees by the CF to Afghan authorities is covered by the international humanitarian law of non-international armed conflicts.Footnote 1080 It was Professor Sassoli’s view that paragraph 3 of the Arrangement on the transfer of detainees dated December 18, 2005, between Canada and Afghanistan, which states, “The participants will treat detainees in accordance with the standards set out in the Third Geneva Convention…” could be seen as a unilateral undertaking of a type that has been held to make the Geneva Convention, including possibly article 12 of Convention III, applicable (Report of Professor Sassoli, at p. 12).

In his report, Professor Sassoli stated:

In regard to the transfer of detainees by members of the CF to Afghan authorities, those members had, under the ICTY jurisprudence discussed above, a legal duty to protect detainees under their custody from the possibility of being tortured by other troops to whom they would transfer them. They had the possibility to fulfill this duty by not transferring the prisoners to the Afghan authorities. If it was demonstrated that they knew that the omission of fulfilling this duty would assist the commission of the crime of torture by Afghan authorities, they could, under international criminal law, be held criminally responsible for aiding and abetting the crimes committed by members of Afghan authorities.Footnote 1081

The prohibition of torture and other ill-treatment is universally recognized and has been enshrined in many treaties. Torture and other ill-treatment have been interpreted broadly and prohibit a large range of types of conduct. The prohibition does not only contain a negative obligation for States but also a positive one to secure individuals from prohibited treatment as well as procedural obligations such as an obligation to investigate prima facie allegations of torture and other ill-treatment.Footnote 1082

International law is relevant for assessing the transfer by CF of Afghan detainees to Afghan authorities either because such transfer could constitute an international crime Canada is obliged to repress and has criminalized as a crime, or because such transfer otherwise constituted a violation of Canada’s obligations under International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law, which could inform the interpretation of certain offences in Canadian domestic law, such as assault, criminal negligence, cruel or disgraceful conduct, negligent performance of a military duty and conduct to the prejudice of good order and discipline …

Concerning the probability of torture the transferring officer must know to make him aiding and abetting in that torture, the Commission may want to take into account the jurisprudence of international human rights bodies that legal undertakings by transferee authorities guaranteeing respect for fundamental rights “in principle are not in themselves sufficient to ensure adequate protection against the risk of ill-treatment where, as in the present case, reliable sources have reported practices [of ill-treatment] resorted to or tolerated by the authorities.”Footnote 1083

In Ms. Richards’ closing oral submissions, counsel for seven of the subjects made the following comments with respect to the evidence of the two experts:

Professor Forcese, an expert in law brought forward by this Commission to assist, testified that even he sitting in Canada with the luxury of hindsight and accepting as a fact the most egregious of allegations by the Complainants that the Task Force commanders transferred detainees knowing there was a real risk that they would be tortured he was dealing with unsettled and esoteric developing areas of law. He had to think about it for two weeks and had difficulty concluding whether a criminal offence may have been committed.Footnote 1084

[…]

As you know, and as you have heard multiple times before you, the Federal Court of Canada has considered this issue about the legal standard for transferring detainees in Afghanistan and we say the decision of the Federal Court is binding on you. The Federal Court confirmed the test that we have repeated throughout the course of these proceedings, and that is: Where a commander has substantial grounds to believe that a real risk existed that detainees would be mistreated, he could not transfer them to Afghan authorities.

While we say the Federal Court should be determinative of the issue, your own experts that you called to assist you in this matter have confirmed that test. Both Professors Sassoli and Forcese confirmed that a risk of torture required some knowledge of probability. That was the language used by Professor Sassoli. Professor Forcese opined that the standard for transferring might differ based on which criminal offence was being investigated. But in any circumstances, he never asserted that the test would be as low as a mere risk of transfer; they were a real risk or higher.Footnote 1085

[…]

Indeed, it was the testimony of Professor Sassoli before you that once Canada entered into those arrangements, they clearly met their international legal obligations. Professor Sassoli opined before you on what he saw the standard for Canada ensuring that it had met its international obligations. He set out there issues that he thought were important. First, he said that Canada should make sure that Afghanistan was bound by Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, which it did through the first arrangement.

He said that Canada should ensure itself that Afghanistan was able and willing to not torture detainees, and he opined that it certainly was. There has been considerable evidence before you about the involvement of the Government of Canada and indeed other international forces in Afghanistan with capacity building and ensuring the ability and willingness of the Afghan government.

Third, Professor Sassoli opined that Canada should make inquiries before transferring to ensure that there was not a real risk of torture, and Professor Sassoli opined that the second agreement certainly met those obligations.

In our submission, it’s very important to be precise when you look at this issue about the legal test for transfer. It is a real risk of torture and not, as my friends have asserted throughout, a mere risk.Footnote 1086

It does not seem to the Commission that AIC/BCCLA are actually asserting that a “mere risk” of torture is the test applicable to the commanders who are authorizing transfers. In their final submissions the Complainants refer to a “substantive” risk of torture in discussing the test applicable to commanders, and the possible application of Common Article 3 (Final submissions of the Complainants AIC and BCCLA, January 26, 2011, at p. 34). They also state at page 37 of their written closing submissions:

[…] it is clear that the Canadian military cannot transfer individuals to the jurisdiction of a foreign power if it is established that there are substantial grounds for believing that these individuals may be subjected to torture in the receiving state.

In their questions to Professor Forcese, counsel for the Complainants asked:

Ms. Cheung: I wanted to draw your attention to that and ask you the question, then. Is it your opinion that a transfer to a substantial risk of torture would be a violation of international law?

Mr. Forcese: Yes, not law of armed conflict, but certainly international law.Footnote 1087

Where it does seem the Complainants and the seven subjects differ is on what “substantial grounds” or “substantial risk” means. The Complainants submit the threshold is a low one, and cite Professor Sassoli as saying it is sufficient to show that the transferee “… may simply belong to a category of people who, according to the information, are sometimes tortured.”Footnote 1088 Presumably, detainees transferred to the NDS fall with such a category of persons according to the Complainants. Counsel for the seven subjects argues, on the other hand, that the threshold is higher than just being a member of a category of people who are sometimes tortured, and requires “[…] some knowledge of probability […]”Footnote 1089

The probability test seems to be the one Professors Forcese and Sassoli mainly adopted in their evidence. Professor Forcese testified:

[…] you look to the existence in the state concerned of a consistent pattern of gross, flagrant or mass violations of human rights. So where those indicia exist, that goes to the issue as to whether there is substantial grounds. That doesn’t answer the question: What does “substantial grounds” mean?

The Americans take the view it is very much a balance of probabilities analysis.

[…]

So how sure do you have to be of the prospect they’re going to be tortured in order to have the guilty state of mind? Well the language is “probability”. You have to be – you have to have knowledge of the probability. So all I am doing is reading in, you know, a colloquial understanding of probability. It is not certainty. It is not clear and convincing proof. It is probability. This probably reflects my doctrinal background, but, in my view probability means basically a balance of possibilities or balance of probabilities, not anything more than that.

[…]

So you have to be able to prove what they had in their mind, but what do they have to have in their mind? They have to have knowledge of the probability. They don’t have to have knowledge of the certainty of torture.Footnote 1090

Professor Sassoli agreed with Professor Forcese’s reference to “balance of probabilities analysis”. Both also agreed the test was not an empirical assessment.

Professor Sassoli also stated:

Personally, I think that there is a misconception there, because the problem is, when you transfer, you don’t know. All you know is what happened to others. And so it should be, in my view, compared with -- and this is what courts, in my view, actually do -- simply the general information one has about the treatment of detainees of this kind in the power of that state.Footnote 1091

[…]

Ms. Cheung: But I believe as you said earlier, the evidence that is required for showing substantial risk, even if it means only Canadian-transferred detainees, would only require that there be evidence that this category of persons -- that is, CF-transferred detainees – had been tortured or at risk of torture; is that correct?

Mr. Sassoli: Sorry, CF?

Ms. Cheung: CF-transferred detainees.

Mr. Sassoli: Yeah, yeah. Obviously you can never -- you can never have evidence for a future fact. So you will never have evidence that someone will become tortured, but that other people in the same situation were tortured.Footnote 1092

In a real sense, then, it appears the analysis of the probable risk of torture necessarily includes knowledge about the fate of previous transferees.

In the end result, recourse must be had to the language of the enactment that creates the offence. In addition, a different evaluation of probability is involved where the decision is whether to investigate, as opposed to registering a conviction:

Mr. McGarvey: I take it it is fair to say, then, when assessing, as we are to assess, whether a police officer should have investigated a commander, attention will have to be paid to which of the particular heads of criminal culpability we’re discussing and the different applicable standards that relate to each of those potentially applicable criminal heads. In other words, if we’re talking about negligence, it may be one standard. If we’re talking about aiding and abetting, it may be another standard. All of those will have to be parsed out individually before assessing whether a police officer had any basis to go forward with an investigation. Is that –

Mr. Forcese: That would be my view.

Mr. Sassoli: I would perhaps simply mention, but this is not really international law but what I think logic under domestic law, that obviously for the question whether you have to start an enquiry, the level of probability must be lower than the one for sentencing someone, for convicting someone. So this has also to be taken into account in the probability evaluation.Footnote 1093

In terms of the threshold applicable to the MP to determine whether a duty to investigate arose, the Complainants argue that the “mere fact” detainees were transferred to likely torture was sufficient to trigger a duty on the MP to commence an investigation:

It was my client’s contention that the fact, the mere fact that individuals transferred by the CF were likely tortured is, on its own, a sufficiently good reason to initiate a MP investigation.Footnote 1094

The question before the Commission, however, is whether a legal duty to investigate was triggered, as opposed to there being “sufficiently good reason” to initiate an investigation. The case law is clear that this duty is not automatically applicable in every situation.

The Commission concludes there are offences known to law which could have formed a reasonable basis for a police investigation. In making this finding, the Commission has borne in mind that, while the legal issues may be complex, the police are not expected or required, during the course of an inquiry or investigation, to evaluate the evidence they have gathered against precise legal standards or to make legal judgments as to whether the evidence will support a conviction. That is the task of other participants in the justice system, namely prosecutors, defence counsel and judges.

XV. The Legal Standard of Conduct Applicable to Military Police

15.1 The Standard of the Reasonable Police Officer

In its ruling on the Motion of Standard of Conduct, dated April 1, 2010, the Commission stated it will be guided generally by the standard of conduct set out in the Hill decision of the Supreme Court of Canada:

The Commission will thus be generally guided in the hearings by the standard as set out at para 68 of the Hill judgment, namely, that of a “reasonable police officer in all the circumstances …” To this we would add the further clarification at para 73 of Hill that MPs are not required to make optimal decisions, but instead are to be judged on the basis of prevailing circumstances:

“The standard is not perfection, or even the optimum, judged from the vantage of hindsight. It is that of a reasonable officer, judged in the circumstances prevailing at the time the decision was made – circumstances that may include urgency and deficiencies of information.”Footnote 1095

The Hill case (2007 SCC 41) dealt with the tort of negligent investigation. The Commission is not concerned in this case with the existence, or elements, of this tort. However, the Hill case provides valuable guidance as to the expected standard of conduct when the police are conducting an investigation. In general terms, it is expected police officers will act as a reasonable investigating officer would in the circumstances. The prevailing circumstances may include situations of urgency or deficiencies in information. Police officers are entitled to exercise their investigative discretion as they see fit, so long as they stay within the bounds of reasonableness and their underlying intention is honest, not arbitrary, and not motivated by favouritism or any other dishonest intention. The expected standard of conduct is not perfection, or even the optimum, viewed from the vantage of hindsight. Minor errors, or errors in judgment that any professional might have made, are not “unreasonable mistakes” that breach the expected standard even though they might have unfortunate results.

The applicable principles are discussed as follows in the Hill judgment:

68 A number of considerations support the conclusion that the standard of care is that of a reasonable police officer in all the circumstances. First, the standard of a reasonable police officer in all the circumstances provides a flexible overarching standard that covers all aspects of investigatory police work and appropriately reflects its realities. The particular conduct required is informed by the stage of the investigation and applicable legal considerations. At the outset of an investigation, the police may have little more than hearsay, suspicion and a hunch. What is required is that they act as a reasonable investigating officer would in those circumstances. Later, in laying charges, the standard is informed by the legal requirement of reasonable and probable grounds to believe the suspect is guilty; since the law requires such grounds, a police officer acting reasonably in the circumstances would insist on them. The reasonable officer standard entails no conflict between criminal standards (Charron J., at para 175). Rather, it incorporates them, in the same way it incorporates an appropriate degree of judicial discretion, denies liability for minor errors or mistakes and rejects liability by hindsight. In all these ways, it reflects the realities of police work.

69 Second, as mentioned, the general rule is that the standard of care in negligence is that of the reasonable person in similar circumstances. In cases of professional negligence, this rule is qualified by an additional principle: where the defendant has special skills and experience, the defendant must “live up to the standards possessed by persons of reasonable skill and experience in that calling”.Footnote 1096 These principles suggest the standard of the reasonable officer in like circumstances.

70 Third, the common law factors relevant to determining the standard of care confirm the reasonable officer standard. These factors include: the likelihood of known or foreseeable harm, the gravity of harm, the burden or cost which would be incurred to prevent the injury, external indicators of reasonable conduct (including professional standards) and statutory standards.Footnote 1097 These factors suggest a standard of reasonableness, not something less onerous. There is a significant likelihood that police officers may cause harm to suspects if they investigate negligently. The gravity of the potential harm caused is serious. Suspects may be arrested or imprisoned, their livelihoods affected and their reputations irreparably damaged. The cost of preventing the injury, in comparison, is not undue. Police meet a standard of reasonableness by merely doing what a reasonable police officer would do in the same circumstances — by living up to accepted standards of professional conduct to the extent that it is reasonable to expect in given circumstances. This seems neither unduly onerous nor overly costly. It must be supposed that professional standards require police to act professionally and carefully, not just to avoid gross negligence. The statutory standards imposed by the Police Services Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.15, although not definitive of the standard of care, are instructive (s. 1).

71 Fourth, the nature and importance of police work reinforce a standard of the reasonable officer in similar circumstances. Police conduct has the capacity to seriously affect individuals by subjecting them to the full coercive power of the state and impacting on their repute and standing in the community. It follows that police officers should perform their duties reasonably. It has thus been recognized that police work demands that society (including the courts) impose and enforce high standards on police conduct (Cory Report, at p. 10). This supports a reasonableness standard, judged in the context of a similarly situated officer. A more lenient standard is inconsistent with the standards that society and the law rightfully demand of police in the performance of their crucially important work.

72 Finally, authority supports the standard of the reasonable police officer similarly placed. The preponderance of case law dealing with professionals has applied the standard of the reasonably competent professional in like circumstances. (See Klar, at p. 349; see also the reasons of the trial judge at para 63.) The Quebec Court of Appeal has twice stated that the standard is the ordinarily competent officer in like circumstances.Footnote 1098

73 I conclude that the appropriate standard of care is the overarching standard of a reasonable police officer in similar circumstances. This standard should be applied in a manner that gives due recognition to the discretion inherent in police investigation. Like other professionals, police officers are entitled to exercise their discretion as they see fit, provided that they stay within the bounds of reasonableness. The standard of care is not breached because a police officer exercises his or her discretion in a manner other than that deemed optimal by the reviewing court. A number of choices may be open to a police officer investigating a crime, all of which may fall within the range of reasonableness. So long as discretion is exercised within this range, the standard of care is not breached. The standard is not perfection, or even the optimum, judged from the vantage of hindsight. It is that of a reasonable officer, judged in the circumstances prevailing at the time the decision was made — circumstances that may include urgency and deficiencies of information. The law of negligence does not require perfection of professionals; nor does it guarantee desired results (Klar, at p. 359). Rather, it accepts that police officers, like other professionals, may make minor errors or errors in judgment which cause unfortunate results, without breaching the standard of care. The law distinguishes between unreasonable mistakes breaching the standard of care and mere “errors in judgment” which any reasonable professional might have made and therefore, which do not breach the standard of care.Footnote 1099 (Emphasis added).Footnote 1100

The Hill judgment also considered the role of the police in the justice system, namely, to be concerned primarily with gathering and evaluating evidence. Police officers are not expected or required to evaluate evidence according to legal standards, or to make legal judgments. It is the job of prosecutors to determine whether the evidence will support a conviction at law:

49 It was argued that the decision of police to pursue the investigation of a suspect on the one hand, or close it on the other, is a quasi-judicial decision, similar to that taken by the state prosecutor. It is true that both police officers and prosecutors make decisions that relate to whether the suspect should stand trial. But the nature of the inquiry differs. Police are concerned primarily with gathering and evaluating evidence. Prosecutors are concerned mainly with whether the evidence the police have gathered will support a conviction at law. The fact-based investigative character of the police task distances it from a judicial or quasi-judicial role.

50 The possibility of holding police civilly liable for negligent investigation does not require them to make judgments as to legal guilt or innocence before proceeding against a suspect. Police are required to weigh evidence to some extent in the course of an investigation: Chartier v. Attorney General of Quebec, [1979] 2 S.C.R. 474. But they are not required to evaluate evidence according to legal standards or to make legal judgments. That is the task of prosecutors, defence attorneys and judges. This distinction is properly reflected in the standard of care imposed, once a duty is recognized. The standard of care required to meet the duty is not that of a reasonable lawyer or judge, but that of a reasonable police officer. Where the police investigate a suspect reasonably, but lawyers, judges or prosecutors act unreasonably in the course of determining his legal guilt or innocence, then the police officer will have met the standard of care and cannot be held liable either for failing to perform the job of a lawyer, judge or prosecutor, or for the unreasonable conduct of other actors in the criminal justice system.

15.2 The Duty to Self-Initiate an Investigation

15.2.1 Case Law

The police have a duty to investigate crime. However, this duty is not absolute; it is subject to the discretion afforded to police officers, with which the Courts will not readily interfere if the discretion is exercised honestly and in an objectively reasonable manner.

Police officers have a duty to use their judgment to adapt law enforcement to individual circumstances and the real-life demands of justice. This is the basis of police discretion. In R. v. Beaudry, 2007 SCC 5, the essence of police discretion was described in the following terms:

35 There is no question that police officers have a duty to enforce the law and investigate crimes. The principle that the police have a duty to enforce the criminal law is well established at common law: R. v. Metropolitan Police Commissioner, [1968] 1 All E.R. 763 (C.A.), per Lord Denning, M.R., at p. 769; Hill v. Chief Constable of West Yorkshire, [1988] 2 All E.R. 238 (H.L.), per Lord Keith of Kinkel; P. Ceyssens, Legal Aspects of Policing (loose-leaf ed.), vol. 1, at pp. 2-22 et seq.…

36 Nevertheless, it should not be concluded automatically, or without distinction, that this duty is applicable in every situation. Applying the letter of the law to the practical, real-life situations faced by police officers in performing their everyday duties requires that certain adjustments be made. Although these adjustments may sometimes appear to deviate from the letter of the law, they are crucial and are part of the very essence of the proper administration of the criminal justice system, or to use the words of s. 139(2), are perfectly consistent with the “course of justice”. The ability — indeed the duty — to use one’s judgment to adapt the process of law enforcement to individual circumstances and to the real-life demands of justice is in fact the basis of police discretion. What La Forest J. said in R. v. Beare, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 387, at p. 410, is directly on point here:

Discretion is an essential feature of the criminal justice system. A system that attempted to eliminate discretion would be unworkably complex and rigid.

37 Thus, a police officer who has reasonable grounds to believe that an offence has been committed, or that a more thorough investigation might produce evidence that could form the basis of a criminal charge, may exercise his or her discretion to decide not to engage the judicial process. But this discretion is not absolute. Far from having carte blanche, police officers must justify their decisions rationally.

38 The required justification is essentially twofold. First, the exercise of the discretion must be justified subjectively, that is, the discretion must have been exercised honestly and transparently, and on the basis of valid and reasonable grounds (reasons of Chamberland J.A., at para. 41). Thus, a decision based on favouritism, or on cultural, social or racial stereotypes, cannot constitute a proper exercise of police discretion. However, the officer’s sincere belief that he properly exercised his discretion is not sufficient to justify his decision.

39 Hence, the exercise of police discretion must also be justified on the basis of objective factors. I agree with Doyon J.A. that in determining whether a decision resulting from an exercise of police discretion is proper, it is important to consider the material circumstances in which the discretion was exercised. However, I do not agree with him on the importance of the factors he regarded as part of the legal context, that is, the administrative directives and the administration of justice in the province.

40 First, it is self-evident that the material circumstances are an important factor in the assessment of a police officer’s decision: the discretion will certainly not be exercised in the same way in a case of shoplifting by a teenager as one involving a robbery. In the first case, the interests of justice may very well be served if the officer gives the young offender a stern warning and alerts his or her parents. However, this does not mean that the police have no discretion left when the degree of seriousness reaches a certain level. In the case of a robbery, or an even more serious offence, the discretion can be exercised to decide not to arrest a suspect or not to pursue an investigation. However, the justification offered must be proportionate to the seriousness of the conduct and it must be clear that the discretion was exercised in the public interest. Thus, while some exercises of discretion are almost routine and are clearly justified, others are truly exceptional and will require that the police officer explain his or her decision in greater detail.Footnote 1101

In Chief Constable of the Hertfordshire Police v. Van Colle, [2008] UKHL 50, the UK House of Lords considered a case where the police had failed to act on a threat against a person which culminated in his murder. Much of the reasoning was addressed at the point whether the police owed the victims of the threatened violence a duty to prevent the threatened violence from occurring, and whether they could be sued for breach of such a duty. In his opinion, Lord Bingham stated:

[…] the court should endeavour to place itself in the chair of DC Ridley and assess events as they unfolded through his eyes. But the application of the test depends not only on what the authorities knew, but also on what they ought to have known. Thus, stupidity, lack of imagination and inertia do not afford an excuse to a national authority which reasonably ought, in the light of what it knew or was told, to make further inquiries or investigations: it is then to be treated as knowing what such further enquiries or investigations would have elicited.Footnote 1102

In the case of R. Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis, Ex Parte Blackburn, [1968] 1 All E.R. 763, Blackburn sought mandamus to compel the police to enforce the gaming laws. In holding that the police had a duty to enforce the law, Lord Denning described the discretion of police officers as follows:

Although the chief officers of police are answerable to the law, there are many fields in which they have a discretion with which the law will not interfere. For instance, it is for the Commissioner of Police, or the chief constable, as the case may be, to decide in any particular case whether enquiries should be pursued, or whether an arrest should be made, or a prosecution brought. It must be for him to decide on the disposition of his force and the concentration of his resources on any particular crime or area. No court can or should give him direction on such a matter.

As to the outcome of the case, no decision was ultimately necessary due to a policy change and an undertaking by the police to look into the “goings-on” in gaming clubs. The Court said that was all that the Complainant could expect.

In an Australian case, O’Malley v. Keelty, CMR of the Australian Federal Police, [2005] FCA 861, the Australian Federal Court considered whether the police had breached a duty to investigate allegations by O’Malley that his telephone communications had been illegally intercepted:

31 The primary question in this case is whether the Commissioner, or his officers, have breached any duty by failing to investigate further the allegations made by Mr. O’Malley. In determining whether a breach occurred, the issue to consider is whether a reasonable, honest police officer would have decided to investigate in this case after having given the matter due and proper consideration. […]

36 Nevertheless, a court cannot and should not compel a police force to investigate every breach of the law. There are many mysteries in this world. Some of them involve possible commissions of crime. It is not, however, the responsibility of police officers to investigate all of them. Indeed, the role of the police is not to investigate whether, at large, there has been a breach of the law.

In the result, the Court did not find in the O’Malley case the police had breached a duty to investigate. Relevant factors considered by the Court to assess the reasonableness of the police actions were:

  • there was no material that would require an honest and reasonable police officer to conclude that any identifiable person might be successfully prosecuted for any wrongdoing. Consequently, there was no reason why an honest and reasonable police officer might not decide against commencing or continuing an investigation.
  • when viewed in relation to the full spectrum of criminal behaviour, it would be difficult to classify this complaint as a relatively major matter. The relatively small penalty attached to such a breach would relegate it to a low priority matter. While such a breach would at least constitute an invasion of privacy, when the degree of individual and social harm likely involved in such a breach is compared to the harm associated with more serious crimes, it is clear that a reasonable and honest police officer might consider the matter to be of such low priority as to warrant the devotion of no further resources to it.
  • the lack and difficulty of obtaining any legally admissible evidence identifying those responsible for the alleged interference with Mr. O’Malley’s home telephone lines, and the long supposed time frame of events, (spanning more than a decade) made it unlikely that the Director of Public Prosecutions would ever be prepared to prosecute the matter.

In conclusion, the principle to be derived from the case law is that so long as police officers have exercised their discretion honestly and in an objectively reasonable manner, and can justify their actions rationally, they will not be found culpable for a decision not to investigate since such a decision falls within their legitimate exercise of police discretion.

15.2.2 MP Policies and Directives

As was noted by counsel for seven of the subjects in written submissions, the CFPM has issued Technical Directives on the conduct of policing duties and functions. The CFPM has also issued, on behalf of the VCDS, the Military Police Policies and Technical Procedural Manual (MPPTP) providing the CFPM’s technical guidance on policing duties and functions. Finally, the CFPM, through the office of the Deputy Provost Marshal (DPM) Police, issues mission specific Technical Directives to the Task Force Senior MP Adviser.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, the CFPM at the time in question, testified the mission-specific Technical Directives did not have the binding effect of orders.Footnote 1103 In written submissions on behalf of Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, the status of CFPM Technical Directives was described as follows:

These directives were the articulation of the CFPM’s expectations on policing. They were described as guidelines for the performance of policing functions. Although consequences could flow from a failure to follow a Technical Directive, they did not constitute an Order. (At p. 18)

There is some interplay between non-binding police directives and policies relating to the performance of policing functions, and the legal duties and discretion of police officers as defined by the common law. Such directives or policies do not define or limit the common law responsibilities and discretion of police, although they are relevant to the prevailing circumstances under which individual police conduct will be evaluated.

In R. v. Beaudry, the Court considered the relationship between directives to police, and the legal duties of police as these are defined by common law:

44 While the existence of administrative directives that apply to the situation in issue is far from being totally irrelevant, it cannot be as conclusive a factor as Doyon J.A. suggests. After quoting the passages from the police practices manual of Repentigny’s public safety service on the procedure to follow in impaired driving cases, he concluded as follows:

[…] In my opinion, these passages demonstrate the authorities’ clear intention that impaired driving offences should first be thoroughly investigated, although this does not preclude a subsequent decision not to prosecute. It must be noted that the period of time for taking breath samples is relatively short, which means that the investigation must be completed diligently and that this directive should be followed.

A police officer who is familiar with such a directive and who has solemnly affirmed, under the Police Act (R.S.Q., c. P-13.1), that he or she will perform the duties of his or her office honestly cannot be unaware of how serious the state considers this type of offence to be. In fact, the appellant’s superior officer himself concluded, after being informed of the events, that breath samples should have been taken.Footnote 1104

45 Doyon J.A. seems to be attributing to the administrative directives set out in the police practices manual a normative value that they do not have. It should be pointed out that these directives do not have the force of law. They therefore cannot alter the scope of a discretion that is founded in the common law or a statute […]

46 In R. v. Jageshur (2002), 169 C.C.C. (3d) 225, the Ontario Court of Appeal addressed this question in a context that was very similar to the one now before us. That case concerned the legality of a police operation carried out in compliance with the applicable law but not with the applicable administrative directives. Doherty J.A. wrote the following for a unanimous court:

An officer’s duties and hence his or her responsibilities cannot be equated with instructions as to how those duties and responsibilities should be carried out. Police policies speak to the manner in which police should carry out their responsibilities, but do not define or limit those responsibilities.

[…]

My conclusion that the officers’ responsibilities were not circumscribed by the RCMP policy concerning major drug operations and reverse stings is fortified by a consideration of the nature of these policies. Section 21(1)(b) of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP. Section 21(2)(b) authorizes the Commissioner of the RCMP to make rules (standing orders) for the conduct and performance of duties by members of the RCMP. Section 38 of the same Act authorizes the Governor in Council to make regulations governing the conduct of members (Code of Conduct). The policies in issue on this appeal did not spring from any of these statutory sources… . [Emphasis added; paras 50 and 52.]

In short, evidence of the existence of directives of this nature and evidence that the accused was, or is presumed to have been, aware of them at the time of the conduct in issue can shed light on the circumstances of the alleged exercise of his discretion. The same is true of evidence about the police service’s usual procedures, such as the testimony of Assistant Director Rocheleau and retired officer Lapointe in the case at bar. However, such evidence cannot be conclusive.Footnote 1105

Because police policies and directives can shed light on the circumstances which are alleged to give rise to a duty to investigate, they are a relevant factor for the Commission to consider. In the MPPTP, referred to above (Exhibit P-3, tab 3), guidance was given to MP on their roles and responsibilities, and the conduct of investigations, as follows:

Chapter One

3. General. The roles and responsibilities of the MP are contained in the Department Administrative Orders and Directives (DAOD). The MP tasks and priorities will vary according to the commander’s requirements, geographical location, and the operational environment concerned. Duties include:

  1. crime prevention;
  2. detection and investigation of service, criminal, and security offences; […]

6. Constraints. The following constraints are to be adhered to when MP policies and procedures are being evaluated: […]

  1. current acceptable police standards and practices; […]

Chapter Six

3. General. The independence of policing is aimed at ensuring the integrity of our judicial system. The purpose and objectives of an investigation are to reconstruct events, gather evidence, identify the elements of the alleged offence, and identify those responsible for it. Each of these purposes must be fulfilled, and each of these objectives must be achieved with integrity and fairness. […]

5. Independence of Investigations. MP authority is derived from the NDA and the C.C.C. [Criminal Code of Canada]. When exercising MP powers under the NDA, the individual MP member is held personally accountable.

6. Ethical Principles. MP investigations shall be conducted IAW accepted CF Military Police policies and procedures, with particular attention to the following:

  1. MP shall not accord immunities or undue advantages to any person notwithstanding their rank or position;
  2. Investigations and other law enforcement activities must be conducted in such a manner, within the law, that facilitates and supports the Commander’s legitimate mission, and reinforces military values;
  3. MP shall not attempt to dissuade a complainant from pursuing a complaint, nor will the MP display scepticism about the allegations. MP may attempt to reconcile inconsistencies in a complainant’s statement(s) of present, however, failure to do so may not prevent the complaint from being pursued; and
  4. MP shall investigate complaints without bias or prejudice to any particular individual. Identification and elimination of suspects shall be based on objective evidence and reasonable grounds.

1. [sic] Initiating an Investigation. An MP investigation may be initiated whenever:

  1. an MP observes the commission of any criminal or service offence;
  2. an MP is in receipt of a complaint originating from any other person in which a criminal or service offence is alleged;
  3. at the request of a Commander/CO;
  4. MP learns of an incident through an informant (i.e. local police, a witness, a confidential informant, an anonymous tip, etc.);
  5. MP are tasked directly by DPM Police or DPM NIS; and
  6. an authority in the MP Technical Chain so directs. […]

20. General. The CFNIS provides DND and the CF an efficient, accountable, and independent organization for criminal investigation services in Canada and abroad, in support of the military justice system.

The direction provided in the MPPTP was amplified by mission-specific Technical Directives issued by the CFPM. During the time period of this complaint, there were three such Technical Directives. The language relating to the investigative duties of MPs remained substantially unchanged in the three versions:

MP Technical Directive for Roto 3, March 15, 2006Footnote 1106

9. GENERAL. […] The authority for MP to conduct investigations is derived from the NDA and the Criminal Code of Canada, not from the operational chain of command. It is critical that commanders understand the authority of the MP to conduct independent investigations. […]

11. SPECIFIC GUIDANCE. While deployed on multi-national operations, the appropriate component of Canadian MP (MP or CFNIS) shall investigate allegations or instances of the following occurrences (attributed to CF personnel), in addition to the normal investigations required IAW Ref B: […]

11.C. Allegations of violations of the law of armed conflict or international law. […]

14. DETAINEES. […] The TFPM is responsible for:

14.A. The provision of advice on prisoner handling and transfer policy and procedures.

[…]

14.F(1). Ensure investigation of the following types of incidents is conducted by appropriate CF investigative organization ( i.e. CFNIS): […]

14.F.(1)(B): Allegations of crimes committed by CF members against detainees.

14.F.(1)(C): Allegations of violations by CF members of the law of armed conflict or international law.Footnote 1107

In its Final Report into a complaint submitted by Dr. Amir Attaran, as reissued on November 3, 2009, the Commission interpreted the MP Technical Directives as intending a proactive posture by MPs in the highly sensitive area of detainee treatment. Unlike the present complaint, the Attaran complaint involved an alleged failure by the MP to investigate visible injuries to three detainees upon their arrival at KAF. The Attaran complaint raised different circumstances from those in the complaint currently under consideration.

15.2.3 The Means of Knowing Standard

On motion by counsel for seven of the subjects, the Commission issued a decision on November 3, 2010, setting out the test that it would apply to determine if information was within the subjects’ “means of knowing”. In that decision, the Commission stated:

30. It therefore appears to the Commission that there is at least some measure of agreement that the “means of knowing” standard captures information which a reasonable MP officer would have obtained by making reasonable inquiries. In the Commission’s view, this entails a subjective element based on what the MP Officer knew, and an objective element as to what a reasonable MP Officer would have done in the circumstances to seek out more information to fill the gaps. Whether a MP Officer acted reasonably in the circumstances is an issue relating to the expected. standard of conduct and depends on the evidence.

For the purposes of applying this test in the context of this complaint, the Commission’s view is that MPs are accountable for information which they knew, or to which they were wilfully blind. In addition, they may be held accountable for the fact they did not know information which a reasonable police officer in the circumstances would have known.

XVI. Did the Subjects Possess Knowledge that Triggered a Duty to Investigate?

16.1 Major Bernie Hudson

Major Bernie Hudson was the Task Force Provost Marshal during ROTO 3. At the time of his testimony, he had served 23 years in the Canadian Forces, 20 as a commissioned officer, and 18 as a member of the military police. He has served in both staff and command positions at various locations across Canada, and has commanded MP detachments both in Canada and abroad. His international deployments included the Golan Heights as part of the United Nations observer mission as both the Canadian Provost Marshal and the Provost Marshal for the multi-national force. He also served on exchange to the British army for three years, during which time he was deployed to Iraq, where he was a second-in-command of a British provost company in Basra.

Most recently, he spent almost seven months in Afghanistan as the ROTO 3 TFPM, from the beginning of February 2007 to mid-August 2007. His deployment to Afghanistan overlapped for a short period of time with that of Maj Zybala, during which time he provided Maj Zybala with briefings and brought him up to date. On the 17th of August, the change of command between the two TFPMs took place, and Maj Hudson left theatre two days later.Footnote 1108

Since returning from Afghanistan, Maj Hudson has been serving at Land Forces Doctrine and Training System in Kingston, where he is the military police desk officer for operational-type training, lessons learned, doctrine and any kind of military police issue that fits into the greater body of army doctrine. He works both here in Canada and internationally representing the military police on this front.Footnote 1109

During his time in Afghanistan, Maj Hudson was not only the TFPM, but also the commanding officer of the MP company. He was located in Kandahar Air Field, at Task Force Headquarters, in the same compound as the Task Force Commander, but his office was in the building next to the commander in that compound.

Maj Hudson, because he was the senior military policeman in theatre, was also wearing a third hat in Afghanistan – that of Provost Marshal for KAF as a whole. He described his three sets of duties as follows:

In the first job as commanding officer of the military police, I was a line commander, worked directly for the Force commander commanding all of the Canadian Military Police in theatre. I was responsible not only for their welfare, their administration, but also any operations that the Canadian Military Police were tasked to support by the commander.

If the commander needed military police to do mentoring jobs, to do detention, taking care of detainees or any of those kind of command-type operational tasks that aren’t germane to police work, he could then task me to do that and I would use the military police at my disposal to actually execute those tasks on his behalf.

As the Task Force Provost Marshal, I had sort of two main responsibilities. One, I was the commander’s adviser for anything to do with policing in theatre. That is really an advisory role. Second, I was also the technical authority for all military police activities in theatre, to which I effectively worked to the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal as the technical head of the military police, in this case for law enforcement investigations, for the enforcement of Canadian law, both civil and military. In some ways I shared that responsibility somewhat with the NIS who have a similar mandate in that respect, but slightly different.

My third hat as Kandahar Airfield Provost Marshal, I was the senior international military policeman on Kandahar Airfield. Kandahar Airfield is multi-national: Americans, British, Dutch, Australians, you name it, everybody is there. But I was the senior military policeman, so I was sort of the doyen of the military police community on the airfield. If there was trouble between the families or there was friction between the different military police with overlapping jurisdictions, I would get them around the table and sort of thrash out the differences.

I was also the adviser to the Force Protection commander of the Airfield for the military police contribution to the protection of the airfield.Footnote 1110

Relating back to his technical net, Maj Hudson explained his contact with the CEFCOM PM was quite frequent, at least every second day by telephone, and perhaps daily when taking email into account. Majors Boot and Laflamme were his CEFCOM PMs. He did not recall speaking to the CFPM while in theatre, but did speak to him before deployment, at a training event. He gave the CFPM a presentation on the MP company, explaining its organization, what they were doing and describing problem areas. Detainee issues were not discussed between the two because, according to Maj Hudson, in January 2007 they were not prominent.Footnote 1111

Maj Hudson had no discussions with LCol (ret’d) Garrick, the NIS commanding officer at the time. He did say there was a briefing protocol in place with the NIS in the Afghanistan theatre. Master Warrant Officer Watson (as he then was, now a Chief Warrant Officer) was the NIS commander in theatre during ROTO 3. Maj Hudson had a formal briefing protocol with CWO Watson, but they would also meet informally. He said the two would meet every couple of days, or almost daily, and described the nature of that informal contact:

Informally, he would come and see me or I might be down in the platoon area visiting my troops and I would see him. Generally we would have discussions. He was a sounding board. He was a senior military policeman with a lot of experience. So if I had things I was wrestling with, I could always ask him questions and vice versa, he would seek my advice on different things too that he was working on.Footnote 1112

In terms of his knowledge about the detainee controversy itself, Maj Hudson was newly deployed to Afghanistan when the February 21, 2007 complaint from Amnesty/BCCLA was filed with this Commission.Footnote 1113 Maj Hudson was aware this complaint had been submitted, but not aware of the details. He never saw a copy of it while in theatre. He was more aware of the Attaran complaint that preceded it, alleging abuse by MPs of detainees while in Canadian custody. Maj Hudson was also involved, likely through the CEFCOM PM, with gathering certain documents in response to the MPCC complaints, although it is not clear whether this was in relation to the Attaran complaint, the first Transfer Complaint or both.Footnote 1114

During his time in theatre, proceedings initiated by the Complainants were ongoing before the Federal Court of Canada. Maj Hudson was aware this involved a motion for an injunction to stop the transfer of detainees. This was something he discussed at length because “it would directly affect operations.”Footnote 1115 In a general sense, as well, he understood the Complainants’ concerns related to allegations of torture.Footnote 1116

He did not see the DFAIT country reports on Afghanistan prior to deployment or while in theatre. He was unaware they existed, and pointed out in testimony these were classified documents. He did see one report from the U.S. State Department prior to deployment, which he heard about and took the initiative to read even though it appears not to have been required reading:

I think I saw one report from the U.S. State Department, probably the one for the year before I was deployed. It was being passed around while we were doing our pre-deployment training through some of the staff and I managed to knuckle onto it and have a look at it.

  • It was passed around to yourself and who else?
  • When we were doing some of our pre-deployment training in Gagetown, the Task Force headquarters was being trained and we had access to various documents. Someone had shown that document to me, probably in the Ops, the G3 side of the Task Force headquarters. It might have been the Ops officer who showed it to me. I read it and handed it back kind of thing.Footnote 1117

He recalled the document contained information “about torture, abuse and those things in a past context”, but described it as evidence that “[...] there is a history of it in that country. There were no specific examples in those documents saying it is still going on today or here are case studies and that sort of thing, but in a context it said that there is a history of this in the country.”Footnote 1118

Maj Hudson saw no reports from the AIHRC, nor was he aware of that organization’s existence prior to arriving in theatre. Once in theatre, though, he was the person tasked with ensuring they received the necessary information on Canadian detainees. This meant he met with two of their representatives from the local Kandahar office, who inspected the detention facilities. The Provost Marshal and these representatives also “discussed how we would provide them information with respect to detainees that move through our custody.” He said in the course of this visit, the AIHRC discussed the risk of torture in a general sense, but without any specifics: “We never discussed any specific examples, had they seen it here or had they seen it there sort of thing. I knew they were one of the checks and balances that we had to create assurances that it wasn’t going on.”Footnote 1119

Maj Hudson knew the agreement with the AIHRC (signed Feb. 20, 2007 while he was in theatre) was they would report back to Canada any mistreatment of Canadian-transferred detainees. He never did any personal follow-up with the AIHRC, other than the tour of the detention facility mentioned. However, he was privy to a conversation in which Canada’s Minister of Defence reinforced the importance of the AIHRC arrangement and the proper treatment of Canadian detainees:

The only other time was when I met Engineer Noorzai with Gordon O’Connor, the Minister of Defence, at some point in March, I believe. We actually toured him around the facility. I was there when the Minister of National Defence talked to him specifically about how important post transfer assurances were and that we, Canada, would provide whatever support they required. Specifically he was asked if he required any additional support from Canada to conduct the review of detainees and that sort of stuff. So I was the fly on the wall in that conversation.Footnote 1120

Beyond these interactions, Maj Hudson did not consider he was to be the point of contact if the AIHRC had actual allegations of mistreatment. This was despite the passage in the agreement, discussed earlier, that would seem to indicate the TFPM was meant to be that point of contact. He said it was possible the AIHRC would contact him, but the more likely contact point would be DFAIT.Footnote 1121

As ROTO 3 TFPM, he was not privy to any reports sent by Mr. Colvin. This appears to be corroborated by Mr. Colvin’s evidence. With the exception of Mr. Colvin’s site visit to Kabul in June 2007, his two key reports describing problems with detainee tracking and concerns about abuse of Canadian-transferred detainees, were circulated some eight months before Maj Hudson’s time in theatre. Nor was Maj Hudson aware of any details about the inter-agency meeting held in March 2007 where Mr. Colvin said if Canada did not want its detainees tortured, it should not send them to the NDS.
