Maj Hudson was only generally aware of political discussion about the detainee issue prior to May 2007, between CEFCOM and DFAIT: “I was aware that there was interaction between CEFCOM and DFAIT at the political level on the detainee file. Specifically what was being discussed and who was discussing what, no idea, well above my pay grade.”Footnote 1122

Maj Hudson said he was generally aware of all the media attention surrounding the detainee issue: “I read anything that came out in the media on the detainee issue, definitely.”Footnote 1123 He was most definitely aware of the Graeme Smith articles while in theatre. In fact, this was the key turning point for him, the point at which he himself developed concerns about post-transfer treatment of Canadian-transferred detainees. Maj Hudson was advised by either the Task Force Commander or his Chief of Staff in theatre that the first article was going to be released, about a day ahead of time. When it was published, the media affairs people at the Task Force passed it around and “obviously it was brought to my attention immediately.”Footnote 1124

Around the time of the Graeme Smith articles, Maj Hudson said he also viewed a site visit report authored by Gavin Buchan of DFAIT. This was the report that stated: “To our surprise, even though NDS officers accompanied us throughout the visit, two prisoners nonetheless came forward with complaints of mistreatment.”Footnote 1125 The Buchan report was actually circulated directly to him by the Deputy Commander, even though it was C4 traffic. Major Hudson ordered one of his MPs to check the names mentioned against the names of detainees who had been in Canadian custody, as he expected queries on this front. The Buchan report would end up being the only site visit report he ever received. He recognized this was not normal as compared to the later site visit reports, instituted pursuant to the May transfer arrangement. Those reports had a limited distribution list.Footnote 1126

Maj Hudson displayed a keen awareness of the legal issues at stake in the detainee controversy. During testimony, he was referred to a passage at the end of the first Graeme Smith article referencing Article 12 of the Third Geneva Convention, which read:

Prisoners of war are in the hands of the enemy Power, but not of the individuals or military units who have captured them. Irrespective of the individual responsibilities that may exist, the Detaining Power is responsible for the treatment given them. Prisoners of war may only be transferred by the Detaining Power to a Power which is a party to the Convention and after the Detaining Power has satisfied itself of the willingness and ability of such transferee Power to apply the Convention.Footnote 1127

Maj Hudson was then asked whether he was aware the article had raised the idea of a breach of the Geneva Conventions at the time. His answer revealed a good understanding of this particular requirement of the third Geneva Convention, i.e., the responsibility for detainees post transfer:

  • My knowledge at the time, it was very clear in my mind that according to the Geneva Conventions, we are responsible for detainees post transfer. That’s basic training for military police officers. That’s part of the laws of armed conflict and that sort of stuff.
  • Responsible for what might happen to them post transfer.
  • Yes, according to the Geneva Conventions, the original capturing power is ultimately responsible for prisoners of war post transfer. If they transfer them to a third state, they are still responsible. If that third state abuses them in some way, they are supposed to reassert custody of them or fix that in some other way.Footnote 1128

Maj Hudson was also aware of the importance of being able to track Canadian detainees after they had been sent to the NDS, and recognized this as a requirement of the Geneva Convention and international humanitarian law.Footnote 1129

If faced with a potential breach of the Geneva Conventions, Maj Hudson said his first step would be to call a lawyer to get advice on the nature of the offence potentially in issue, if he were the one dealing with the file. He explained, though, it would more likely be handled by the NIS: “We have military prosecutors that can put together the articles of the offence and all that sort, so we would be in constant discussion with them. And arguably, it would be an NIS led investigation anyways, so it wouldn’t be me deciding what to charge them under.”Footnote 1130

Maj Hudson had a sound grasp, as well, of the technical/doctrinal documents that governed his actions as a police officer while in the Afghan theatre. The technical directive was one of his primary documents, along with the Military Police Policies and Procedural Manual.Footnote 1131 Maj Hudson was referred to a key passage in the applicable technical directive during his time in theatre, para. 11(c), which states that while deployed, the “appropriate component of Canadian MP or CFNIS shall investigate allegations or instances of the following occurrences attributed to Canadian Forces personnel [...] (c) Allegations of violations of the law of armed conflict or international law [...]”Footnote 1132

Asked about the very specific language in this section, saying one “shall” investigate allegations of violations of international law, Maj Hudson agreed in these areas the technical directive did not leave much discretion: “The technical directive clearly says that we need to do that. It actually directs me to do it. This here, what this tells me is one of my roles and responsibilities is to do that.”Footnote 1133

Maj Hudson was referred to para. 14(f) of the same Technical Directive, which states the TFPM, in particular, is responsible to “Ensure investigation of the following types of incidents is conducted by appropriate CF investigative organization (i.e. CFNIS): [...] 14.F.1(C) Allegations of violations by CF members of the law of armed conflict or international law.” He explained what he understood his obligations to be in respect of this passage:

If a Canadian Forces member breached the laws of armed conflict or international law or international humanitarian law, then we could investigate that because potentially that is a crime committed by a Canadian person under our jurisdiction. [...] If I had sight of that, my first thing would be to discuss it with the NIS because it would probably be an NIS investigation. I would be very surprised if it was left in my purview to investigate.Footnote 1134

Maj Hudson explained he would contact the NIS to ensure an investigation took place. In the hypothetical circumstance where the NIS refused to pursue the investigation, and he continued to think it necessary to investigate, he said he would seek advice up his technical chain.Footnote 1135

Under MGen (ret’d) Grant and pursuant to TSO 321A, Maj Hudson considered that his input into the detainee transfer process was limited to the care and handling of detainees while in Canadian custody. Maj Hudson recalled no discussions with the general or his advisors on the question of post-transfer risk prior to the Graeme Smith articles.Footnote 1136 He was asked whether MGen (ret’d) Grant had a decision making committee, in the same way that MGen Laroche described. Maj Hudson said no - MGen (ret’d) Grant’s decision making process was very informal. Indeed, he wanted to formalize the process somewhat, and assisted the TF Commander in doing so while in theatre:

The process itself, in my mind, was – I wanted to have it better documented. One of the things that I did as we were rewriting the TSOs, we created a form where we would actually collect all the inputs so that it would be clearly in front of the General, all the advice he has been provided [...]

Not that the decisions made were wrong, not that he didn’t get all the information, I have no suspicions in that regard, but I thought for the sake of posterity and whatnot that it was a bit loose and I would have liked to have seen it much more delineated, so we created this process toward the end of May.Footnote 1137

The document Maj Hudson helped create did not have a section on risk-assessment. The risk assessment matrix referred to during the testimony of Generals Laroche and Juneau was not created until ROTO 4. The document used during ROTO 3 was focused on whether the detainee was an enemy combatant that needed to be transferred, or an innocent that needed to be released. His document assessed whether the detainee was fit, operational reasons to believe he was Taliban, the results of tactical questions and gunpowder residue tests, and other such indicators.Footnote 1138

Maj Hudson believed at first this form included a box for the JAG to check off with respect to legal advice, presumably encompassing the question of post-transfer risk, but corrected himself when he viewed the actual document.Footnote 1139 He did know his commander was getting legal advice, or at least strongly presumed that to be the case: “He was getting legal advice on everything. Specifically on detainees? I would be surprised if he wasn’t getting legal advice on detainees. The JAG officer was very […] conscientious.”Footnote 1140

Maj Hudson did say there were, on occasion, actual meetings to discuss a transfer decision. It appears if such a meeting occurred, he was involved:

[…] It depended on the actual circumstances. Some [transfer decisions] were very cut and dry, very clear, in which case a meeting was probably not required and the results would come back to me informally – I shouldn’t say “informally”, but the results could come back verbally or whatnot.

Sometimes when there was more debate, we would actually have a formal meeting. Generally, at that meeting you would see representation from the Op side, representation from the intelligence side, myself, possibly medical if there were medical issues, and usually the JAG as well.

  • What about the PolAd?
  • Possibly, yes. I am trying to remember. I can’t recall exactly. Again, the decision to release is a military decision.Footnote 1141

Maj Hudson explained the main issue at these meetings was figuring out whether a detainee was a Taliban or an enemy. This remained the case after the new arrangement was put in place. That is, before the Graeme Smith articles, post-transfer treatment was not discussed because no red flags had yet been raised, while afterwards, the TFPM continued to provide advice only on his areas of expertise, which did not include post-transfer risk. Moreover, such advice was usually provided only in written form, via the detainee officer:

As far as we were concerned, up to the middle of April point when the Globe and Mail article came out, there was no indication that post transfer was an issue. There was no red flags that had come up. So up until that point, I am sure that -- I shouldn’t say I am sure, but I assume the General had thought those things through. I thought about them as well, but that wasn’t an issue we put on the table every week and said, okay, is there any -- because there was no evidence that there was a problem yet.

  • And after the Graeme Smith article and the new arrangement in May 2007, was there heightened awareness about that issue?
  • There definitely was because once that article came out, we stopped doing transfers until we had assurances that the system was more robust.
  • Was the process essentially the same prior as after?
  • After, we actually implemented this form that I mentioned. So that changed the process significantly.
  • But physically it would happen in more or less the same way. Sometimes you would meet, sometimes you wouldn’t.
  • Generally, all the information would be put to the commander by the detainee officer. We would gather it all together and he would submit it. We wouldn’t necessarily have to meet. If the commander had questions, he may call some of us in to elaborate or discuss, but there was no requirement for a physical meeting once we had the form.Footnote 1142

Maj Hudson said he could not recall any specific discussions of post-transfer risks after the May 2007 re-start of transfers. Significantly, though, he appears to have been regularly involved in these types of discussions during the stoppage period:

[…] we had many discussions of post transfer risk. But once we were assured by DFAIT that the conditions were now in place to do proper follow-ups, then that issue – although we kept our ears open and our eyes open and kept a watch on it, that issue wasn’t forefront in the decision-making process because we had assurances from DFAIT that everything was working.Footnote 1143

It appears he was asking questions about the nature of the post-transfer monitoring that would take place during that stoppage period, and was informed by his Commander that DFAIT would take care of it.Footnote 1144

Maj Hudson did not feel he was getting any more or any less information about detainees under the new regime, as compared to the old, nor could he recall any discussions or questions put to him about whether, under the new regime, he should be receiving the site visit reports or otherwise be kept out of the loop.Footnote 1145 Maj Hudson’s troops continued to keep detainee records, such as capture reports, DNA samples, and the individual case files. This did not change with the new regime given that MPs were the experts when it came to evidence and case file retention.Footnote 1146

Asked whether he felt he needed to see the site visit reports in order to reassure himself about the propriety of the commander’s transfer decisions, Maj Hudson’s evidence was that he was satisfied with what he knew about the new monitoring regime, and the steps taken after the stoppage in late April/early May. Maj Hudson knew he was not likely to see the site visit reports. What he wanted, though, was a level of comfort things were being done properly:

From my point of view, what was most important was that there were organizations that were monitoring this, that I had assurances from those organizations that they were doing that monitoring. I understood the political sensitivities that this is in that stovepipe, I work over here in this stovepipe, and I am not a political adviser in DFAIT and I am not in the embassy, so I am not going to see these things. But what I did want was comfort that they were doing their jobs and that there were assurances in place and that they were comfortable with the post transfer piece. As long as DFAIT came back and said they were comfortable with it and it was working, I was happy because I had no reason not to trust DFAIT.Footnote 1147

Maj Hudson had conversations with the POLAD (Mr. Martin Laflamme of DFAIT) once the new transfer regime was in place. Those discussions revolved around the role the POLAD was to play in reading out the new agreement to detainees. Maj Hudson could not recall asking the POLAD about whether any adverse reports were coming back. Similarly, he did not ask his Deputy Commander, Colonel Cessford, about the results of the site visits.Footnote 1148 Indeed, Maj Hudson did not even know to whom the site visit reports went specifically. He felt, though, such reports were not likely to be sent directly to someone in his position:

DFAIT is not in the business of passing stuff directly to troops on the ground. This is an international incident so you have to be very careful how they deal with that matter. So I would think this would go back to Ottawa and DFAIT in Ottawa would talk to the Department of National Defence. It would come down through to CEFCOM and this sort of stuff with the actual reports. I wouldn’t expect to see those reports directly.Footnote 1149

Maj Hudson did appear to be somewhat aware of the frequency of the visits during his final months in theatre. He knew them to be occurring at approximately two visits per month. He learned of this through weekly operational meetings, without being privy to the results of those visits. He also knew that on two occasions his MP troops at the PRT provided visit security. Thus, with the exception of his leave period from June 3rd to 27th, approximately, he had a general awareness that visits were occurring.Footnote 1150

Throughout his testimony, Maj Hudson was asked whether he ever considered investigating the legality of the TF Commander’s transfer decisions. Maj Hudson stated he trusted the Commander’s decisions, and had seen good evidence that the Commander would do the right thing when required. Maj Hudson gave many examples and explanations for why he never doubted the Commander, or thought he was potentially engaging in war crimes by knowingly transferring detainees to an unacceptable risk of torture or mistreatment. One such example relates to the particular detainee who was forced to stay at the temporary detention facility, under the very difficult conditions described by Sgt Utton and Capt Worsfold. Maj Hudson felt this man’s unfortunate plight showed the Commander’s resolve not to transfer again until DFAIT had an appropriate visits regime in place:

The fact that he was willing to not transfer and have me keep this guy reinforces my confidence in the commander that he is above board and that he is not committing a contravention of the international law of armed conflict or something like that because he doesn’t want to transfer this guy into a position where he could be tortured, and he refuses to transfer him.Footnote 1151

It appears also to have been around this same time Maj Hudson had discussions with his MP troops about their legal liability. His troops at the platoon level and below were concerned about their personal liability in the detainee affair, so he had “town hall type” conversations with them to reassure them they would not be found individually liable for their part in the transfer process.Footnote 1152 He described the essence of what he related to his troops as follows:

I provided them information that they didn’t have. I provided them information as to what DFAIT was doing, what CEFCOM was doing, I provided them information as to what the Afghan Independent Human Rights Commission was responsible to do. I was providing them all that background. The reasons why I was comfortable, I was explaining to them … Also, about the Commander and how the Commander’s decision process is based and what information he has access to […]Footnote 1153

Maj Hudson specifically recalled Capt Worsfold was one of the people to have expressed her concerns about her liability in the transfer process, although her particular concern may have related to the difficult conditions under which a detainee was being held for an extended period in May 2007.Footnote 1154

As a result of these discussions, and his own consideration of the situation, Maj Hudson was clearly turning his mind to the legality of the new transfer arrangement, albeit perhaps not in the policing/investigative sense:

  • Listening to the way you looked at this and the discussions you had with your troops, is it safe to say that you did turn your mind to the question of whether this new régime was legal, whether it was something that could meet the Geneva Convention standard?
  • There is no standard in the Geneva Convention, there is no clear standard. But if I follow your thinking here, yes, I looked at the new transfer agreement. I could see how it was significantly better than the old one. It’s more clear, there’s additional levels of access built into it and reporting. I said good, that to me seems to meet that requirement. Then I also had access to see the actual SOPs used by DFAIT and I could see how they were putting pieces into place and requiring so many visits and how they would be done and everything. So I could see that they were putting a lot more thought into how they do their jobs.

    So between the two of these things, I have a reasonable assurance that we are doing the right things. That’s not to say it’s perfect or it’s not to say that something couldn’t happen in the future, but these two documents built a lot of confidence in my mind in the system.
  • You didn’t have a particular legal test in your mind other than you understood generally this earlier obligation you described to me under the Geneva Convention that we are responsible for our detainees post transfer.
  • Yes. My understanding is we are responsible and ultimately we are not going to transfer someone into a situation where torture is imminent. But as far as having a specific legal test in mind, no.Footnote 1155

Maj Hudson’s evidence also clearly indicated he turned his mind to the obligations of MGen (ret’d) Grant not to transfer people to a situation of potential torture:

General Grant would have to satisfy himself that he wasn’t transferring people into conditions where they could be tortured. That was what he would have to -- because he is authorizing the transfers. Fair enough. I can’t say how he satisfied himself of that. You would have to ask General Grant that question, how he satisfied himself that he wasn’t doing that.

  • But it’s fair to say you understood he had that obligation.
  • That he had an obligation not to transfer people into a situation where they would be potentially tortured.
  • Did you think that at the time you were in Afghanistan with him?
  • That he had that obligation?
  • Yes.
  • Yes, definitely.Footnote 1156

At another point in Maj Hudson’s testimony he explained again why he did not investigate the commander’s orders to transfer. His answer is lengthy, but embodies the bulk of his reasoning:

There is a whole host of reasons why. The first thing is, as a policeman, I can’t just run out and investigate something because I feel, I feel it is of interest. I need to have probable cause. I need to have a complaint brought to me. I need to have a pattern of activity that I can link together. I have to build up at least some concrete suspicion and then I have to have a basis in law to actually act on it, right. I just can’t go open people’s shades and look in their rooms. You know, this sort of stuff. So I need some stuff.

So bottom line is I had throughout my entire tour I had confidence in my commander and his ability to make those decisions. And at no time did I feel that -- did I lose -- sorry, at no time did I lose my confidence in him and in his ability to make those kind of decisions. And a whole host of reasons.

First off, we have a bilateral agreement between two countries with assurances built into it and those insurances (sic) include not only obligations to support the Geneva Conventions by Afghanistan as well as Canada but also obligations by Afghanistan to make information available and to allow us to inspect. And that assurance actually gets tighter once the second agreement is signed.

And we also have four different organizations in theatre which are actually doing prison visits. Right? We have the ICRC, we have the Afghan Independent Human Rights Commission, we have DFAIT, and we have Corrections Services CanadA. So we have force organs that are actually monitoring these prisons. And my belief is that any of these organizations with the exception of ICRC would have brought to our attention failings in that area that were grave of that sort.

On top of that, when allegations -- and at no time do I actually have a hard, specific allegation to investigate. When the allegations from Graeme Smith come forward, and the Buchan report, the first thing that happens is we shut down transfers. The commander actually makes the right decision. There is enough pattern of activity here on the table. Nothing is proven or substantiated yet that this is a Canadian detainee, but there is enough doubt that we need to shut down transfers.

And the commander did that. He refused to allow any transfers to happen during that period. And to me that was the right decision. Had my commander not done that, we might be having a different conversation here. But he did shut down transfers during that period and he would not reinstate transfers and he made it very, very clear to me he wouldn’t until such a time as he was assured that not only did we have this new monitoring agreement between the two countries but that DFAIT could actually fulfil its obligations.

Once he was confident that -- and I seen the DFAIT SOPs and they looked good to me as well. Once he was confident that DFAIT could fulfil its obligations then he reinstigated transfers.

So I mean, in my mind, the commander did not, early on did not have enough information to doubt that there was a problem or to believe that there was a problem. He trusted DFAIT was doing their job and everyone else. Once allegations came to light he shut down transfers, and then he wouldn’t start them up again until the system was corrected. And once DFAIT had corrected the system we started transferring again.

So to me he has done all the right things. There is no reason in my mind to build a suspicion that he is not doing the right things.Footnote 1157

Maj Hudson also never considered whether the Commander committed some type of a war crime by transferring detainees prior to the Graeme Smith articles and the April/May stoppage. He simply did not come to the conclusion prior to that stoppage the Commander had knowledge of a real risk of torture:

I didn’t believe he did to be honest with you. Based on I didn’t believe that I had any knowledge that there was torture. There was a past history but we had so many organizations, again in theatre, monitoring, that my belief was if there had been anything up to that point that they would have been telling us, they would have been putting out reports.Footnote 1158

On one occasion, upon returning from his leave in late June 2007, Maj Hudson did learn that a site visit had uncovered allegations of abuse. His deputy, who stood in for him on leave, informed him of the visit.Footnote 1159 He was asked whether his faith in the Commander to make the right transfer decision was shaken when he learned, upon returning from leave, a site visit had resulted in allegations, but transfers were not stopped. He said this news still did not provide him with enough evidence to suspect the Commander of having committed an offence because he saw no evidence the Commander kept on transferring in the face of the adverse report, or in the absence of a reassurance from DFAIT that transfers could continue for some reason:

The question here is: Did we commit an offence by knowingly transfer someone into a condition with torture? If we transferred someone and they are tortured and that wasn’t our intent or we didn’t know that would happen, then that’s not an offence. It’s only if the commander saw this and the next day decided to transfer someone, that would be of interest to me.

The other thing to keep in mind is we weren’t transferring detainees every day. We were transferring a few a month. There are periods when there are no detainees in the facility. This could come in and the commander could be in a position where he is not asked to transfer a detainee for a week or two weeks, which is plenty of time for DFAIT to fix this or to look into it or to provide that additional level of assurances. We are not dealing with hundreds and hundreds of people here. We are dealing with handfuls.Footnote 1160

Elsewhere, he said just because a report had been received did not mean a crime had been committed by transferring thereafter. He was told DFAIT was dealing with it: “I was told at the time that it was sufficient and I was trusting the people that were talking to me.”Footnote 1161 Most importantly, though, he said that at that point in time the Commander had established a pattern of behaviour which caused him to trust: “He had already established the fact if he [saw] reasonable allegations or a pattern of activity, that he was going to shut down transfers.”Footnote 1162

Maj Hudson was not aware during his time in theatre, but was shown a document during his testimony that indicated his faith in the Commander to proceed carefully was justified, given that a short moratorium or pause in transfers did occur in June 2007 in order to assess the import of the June allegations received.Footnote 1163

Finally, in terms of why he never came to suspect his Commander of illegal activity, Maj Hudson related a conversation he had with his Commander where MGen (ret’d) Grant told him he would keep detainees indefinitely rather than transfer them improperly.Footnote 1164

Thus, for all the foregoing reasons, Maj Hudson never really saw cause to turn his mind to the question whether he should investigate or cause to be investigated the Commander’s transfer decisions. He simply “didn’t feel it was necessary.”Footnote 1165 The Commander’s actions were such, he explained, that he never had to sit down to consider whether his Commander was committing some type of a crime.Footnote 1166

In terms of the standard he set for assessing his Commander’s conduct, he said at one point he would have needed a “clear indication” his Commander committed a breach of international law. Elsewhere, though, he spoke of needing a “concrete suspicion” and a “reasonable suspicion”.Footnote 1167

On a final point, Maj Hudson physically witnessed the transfer of certain detainees, and saw no signs of resistance, physical or otherwise, nor did he receive reports back about the NDS threatening detainees.Footnote 1168 He also appears not to have been aware of the fact CEFCOM/J9 initiated a fact check to confirm whether some of the detainees mentioned in the Graeme Smith article were Canadian-transferred detainees. He did, on more than one occasion, when allegations were being made, check his own database to confirm the names of some detainees. One such case was discussed earlier. He said had he known about the CEFCOM fact check, it would not have changed his view of the Commander’s behaviour because MGen (ret’d) Grant stopped transfers even before confirming that the names mentioned in the Globe and Mail articles were actual Canadian transferees.Footnote 1169

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submitted Maj Hudson bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. Generally, they said he bore responsibility as one of the TFPMs during the time period of this complaint for the failure to investigate or inquire into the legality of past and ongoing transfer orders. They submitted Maj Hudson had, or had the means of knowing, the following information which should have led him to conduct an investigation:

  • Maj Hudson was generally aware there were allegations of post-transfer abuse of detainees by the NDS.
  • Maj Hudson reviewed a U.S. State Department country report outlining the use of torture in Afghan prisons during his pre-deployment training.
  • Maj Hudson knew about a historical concern of detainee torture and abuse by Afghan officials.
  • Maj Hudson continued to be made aware of the risk of post-transfer abuse during his tenure as TFPM:
    • He was tasked to fulfil documentation requests related to the February 2007 complaint.
    • He knew there was a Federal Court proceeding seeking an injunction to halt detainee transfers. Maj Hudson discussed this subject at length because it would directly affect detainee operations.
    • He knew of the April 2007 Graeme Smith articles in The Globe and Mail.
    • He assisted in identifying whether the detainees alleging abuse in the Graeme Smith articles had been transferred by the CF.
    • He received a copy of the “Buchan report”, a DFAIT site visit report documenting allegations of torture by the NDS, shortly after the Graeme Smith articles were published.
    • He knew transfers were temporarily suspended after the Graeme Smith articles were published.
    • He knew another DFAIT monitoring visit had unearthed additional reports of torture, upon returning from leave in June 2007.
  • Maj Hudson held an open town hall type meeting with members of the MP Coy under his command in order to assuage fears of individual criminal liability relating to the role MPs played in transferring detainees to Afghan officials and allegations of torture.
  • Maj Hudson participated in a detainee committee to provide the Comd JTF-Afg with advice on the transfer decision.
    • He viewed the decision to transfer detainees primarily as one that focused on whether the detainee was a belligerent, and not on whether it was safe to transfer him.
    • Except during a limited period of time after the Graeme Smith articles were published, post-transfer risk of torture or abuse was not emphasized during these committee meetings.
    • He created a transfer matrix in order to document the advice provided to the Comd JTF-Afg in making a decision to transfer, hold or release detainees. The Complainants point out the transfer matrix created by Maj Hudson did not contain any space for assessing post-transfer risk of torture or abuse, whereas subsequent forms did contain such a space.
  • “Maj Hudson was aware that the CF had responsibility for ensuring that detainees were not transferred to risk of torture”.Footnote 1170

Based on this information, the Complainants submitted Maj Hudson should have made further inquiries or initiated an investigation into the legality of the transfer decisions. The Complainants submitted:

[...] despite his admitted awareness of reports and articles documenting torture of detainees, a general understanding that there were ongoing allegations of detainee abuse by the NDS, and his own MP detachment’s concern about personal liability for breaches of international law, Major Hudson made no efforts to inquire or investigate into whether past and ongoing orders to transfer detainees were legal. Moreover, he never sought any advice from the technical chain of command about whether ongoing transfers in the midst of allegations of torture required some sort of investigation.Footnote 1171

The Complainants also submitted Maj Hudson understood it was his duty as an MP to investigate any breaches of the laws of armed conflict or international law by a Canadian person under the MP’s jurisdiction. The Complainants submitted that, as TFPM, Maj Hudson had a responsibility to ensure that any investigation into such offences was initiated if there was a report of such conduct, or if he somehow learned of such conduct. The Complainants submitted Maj Hudson:

[...] generally understood that it would be a violation of international law to issue an order to transfer a detainee where there were grounds for believing that the detainee would be transferred to substantial risk of torture.”Footnote 1172

[...]

He also understood that with respect to discretion to start an investigation, a peace officer’s level of discretion is inversely proportional to the seriousness of the offence.Footnote 1173

The Complainants also took issue with the level of trust and deference that Maj Hudson placed in the chain of command and the Government of Canada to communicate allegations of torture. The Complainants noted Maj Hudson testified he would require “clear evidence” the Comd JTF-Afg intended to transfer a detainee to a risk of torture before he began an investigation. Although the Complainants conceded Maj Hudson later testified he would have to “formulate a belief or at least a reasonable suspicion” the Comd JTF-Afg intended to transfer to a risk of torture, they suggested the earlier statement is revealing.Footnote 1174 The Complainants submitted that:

[i]n short, Major Hudson simply trusted his commander to make correct decisions. However, there is no evidence that he made any inquiries whatsoever to support his assumptions that DFAIT was conducting adequate investigations, or that the [Comd JTF-Afg] had adequate information. There is no evidence that he had any knowledge of DFAIT’s activities or the Commander’s access to information. His assumption of best efforts and good faith conduct are not based on any actual knowledge, but simple faith.Footnote 1175

[...]

In this case, Major Hudson’s approach to policing started off with the strong presumption that there was no misconduct, [...]Footnote 1176

The Complainants pointed to the following factors as evidence of Maj Hudson’s failure to investigate:Footnote 1177

  • He did not investigate or make any inquiries into the legality of any orders to transfer detainees to Afghan custody.
  • He did not direct anyone under his command to investigate or make inquiries into the legality of any orders to transfer detainees to Afghan custody.
  • He did not make any recommendation to the NIS to investigate the legality of the transfers.
  • He did not ask any questions to determine if there was a pattern of activity – such as continued transfers in light of ongoing reports of post-transfer torture – which might suggest misconduct.
  • He did not ask any questions to determine whether allegations of abuse were substantiated; rather, he assumed he would be informed if they were substantiated.

The Complainants submitted, “given Maj Hudson’s awareness of historical and ongoing reports of detainee torture by Afghans, his failure to make even the most basic inquiries into the legality of the transfer orders is objectively unreasonable. [...] Given the seriousness of the allegations at issue, Major Hudson’s discretion to investigate is narrow, and his reliance on untested assumptions cannot be considered reasonable.”Footnote 1178

Submissions on Behalf of Maj B. Hudson

The submissions made on behalf of Maj Hudson pointed to a number of factors to demonstrate his actions were reasonable and met all professional standards.Footnote 1179 It was submitted Maj Hudson acted reasonably and appropriately in carrying out his policing mandate, as he did not receive a complaint or allegation regarding the legality of the command decisions to transfer detainees. It was also argued Maj Hudson had full confidence in the command decision making process based on his experience as an MP and as a CF member on operations. Similarly, it was argued Maj Hudson knew the Comd JTF-Afg placed a great deal of importance on the detainee issue and had no reason to doubt the appropriateness of the decisions to transfer detainees.Footnote 1180

In support of these submissions, counsel made several representations as to the state of Maj Hudson’s knowledge. Counsel for Maj Hudson submitted:

Maj Hudson was aware that a complaint had been filed with this Commission in 2007 but was not aware of the details and did not see a copy of it. He was aware of the OP Camel Spider investigation which was ongoing while he was in Afghanistan. He did review one US State Department [country] report during pre-deployment and was aware of historical issues with regard to the treatment of detainees.Footnote 1181

Counsel also submitted:

To Maj Hudson’s knowledge, there were no concerns regarding post-transfer treatment of detainees prior to April 2007. Maj Hudson was aware of the Graeme Smith article, and had been advised in advance that the article would be published. Once published in the Globe and Mail, it was immediately brought to his attention. He was also provided with a copy of a report from the April 25, 2007 prison visit conducted by Gavin Buchan (of DFAIT) and a CSC representative (“Buchan report”).Footnote 1182

It was acknowledged Maj Hudson knew of the 3 May 2007 Supplementary Arrangement, but was not involved in its negotiation. Maj Hudson noted that under the Supplementary Arrangement, he was responsible for providing the AIHRC with information regarding detainees and he knew “[…] that the AIHRC was one of the checks and balances in place to ensure that detainees were not mistreated.”Footnote 1183

Maj Hudson noted he met with the AIHRC on two separate occasions, and was also present at a meeting between Minister O’Connor and Engineer Noorzai of the AIHRC in March 2007 where detainee treatment was discussed. However, Maj Hudson was never privy to AIHRC reports about detainee abuse, and the AIHRC did not raise any concerns regarding its ability to access detainees during monitoring visits during those meetings.Footnote 1184

Counsel submitted Maj Hudson believed Canada “[…] was responsible for detainees post-transfer”, and if those detainees were mistreated, then Canada had a state responsibility to reassert custody or to fix the issue in some other way. Accordingly, Maj Hudson did not consider this to be a CF or MP responsibility. Maj Hudson also believed the 3 May 2007 Supplementary Arrangement met Canada’s international legal obligations and was designed to protect detainees transferred to Afghan authorities. It was also noted Maj Hudson knew the ICRC, AIHRC, DFAIT and CSC visited the Afghan authorities, and he expected all but the ICRC to report any problems relating to detainees to the CF.Footnote 1185

In regards to the monitoring role of DFAIT, counsel stated:

Maj Hudson also knew that the new arrangement negotiated in May 2007 provided for monitoring and that DFAIT had committed to doing this monitoring. He was satisfied that DFAIT was responsible for the issue (of detainee treatment post-transfer), had developed SOPs which demonstrated their capability to conduct the monitoring visits and he trusted their ability to deal with the issue. All of this information gave him confidence in the monitoring system and satisfied him that the risk of torture was low enough that transfers could proceed.

Maj Hudson did not receive information about post-transfer detainee issues. He was aware that DFAIT was conducting site visits but did not receive site visit reports.Footnote 1186

Counsel submitted Maj Hudson was not responsible to ensure that Canada met its international legal obligations regarding post-transfer treatment of detainees. Counsel further noted “[t]here were other Canadian government agencies, such as DFAIT and CSC, which were specifically responsible for that.” Counsel reiterated Maj Hudson trusted the whole-of-government approach adopted by the Government of Canada in addressing the detainee issue, and noted Maj Hudson knew of the NIS investigation into the Attaran complaint in support of this assertion.Footnote 1187 Additionally, counsel stated Maj Hudson knew that the Comd JTF-Afg was advised by “a dedicated legal advisor and expected he was getting legal advice on detainee issues.”Footnote 1188

It was submitted Maj Hudson could not investigate the Comd JTF-Afg transfer decisions without probable cause. Maj Hudson submitted “[t]he threshold for commencing an investigation would be a complaint against the Commander or information of a pattern of activity by the Commander which demonstrate that he had likely committed an offence.” Maj Hudson said in testimony he would not investigate an operational command decision unless the decision led to the commission of a criminal act. Counsel submitted “Maj Hudson would consider the severity of the alleged offence, whether there was a substantive complaint and whether there was clear evidence the Commander had intent to transfer detainees knowingly to torture” when deciding whether to begin an investigation into the transfer decisions. Maj Hudson reiterated he “would not investigate an operational command decision unless the decision could constitute a criminal act.”Footnote 1189

In determining if the Comd JTF-Afg had possibly committed a criminal act, Maj Hudson said he would have considered whether the Commander had committed a crime by knowingly transferring a detainee into a condition of torture. Maj Hudson submitted “[i]f the Commander did not know or did not intend the torture to happen, then there would be no evidence of an offence having been committed.”Footnote 1190 Maj Hudson also considered reports of abuse and torture occurring before the new transfer arrangement of May 3, 2007 not to be indicative of the commission of an offence because the new transfer arrangement was intentionally created to improve the existing arrangement.

Maj Hudson also submitted that if he had received a report a CF member had transferred a detainee knowingly to a risk of torture, or he knew of such an offence being committed, he would have caused an investigation to be commenced by the appropriate body. Maj Hudson also submitted he would have sought legal advice regarding any potential offence that arose. However, he maintained he never received any such allegation, and he never formed a reasonable suspicion the Comd JTF-Afg had ordered the transfer of detainees knowing they could face torture or abuse. Maj Hudson submitted he had constant trust in the Commander and his trust was affirmed in that the Commander demonstrated his willingness to cease transfers when allegations of torture arose. Accordingly, Maj Hudson submitted he acted in a reasonable manner and his actions met the professional standards expected of an MP.

Conclusions Regarding Maj B. Hudson

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Hudson’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We repeat here that the applicable legal standard is reasonableness, not perfection, or even the optimum as viewed with the benefit of hindsight. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • Maj Hudson was aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, to take steps to cause the investigation of allegations of breaches of international law.
  • Maj Hudson demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees, including the nature of Canadian responsibility for detainees post transfer.
  • Maj Hudson did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees in general, or to transfer any detainee in particular, could be illegal. He only had some knowledge of the substance of the complaint to this Commission in February 2007, the Federal Court injunction process, and the media attention the detainee question received. He reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he observed his Commander and the Government taking to guard against potential mistreatment of detainees following transfer, such as the AIHRC monitoring agreement put in place at the start of his rotation.
  • Maj Hudson did not neglect his responsibilities as a TFPM in order to avoid acquiring information about mistreatment of detainees post transfer. Maj Hudson made inquiries and generally involved himself in matters related to detainees, to the extent that he was reasonably able to do so. In particular, during the stoppage of transfers in late April/early May, he actively sought out information from his Commander and others about the propriety of the new transfer regime.
  • Maj Hudson was proactive in creating a form to document the Commander’s decision making process for transfers, again showing a willingness to engage in and improve that process.
  • Maj Hudson reasonably considered his Commander’s actions to have demonstrated a willingness to stop transfers where necessary, despite the operational obstacles this created.
  • When in June 2007, after returning from leave, he learned that allegations of mistreatment had been received following a site visit, it was reasonable for him not to harbour suspicions whether his Commander had engaged in illegal transfers. The Commission must, as far as possible, try to put itself into the shoes of Maj Hudson at the time and assess events through his eyes. These include his inherent trust in the Commander, whom he knew and with whom he worked. His opinion of his Commander’s trustworthiness and adherence to duty was a legitimate factor for him to consider. Further, the information available to him indicated that DFAIT had looked into the matter, and the fact that another Government agency appeared seized of the issue reasonably allayed any concerns he might have been expected to have.
  • Maj Hudson did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports from May onwards and C4 traffic pertaining to detainees. This was not due to personal failings on his part. Rather, it was mostly a consequence of the “siloing” phenomenon discussed earlier. In the absence of this information, and combined with his observations of the Commander’s prior willingness to stop transfers in the face of allegations of mistreatment, it was reasonable for Maj Hudson not to have suspicions his Commander was illegally ordering detainee transfers.
  • Maj Hudson did have some information indicating torture was a serious concern in Afghanistan, from sources such as the Complainants’ Federal Court action, his general understanding of the February 21, 2007 complaint to this Commission, the US State Dept report which he sought out and read, and the media attention given to the detainee transfer question. He had, on the other hand, information that the AIHRC was monitoring detainees post transfer. Furthermore, he had the evidence that as soon as the Globe and Mail allegations came out, his Commander had ceased transfers.
  • Maj Hudson believed his Commander was getting appropriate legal advice on the propriety of transfers, something that, on these facts, and in consideration of the other factors known to Maj Hudson, could reasonably have assuaged any concerns about the legality of the transfer orders.

Finding #1: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Hudson in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that Maj Hudson should have investigated his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer.

16.2 Chief Warrant Officer Barry Watson

CWO Watson joined the Canadian Forces as an infantryman in 1985, and stayed in the infantry until 1990 when he became an MP. He worked first as an investigator and basic patrolman. In 1994, he was promoted to Master Corporal, and was posted to 4 Wing, Cold Lake, Alberta, where he did duties as a patrolman and in security operations. In 1997, he was promoted to Sergeant and posted to Wainwright, doing police operations. From Wainwright, in 2001, he was promoted to the rank of Warrant Officer and posted to Dundurn, Saskatchewan as MP detachment commander. In 2004, he was promoted to Master Warrant Officer and posted to the NIS in the Western Region, Edmonton, Alberta. It was during this stint with the NIS he was sent to Afghanistan for his ROTO 3 tour. Upon his return from Afghanistan, he stayed in Edmonton until 2008, when he was promoted to Chief Warrant Officer. He then took on the position of Regimental Sergeant Major for 1 Military Police Unit, Edmonton, Alberta. As of 2008, he was no longer a member of the NIS.

During his career, CWO Watson completed four overseas postings, first in Cyprus in 1988, in Bosnia in 2000, in Israel/Syria in 2002, and his Afghanistan posting in 2007. In Afghanistan, CWO Watson was the NIS detachment commander. He described his mandate as being similar to a domestic mandate. He managed NIS operations in Afghanistan, including investigations of serious and sensitive matters. The big difference in theatre was that he also investigated personnel killed in action (KIAs) and escalations of force resulting in injury and death.

CWO Watson arrived in Afghanistan on January 31, 2007 and left theatre, as best he could recall, on August 8, 2007. The NIS offices were located at KAF, close to the detention facility. CWO Watson’s barracks were quite some distance from the facility.Footnote 1191

Unlike the TFPM in theatre, CWO Watson did not report up the technical chain to the CEFCOM PM. He had no relationship whatsoever with the CEFCOM PM, and could not even recall who held that position while he was in theatre. Instead, his operational command was his technical chain, and it went straight up to the Commanding Officer of the NIS, LCol (ret’d) Garrick. He was OPCON to the TFPM in theatre, which meant the TFPM provided administrative support and could employ the NIS for general military police duties if they were not occupied with NIS duties. This scenario did not arise for CWO Watson.Footnote 1192

CWO Watson’s dealings up the chain of command were first with Lt Utton (NIS) in Canada, with whom he had daily contact. His contact with LCol (ret’d) Garrick was via weekly teleconferences held with NIS detachments throughout the world. CWO Watson’s participation in those conferences was monthly rather than weekly because he became very busy.Footnote 1193

CWO Watson had no contact with the CFPM while in theatre aside from one email he recalled receiving.Footnote 1194 His contact with Maj Hudson was not very frequent, but they ran into each other informally once or twice a week. Generally speaking, Maj Hudson would not know what the NIS was investigating unless the investigation involved his own personnel, in which case he would be briefed.Footnote 1195

As NIS detachment commander in Afghanistan, CWO Watson was independent of the chain of command, but he did have a reporting relationship with the Task Force Commander because he briefed MGen (ret’d) Grant on NIS investigations being conducted that could possibly affect operations in theatre.Footnote 1196

A recurring theme in CWO Watson’s evidence was that the NIS detachment in theatre was seriously overworked. While four NIS members were deployed, the effective number, with leave and vacations, was three. That number was even reduced to two at one point because one member had to go home early for personal reasons.Footnote 1197

CWO Watson knew very little about the post-transfer treatment of detainees while in theatre. He was shown the February 21, 2007 complaint, but explained he had not heard about this complaint while in theatre, nor was he aware of its allegations even in a general sense. He only became aware of it when he learned after his return from theatre he was named as a subject.Footnote 1198

CWO Watson was aware of the Attaran complaint alleging mistreatment of detainees by MPs while in Canadian custody. That complaint spawned Operation Camel Spider. CWO Watson was heavily implicated with the information gathering process for Camel Spider, beginning shortly after his arrival in theatre. This was an information gathering role only, and did not involve providing any actual analysis. This analysis was done by the lead on the Camel Spider operation, Inspector Gfellner back in Canada. CWO Watson was “tasked to assist him in obtaining all the documentation and trying to locate the three detainees who were allegedly abused, as detailed in that complaint.” Indeed, he explained much of his time in Afghanistan would be consumed by trying to find and interview the detainees who were allegedly abused. The three detainees went into hiding, and were not located by CWO Watson during his tour.

During his time in theatre, CWO Watson was unaware of the ongoing Federal Court proceedings instigated by the Complainants Amnesty/BCCLA. He did not view the Globe and Mail articles written by Graeme Smith while he was in theatre. He was not aware they had come out, and did not even have a general sense of what they contained. He only read those articles for the first time in preparation for these hearings. He did not view any type of human rights reports or reporting on the situation in Afghanistan, such as the country reports from DFAIT, Mr. Colvin’s reporting, and reports from the US State Department, the United Nations, and the AIHRC.Footnote 1199 CWO Watson was also not aware of Canada’s agreement with the AIHRC with respect to post-transfer monitoring.Footnote 1200

CWO Watson was briefed on cultural issues before deployment, but beyond those briefings, did not accumulate any information about the human rights situation in Afghanistan. He did not do his own research on the question. He was, however, aware the detainee issue was a sensitive one, something he learned from a briefing he attended prior to deployment, which was given by Maj Hudson:

I was aware of the sensitivity of the detainee issue and that was because the Task Force Provost Marshal on pre-deployment training, Major Hudson, had briefed his upper levels of the chain of command. I was in attendance at that. He briefed us on the seriousness of the detainee issue as it pertained to the Canadians handling the detainees.

Because the Military Police were so intimately involved in the handling of detainees, he stressed the importance of the issue and how they, the Task Force MP company, had to get it right and how it could bring down his command and actually cause serious ripples in the government should they fail with regards to their mission of the handling of detainees.Footnote 1201

He was never told anything about what might happen to detainees after transfer,Footnote 1202 and he was not aware during ROTO 3 of concerns expressed by Maj Hudson’s soldiers about their personal liability relative to the detainee process.Footnote 1203

While in Afghanistan, CWO Watson did say he was privy to vague rumours of incidents regarding detainees post transfer, possibly from the outset of his time there. He could not recall the source of these rumours or their content.Footnote 1204 The rumours he heard did not relate to the possibility his Task Force Commander was making illegal transfer decisions.Footnote 1205

CWO Watson explained “I just don’t feel that the rumours that I hear would give enough credence for me to launch an investigation, enough to raise reasonable suspicion for me to launch an investigation on a specific rumour”.Footnote 1206 Indeed, he said even if he had read the Globe and Mail article in theatre, he would not have initiated an investigation as a result.Footnote 1207 He did not seem to perceive the article as raising allegations against his Commander, so much as raising questions about Afghan treatment of detainees.Footnote 1208 CWO Watson did agree he could look into the veracity of rumours, as an investigator, if he saw fit to do so. It was just not generally his practice to do so. The more sensitive an issue, the more likely he would be to investigate rumours, but, again, this would all depend on the nature of those rumours.Footnote 1209

CWO Watson advised the Commission he did not read or view any media pertaining to the Afghan detainee issue while in theatre. This was due to the sheer volume of work he had to do:

[…] every working hour in Afghanistan, my focus was on the duties at hand and I have already explained which duties those were.

When I was finished, when I did have some down time, I focused on my personnel who had been exposed to some traumatic events to make sure their well-being was taken care of. When that was done, I took the rare opportunity I could to speak with my family. When all that was said and done, I took some down time. If somebody suggested that I had time to sit down, put my feet on a desk and read a newspaper, it did not happen.Footnote 1210

CWO Watson knew the Technical Directive was the primary technical document governing his work as NIS detachment commander in theatre.Footnote 1211 He was referred in particular to para 11, which states the appropriate component of the MP or the CFNIS “shall” investigate allegations or instances of violations of the law of armed conflict or international law, and allegations of mistreatment of detainees in CF custody. CWO Watson agreed the language was quite specific, and obligatory. If a complaint of this nature had come to him, he would have put an entry into SAMPIS, whether an actual investigation occurred or not. He was also referred to para 14, which placed a responsibility on the TFPM to ensure the investigation of these types of allegations, even though such an investigation would “without question” fall under NIS jurisdiction. His view of the section was it required the TFPM to “notify the NIS to conduct an investigation” if he became aware of this type of information. Indeed, he explained he was “absolutely” dependent on the TFPM to alert him to these types of allegations given his NIS team’s enormous workload and given the TFPM’s greater access to information:

[…] he [the TFPM] had eyes on everything pretty much in Afghanistan. I was overwhelmed with the workload the NIS had given us. Overwhelmed might be strong, but there was a lot of work for me to do in Afghanistan, so I had to rely on the Task Force Provost Marshal and his personnel to alert me of any incidents that required NIS investigation.Footnote 1212

CWO Watson explained the NIS worked in a similar way even back in Canada. They relied on the military police at bases and detachments across the country to alert them to information. He personally was “not proactive in my role as the NIS detachment commander in Afghanistan as it related to policing. I relied on Complainants and military police to bring information to me so I could react accordingly and investigate the incident …” Clearly, one reason he had to rely on Complainants and other MPs was his workload in Afghanistan. He explained a major crimes unit like the NIS was never meant to be a proactive police organization: “We are always reactive. We react to the information we receive from other policing agencies, other military police, as well as Complainants who come directly to us. We don’t go out looking for work.”Footnote 1213

CWO Watson shed further light on the nature of his workload during ROTO 3. The Camel Spider investigation became high profile and consuming almost immediately upon his arrival. In addition, he had a murder investigation, a tent line shooting, 22 KIAs to retrieve, investigate and repatriate and investigations into numerous escalations of force resulting in injury or death. Again, he said it was “overwhelming”. Given that NIS numbers in Afghanistan were sometimes as low as two, CWO Watson said they had to get extra resources from the MP company and from a Strategic Advisory Team (SAT) in Kabul because they simply could not keep up: “…I didn’t have time to be out there asking questions or conduct[ing] proactive policing. I really did not. Our days started early in the morning and went 15, 16, 17 hours. There were time[s] when we were up 48 hours straight dealing with KIAs.”Footnote 1214

On this point, it should be noted the NIS in theatre was not only responsible for investigating escalations of force and KIAs. They also dealt with the undoubtedly difficult tasks of mortuary affairs and the repatriation of fallen CF members that flowed from these incidents.Footnote 1215

The TSO 321/321A did not apply to the NIS detachment in Afghanistan because they were not under the command of the Task Force Commander.Footnote 1216 The TSO was therefore not a document directed to him personally. CWO Watson was familiar with it only because of the work he did on Operation Camel Spider.Footnote 1217

CWO Watson knew from Maj Hudson’s pre-deployment briefing that, while in CF custody, Afghan detainees were to receive the same standard of treatment as prisoners of war under the Geneva Conventions. He simply had no idea how the detainee process worked.Footnote 1218 CWO Watson provided no advice to the Commander on detainee transfers and never discussed detainees with him, with the exception of the Camel Spider investigation. He also had “no involvement whatsoever with the process of handling or transferring of detainees.” Nor did he ever discuss the workings of the transfer process with Maj Hudson, or see any of the related forms. He did not even know that the detainee officer position in theatre existed, and only knew of the existence of a POLAD, but had no contact with him. In fact, CWO Watson ordered his personnel to stay away from the detainee transfer facility to ensure, if the NIS ever had to investigate a detainee incident, they would do so from an impartial perspective:

I ordered my personnel, directly ordered them, to stay away from the detainee compound because our office was in such close proximity. I knew the sensitivity of the detainee issue as it related to while they were in CF custody. I knew it was a serious issue and such a sensitive issue that should an allegation ever be brought forward by a detainee, we as the NIS would be tasked to investigate that. So because of that, I ordered every one of my personnel to stay away from the detainee compound, not to go near it, not to look at any monitors, don’t have anything to do with detainees.Footnote 1219

In this vein, CWO Watson explained he and Maj Hudson did not discuss detainees together while in theatre except in relation to Operation Camel Spider. They would have discussed this investigation to some extent because CWO Watson needed to go into Maj Hudson’s building to view related detainee files. CWO Watson most certainly did not ask Maj Hudson questions about how detainees were treated in custody, and did not interview Maj Hudson for Operation Camel Spider. They also never spoke about post-transfer treatment of detainees. CWO Watson followed the same order as his personnel, and stayed away from the detainee questions so as to maintain impartiality.Footnote 1220

CWO Watson understood Canada had a responsibility not to transfer Afghan detainees to harm. He knew this from his own common sense, and perhaps as a result of courses he had taken in military law and on the Geneva Conventions. This question of transfer to harm was not something he turned his mind to while in Afghanistan.Footnote 1221 He had no idea how the transfer decisions were made, and by whom. CWO Watson assumed it was ultimately the Task Force Commander’s call, and thought MPs had input since they were the ones who took the detainees into custody.Footnote 1222

CWO Watson did know detainee transfers stopped in April/May 2007. Being located near the detention facility, he could tell when there were detainees present by noting that guards were posted. When no guards were posted, there were no detainees: “I know that the MP company, the Task Force MP personnel, were getting worked pretty hard doing guard duties, and it’s through that knowledge that I became aware that the transfer of detainees had been halted.” He had no idea why they stopped. He could only assume, and he did at the time, something caused the Task Force Commander to halt transfers. He did not have any particulars, nor did he ask questions of other MPs. He could only guess the suspension lasted three weeks to a month.Footnote 1223

Similarly, CWO Watson did not know a new transfer agreement had been reached in May 2007. He described awareness of such things as being “outside the scope of my duties.” It was for this reason, he believed, the Task Force Commander or the Provost Marshal would not have seen the need to make him aware of these types of documents and information.Footnote 1224 He was aware some site visits to detainees were occurring, but did not know who was doing them and what the results were. He did know the visits took place to ensure Canadian-transferred detainees were treated properly. The information that visits were occurring came to him through general conversations with other MPs - not the TFPM, but perhaps a Sergeant Major in the MP company with whom he spoke.Footnote 1225

With respect to an alleged failure to investigate, CWO Watson said he never actually turned his mind to the legality of the detainee transfers while he was in theatre. He certainly never sought legal advice on the detainee process. More particularly, he said he never turned his mind to the question of MGen (ret’d) Grant’s legal liability for his transfer decisions while he was in theatre. This was because he “never had reason to suspect he was ultimately committing an offence.”Footnote 1226 CWO Watson, like Maj Hudson, had confidence in the commander, and was certain that the commander would not make decisions, such as transfer decisions, until he had the information required.Footnote 1227 CWO Watson did not turn his mind to this type of question while in theatre.Footnote 1228 Reasonable suspicion was his standard for starting an investigation.Footnote 1229

CWO Watson emphasized for the Commission that if somebody had come to him and laid a specific complaint saying the Task Force Commander was transferring detainees contrary to the law of armed conflict, he “would have had no choice but to investigate. I would have immediately engaged my chain of command and sought guidance on how to proceed with this. But that never happened with me […] and I had no reasonable suspicion to believe he did anything wrong whatsoever.”Footnote 1230 He agreed such an investigation might have required him to interview detainees in Afghan custody.Footnote 1231

CWO Watson knew the TFPM was part of the chain of command responsible for detainee transfers, and potentially liable himself, although, this is not something he thought about in theatre. He did not see any conflict for the TFPM in terms of reporting any illegal activity to the NIS. He felt it was every MPs responsibility to report illegal activity:

Because we as military police, part of our job is to police the Canadian Forces regardless of who is alleged to have committed an offence or what the offence is that is alleged to have been committed. It’s every MP’s responsibility to bring it to the attention of the appropriate investigative authority so that the proper investigation can be conducted.

[…] So I would expect anybody in that MP company to come forward to me or to my personnel and lay the complaint or bring the information forward should there have been one. I am satisfied that they would have done that.Footnote 1232

CWO Watson only learned about Operation Centipede after coming back from theatre. He was never involved in providing advice on the start-up or conduct of that investigation.Footnote 1233 He was also not aware LGen (ret’d) Gauthier requested that the NIS to investigate certain aspects of the Globe and Mail articles. CWO Watson explained he would not have been privy to this information, as this would have been handled by LCol (ret’d) Garrick, and tasked to someone else.Footnote 1234

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submit CWO Watson had sufficient knowledge, or had the means of knowing such information, that should have prompted him to begin an investigation into the legality of the Comd JTF-Afg transfer decisions. They submit, as one of the NIS detachment Commanders in Afghanistan during the timeframe for the complaint, CWO Watson’s failure to investigate constituted a “[...] gross breach of the professional standards by which society expects Military Police to conduct themselves.”Footnote 1235 The Complainants submit the following information, which CWO Watson acknowledged he knew, should have prompted CWO Watson to commence an investigation:

  • CWO Watson knew that proper treatment of detainees while in CF custody was of paramount importance to the TFPM, Maj Hudson, and would have significant implications for the Government of Canada.
  • CWO Watson was aware that transfers were suspended in May 2007, but did not know the reason that the Comd JTF-Afg suspended them.
  • CWO Watson was aware that the CF had a residual responsibility for ensuring proper treatment of Canadian-transferred detainees.

Implicit in their submissions, the Complainants take issue with the lack of awareness and, more significantly, curiosity regarding the treatment of detainees displayed by CWO Watson. The Complainants wrote in their final submissions:

CWO Watson claimed to have extremely limited knowledge about allegations of post-transfer torture and abuse of detainees. He was not aware of the fact or substance of the February 2007 Complaint. In particular, he claimed that while he was in Afghanistan he was not aware that there were allegations that MPs could potentially be held liable for Criminal Codeor service offences for complicity in post-transfer abuse. He was not aware that there was a proceeding in Federal Court seeking to halt detainee transfers. He was unaware of news accounts of detainee torture, such as the April 2007 articles in The Globe and Mail. He was entirely unaware of human rights reports from the AIHRC, UNHCHR, Amnesty International and the U.S. Department of State. CWO Watson was aware that “somebody” was visiting detainees after they were transferred to ensure that the detainees were “being treated fairly and properly”, but he did not know it was DFAIT, or that DFAIT prepared reports based on those visits.Footnote 1236

The Complainants were also very critical of CWO Watson’s testimony:

There were many problems with CWO Watson’s testimony and we find that it was unsatisfactory in many respects. At times, it was implausible and was contradicted by other evidence. [...] In our respectful submissions, CWO Watson’s testimony on these issues was a product of his determination to hold to his story, rather than an honest review of the events that transpired and a reflection upon his duties as a Military Police officer.Footnote 1237

In particular, the Complainants took issue with CWO Watson’s testimony regarding rumours of abuse of detainees. They submit CWO Watson initially testified that “while he was in Afghanistan he heard ‘vague rumours of incidents regarding the handling of detainees post-transfer’ but that he could not recall the details of those rumours.” The Complainants note CWO Watson admitted that there were rumours of abuse when he was confronted, during cross-examination, with transcripts of interviews with this Commission two years earlier.Footnote 1238

Accordingly, the Complainants submit “CWO Watson’s claim that he could not remember any details of the rumours was difficult to credit” and they assert accordingly CWO Watson knew detainees were rumoured to be abused, that he had a duty to make further inquiries, and he failed to do so.Footnote 1239

The Complainants believe little weight should be given to CWO Watson’s justifications for why he did not conduct further inquiries into the rumours. They submit CWO Watson’s first justification of ignorance and lack of specificity in the rumours is unreasonable, because the MP technical chain issued a technical directive that clearly contradicted CWO Watson’s reasons. Similarly, the Complainants submit CWO Watson’s second justification, that he did not have sufficient resources or mandate, is unreasonable because NIS officers are expected and trained to conduct investigations to a high standard despite the obvious difficulties when deployed in theatre of operations. The Complainants also submit CWO Watson’s claim he did not have the mandate to be proactive is contradicted by other NIS witnesses and by CWO Watson’s chain of command.Footnote 1240 Moreover, they state CWO Watson would not have had any inclination to investigate even if he did have greater time and resources.

The Complainants submit CWO Watson’s testimony suggested that he did not seem to understand that transferring detainees to the substantial risk of torture could be an offence. Accordingly, CWO Watson never turned his mind to whether or not he should be investigating the Comd JTF-Afg’s transfer decisions. Accordingly, they believe CWO Watson acted unreasonably and breached the professional standard expected of a senior MP.

Submissions on Behalf of CWO B. Watson

The submissions of CWO Watson point to a number of factors which, he submits, demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards.Footnote 1241 Counsel for CWO Watson emphasized the NIS detachment in Afghanistan was extremely small and had a very heavy workload. They argued, given the many demands placed upon the small NIS detachment, there was not sufficient time for CWO Watson to be curious about the treatment of detainees absent a complaint. In written submissions on behalf of CWO Watson, his counsel stated,

During [CWO Watson’s] tour, there were four NIS members in theatre responsible for the conduct of major criminal investigations, including investigations of CF members killed in action, and mortuary affairs.Footnote 1242

[...]

[...] As the equivalent of a major crimes unit, it is normal practice for the NIS to be reactive, particularly in Afghanistan where resources were limited and demands were heavy. [CWO Watson] did not have time to be curious about things that did not even raise a reasonable suspicion in his own mind.Footnote 1243

CWO Watson also pointed to the operational difficulties associated with conducting investigations. He stated in order to “leave the wire” he had to weigh the value of information that may be obtained against the real risk of endangering the lives of other CF members who are tasked with providing security for the investigators.Footnote 1244 In this regard, during his deployment to Afghanistan he left the wire only three times to assist with Operation Camel Spider. This argument implies CWO Watson acted reasonably by not forcing CF members to risk their lives needlessly.

CWO Watson submitted he had no knowledge of the allegations of abuse, and thus it would be unreasonable to expect him to initiate an investigation into a subject matter where he had no knowledge, complaint or allegation. CWO Watson stated he did not know the following:Footnote 1245

  • He did not know of the complaint filed with this Commission, until he was named as a subject.
  • He was not aware and did not read the newspaper articles while in Afghanistan.
  • He did not review any human rights reports by international bodies or DFAIT regarding conditions in Afghanistan.
  • He did not have access to the DFAIT site visit reports and was not briefed on the information contained therein.

CWO Watson also submitted he did not hear any rumours alleging the Comd JTF-Afg was committing “any breach of the law of armed conflict or transferring detainees into a real risk of torture.”Footnote 1246 However, CWO Watson noted he heard vague rumours regarding post-transfer issues but did not recall any details. CWO Watson was aware Canada had a residual responsibility to ensure that Canadian-transferred detainees were treated humanely and he knew someone, although he did not know who, was conducting post-transfer visits.Footnote 1247 In this regard, CWO Watson acknowledges he provided assistance to the NIS HQ in the Operation Camel Spider investigations by assisting in identifying and interviewing the detainees who were subjects of that investigation.Footnote 1248

CWO Watson noted the NIS detachment had no involvement in detainee handling or the transfer of detainees. CWO Watson submits that he specifically ordered the NIS investigators under his command to distance themselves from the detainee compound and detainees to preserve impartiality, in the event the NIS was called upon to conduct an investigation into allegations of detainee abuse.Footnote 1249

Similarly, he observed detainees were remaining at the Transfer Centre for longer periods and thus became aware transfers had been suspended in April or May 2007.
