He noted he had no knowledge of the reason for the suspension of transfers, but argued, in retrospect, the suspension of transfers would have given him confidence the Comd JTF-Afg was handling the transfer of detainees correctly.Footnote 1250

CWO Watson believed he lacked the authority or jurisdiction to investigate allegations of abuse of detainees in Afghan custody. He also indicated he did not believe the allegations contained in the newspaper articles were specific enough to raise a reasonable suspicion to his mind and thus would not have initiated an investigation, even if he had read them while in Afghanistan. Moreover, CWO Watson wrote:

[he] never had reason to suspect that the Task Force Commander was committing an offence. Nobody came to him and alleged that the Task Force Commander was transferring detainees contrary to the law of armed conflict. If they had, he would have investigated that complaint. He felt that the decisions the Commander was making were proper and that the Commander was getting all the information required to make his decisions.

As the NIS detachment Commander, CWO Watson was not responsible for oversight of the Commander’s operational decisions to ensure compliance with the law. CWO Watson would only become involved if there was some evidence which would lead to a reasonable suspicion that the Commander was engaged in illegal activity. No such evidence or information ever came to his attention.Footnote 1251

Thus, CWO Watson submitted that with no direct knowledge of allegations of abuse, given the demanding workload on the NIS, and the risk to CF members, it would be unreasonable for him to go chasing after vague rumours. Similarly, he lacked the jurisdiction to investigate allegations of abuse and never suspected the Commander of illegally transferring detainees to a serious risk of torture or abuse. Accordingly, CWO Watson told the Commission he acted reasonably as the NIS detachment Commander and met all professional obligations expected of an MP.

Conclusions Regarding CWO B. Watson

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that CWO Watson’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police member. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • CWO Watson understood what his obligations to investigate would have been pursuant to his Technical Directive while in theatre, if he had received a complaint about the Task Force Commander’s transfer decisions, or if he had developed a reasonable suspicion those decisions were somehow illegal.
  • CWO Watson knew Canada’s detainees were to be handled in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, and knew, from a common sense perspective, this included not transferring detainees to harm.
  • CWO Watson did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees in general, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He explained, despite his heavy workload, he would have been obligated to investigate a complaint the Commander was acting illegally if one had been made.
  • It is relevant to consider that CWO Watson was overwhelmed with the stressful workload he and his NIS detachment faced in Afghanistan, especially given the KIA and escalation of force investigations, and related duties. Given this workload, the limited resources, and the more reactive role of the NIS, it was reasonable that CWO Watson did not receive or try to seek out information in theatre about the detainee process and the treatment of detainees post-transfer. It was reasonable for him to expect others, such as the TFPM and the MP company, to bring information or concerns to him if they existed.
  • CWO Watson specifically took steps to keep the NIS detachment independent of the detainee transfer process in light of the allegations made by AIC/BCCLA in February 2007. This was sound from a policing perspective, but as a result he was not privy to information about the detainee process and had not acquired information about potential risks post transfer, other than through rumours. Those rumours did not directly call into question the legality of the Task Force Commander’s behaviour. Through no fault of his own, CWO Watson also did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports produced during his rotation. He knew site visits were occurring, and reasonably assumed this was to ensure proper treatment of detainees. CWO Watson knew transfers had stopped for a time in April/May 2007 but did not know why. His lack of knowledge about these matters was, however, reasonable given his workload and his reasonable expectation others more directly involved would brief him should there be policing concerns.

Finding #2: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Chief Warrant Officer Barry Watson in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that CWO Watson should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police member.

16.3 Major Michel Zybala

Major Michel Zybala was the Task Force Provost Marshal during ROTO 4. He first entered the Canadian Forces at age 17, and quickly became a reservist with the Governor General’s Foot Guards in Ottawa. He also spent four summers with the Red Guard (Garde en rouge) on Parliament Hill. It was in 1989 that he entered full-time into the Canadian Forces, as a member of the military police.

Maj Zybala’s career focus has been on security, intelligence, and detention operations. He was a staff officer at National Defence Headquarters in Ottawa, followed by three years in his first command position at a Canadian Forces detention barracks. His next command position was with an MP platoon at Valcartier, followed by a long period with the Canadian Forces intelligence services, both as detachment commander and operations officer at NDHQ in Ottawa. His third command position was as commander of the fifth MP unit in Montreal, where he was responsible for all military police in the Quebec sector.

Prior to 2007, Maj Zybala served on three operational tours prior to Afghanistan, the first in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as commander of the MP platoon in 1999/2000. His second tour, with intelligence services, was also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His third mission was to Kabul, Afghanistan in 2004, again with intelligence services.

His fourth command position and fourth operational tour was as commander of the MP company and Task Force Provost Marshal in Afghanistan. His training for the mission began in February 2007. He was deployed in August 2007, and returned in March 2008. The precise date for change of command from Maj Hudson to Maj Zybala was August 15, 2007. Maj Zybala’s Task Force Commander was MGen Laroche, and his CEFCOM PM was Maj Laflamme, both of whom have testified before this Commission.

Maj Zybala described his contact with Maj Laflamme as frequent, usually involving weekly telephone conversations, and more often if necessary. He also sent a monthly situation report (sitrep) to Maj Laflamme, as related in the latter’s evidence, and weekly reports dealing primarily with ongoing or completed criminal investigations. Maj Zybala said his contact with Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore (CFPM) was limited to two phone conversations.Footnote 1252

Maj Zybala took the initiative, prior to his deployment, to inform himself of issues related to the treatment of detainees and the conditions in prisons in Afghanistan. Based on his research, he understood Canada had what he often referred to as a residual responsibility towards detainees once transferred, which he described as follows:

[...] je crois que le standard légal c’est qu’on ne peut transférer un détenu si on croit qu’il y a un risque substantiel de torture.

  • Donc il y a une certaine responsabilité?
  • Résiduelle, oui.

[unofficial translation] [...] I think that the legal standard is that we cannot transfer a detainee if we believe that there is a substantial risk of torture.

  • So there is some liability?
  • Residual, yes.Footnote 1253

He also knew, specifically, this responsibility flowed from article 12 of the third Geneva Convention.Footnote 1254

Maj Zybala’s prior research involved reading, for example, the Graeme Smith Globe and Mail articles from April 2007. He did not view DFAIT, US State Department or UN reports, but did read at least one report from the AIHRC, which he downloaded from the AIHRC website. He took from that report the AIHRC was flagging problems that existed of abuse and torture in the Afghan prisons.Footnote 1255 Indeed, the report he consulted contained a chart with statistics on reports of torture by province in Afghanistan, with such reports in Kandahar province being double that of the next worst province. He was careful to point out, though, the statistics and reports were somewhat dated (from one to two years prior to his rotation) and, in his opinion, the situation in Afghanistan could change radically in only six months. The information in the AIHRC report was useful for him, but not determinative of the question of risk of torture and abuse.Footnote 1256

Maj Zybala also knew about the February 21, 2007 complaint before going into theatre. He knew it alleged the military police were perhaps committing a crime by assisting in the transfer of Afghan detainees to an unacceptable risk of torture. It appears he found the complaint, of his own accord, by going to the Complainants’ website.Footnote 1257 From it, he understood that the complaint raised the allegation – conveyed by the UN – that torture was common in NDS institutions. He knew this, and considered it to be historical information that did not necessarily have a bearing on what was happening in the present in Afghanistan. Again, he saw it as useful, but not determinative:

Effectivement. C’est de l’information historique qui est d’intérêt, mais non déterminante.

[unofficial translation]

That’s correct. It’s historical information that is of interest, but not determinative.Footnote 1258

As a result of this prior research, and the aforementioned sources, Maj Zybala therefore knew, prior to going into theatre, torture could occur in the Afghan prison system.Footnote 1259

During his training, Maj Zybala familiarized himself with the new Transfer Arrangement created in May 2007. He knew it put in place a site visit process to be carried out by DFAIT, and placed responsibility on the Afghans to investigate all allegations of mistreatment. He would not speculate as to the motive for establishing the new transfer regime. He only knew there had been a suspension of transfers in May 2007. In general, he felt the new arrangement satisfied Canada’s obligations under international law, ensuring, as he understood was required, that Canada’s detainees were treated in accordance with the third Geneva Convention.Footnote 1260 He was also aware there was an arrangement with the AIHRC with respect to reporting on mistreatment of Canadian-transferred detainees, but never saw reports or heard from them in this respect during his time in theatre.Footnote 1261

Maj Zybala was aware of the applicable technical directive during his timeframe in Afghanistan. In similar fashion to Maj Hudson, he described the necessity to converse with the NIS representatives in theatre were there to be a question as to whether the NIS or the regular MP platoon had the mandate to investigate any particular offence, with the debate centering on the serious and sensitive nature of the investigation.Footnote 1262 This is a reference to para 11 of the various Technical Directives.

Maj Zybala also knew if he became aware of a possible violation of international law in theatre, it would be his job to refer this to the NIS.Footnote 1263 He was attuned to the possibility the detainee transfer process potentially implicated the Task Force Commander and the chain of command, in a legal sense. He viewed the directive from LGen (ret’d) Gauthier to MGen Laroche while in theatre, including paragraph 24 of that directive, which sets out this potential liability.Footnote 1264 In fact, it appears he considered himself potentially subject to the same or similar liabilities as part of that same chain of command. He did not perceive, however, a conflict of interest in the fact he might have been required to report the illegal activity of that chain of command to the NIS for investigation.Footnote 1265

Maj Hudson briefed Maj Zybala prior to their exchange of command. However, he did not convey that he was unduly concerned about the post-transfer process. He may, though, have learned from Maj Hudson there had been one suspension of transfers. He understood the suspension was to allow for a period of adjustment and transition to the new regime. Maj Hudson did not speak to him about allegations that had been received from former CF detainees.Footnote 1266

While in theatre, Maj Zybala followed, obviously from a distance, the ongoing proceedings in Federal Court, commenced by the Complainants.Footnote 1267

Unlike Maj Hudson, Maj Zybala’s troops did not come to him with concerns about their liability with respect to detainees, or about what was going on in Federal Court. If such discussions did occur, they were brief and “en passant”.Footnote 1268 In fact, the situation was reversed somewhat. He was the one who was personally a little worried about his potential liability in theatre. This caused him to read up on the applicable international law before he went into theatre, and to brief his troops during training on the importance of treating detainees well.Footnote 1269 His efforts to read up on the human rights situation and the legalities of the transfer regime were grounded in his personal concerns, but also in the general curiosity he felt a military person should have.Footnote 1270

While in theatre, his troops never advised him that detainees had expressed a fear of torture or mistreatment by the NDS if transferred. However, he confirmed Capt Bouchard’s testimony that at least two detainees communicated that they would have preferred to die rather than be transferred to the NDS because they did not have the money to bribe their way out of prison. He described the Afghan request to be killed as a typical Afghan reaction:

  • Est ce que vous avez déjà été mis au courant que des détenus auraient dit, par exemple, qu’ils préféraient mourir que d’être transférés?
  • Oui.
  • Oui? Par qui?
  • Ça aurait été par le Capitaine Bouchard, qui lui était présent très souvent aux transferts. Il m’a rapporté un incident en particulier dont je me souviens; c’est que deux détenus avaient été informés du fait qu’ils allaient être transférés au NDS, et avaient dit qu’ils préféraient mourir. Je vous dirais que c’est là une réaction assez typiquement afghane et que j’ai vue souvent à Kabul en 2004. C’est la réaction assez typique d’un Afghan, lorsque contrarié par un Occidental, surtout quand vous le traitez de menteur. La réaction souvent est « Bien si vous me croyez pas, tuez moi, tuez moi. J’exige d’être tué ».
  • Mais là vous le traitez pas de menteur, là?
  • Non, mais ce qui les achalait c’était pas le fait qu’ils avaient peur du NDS, mais qu’ils n’avaient pas l’argent nécessaire pour donner des pots de vin au NDS pour se faire libérer. Ce n’était pas une question de peur du NDS, mais nous avons tout simplement pas les fonds monétaires pour nous permettre les pots de vin.
  • Est ce qu’ils vous ont dit ça?
  • C’est exactement ce qu’ils ont dit à l’entrevue, au moment du transfert.
  • Ils ont dit ça à M. Bouchard? Est ce qu’ils ont dit qu’ils avaient peur de mourir, ou qu’ils avaient pas l’argent?
  • Non, ils ont dit qu’ils avaient pas l’argent. Ils préféraient la mort, mais n’avaient pas peur de mourir. Comme je vous dis, c’est une réaction typiquement afghane.

[unofficial translation]

  • Were you ever made aware that some detainees had supposedly said, for example, that they preferred to die rather than to be transferred?
  • Yes.
  • Yes? By whom?
  • That would have been by Captain Bouchard, who attended transfers very often. He told me about an incident in particular that I remember; two detainees had been informed that they were going to be transferred to the NDS, and had said that they preferred to die. I would say that it’s a fairly typical Afghan reaction that I often saw in Kabul in 2004. It’s the fairly typical reaction of an Afghan when upset by a Westerner, especially when you call him a liar. Often the reaction is “Well, if you don’t believe me, kill me, kill me. I demand to be killed”.
  • But there you’re not calling him a liar are you?
  • No, but what bothered them was not the fact that they feared the NDS, but that they didn’t have the money to bribe the NDS to secure their release. It wasn’t a question of fear of the NDS, but we simply do not have the funds for bribes.
  • Did they tell you that?
  • It’s exactly what they said at the interview, at the time of transfer.
  • They said that to Mr. Bouchard? Did they say that they were scared to die, or that they didn’t have the money?
  • No, they said that they didn’t have the money. They preferred death, but were not scared of dying. Like I told you, it’s a typically Afghan reaction.Footnote 1271

Whether the interpretation of the Afghan detainees’ reactions was right or wrong, it appears both Maj Zybala and Capt Bouchard took from the detainees’ comments, not that they were frightened of NDS mistreatment or torture, but that they feared indefinite imprisonment due to an inability to bribe their way out of the Afghan prison system.

Maj Zybala was sufficiently concerned about this question of detainees paying their way out of custody that he raised it within the command structure and with members of the Manley Panel when they came to Afghanistan to inquire into Canada’s future role.Footnote 1272

Maj Zybala was also receiving information during his time in theatre from Ms. Garwood-Filbert of Correctional Service Canada. She advised Maj Zybala the situation in the Afghan prisons was improving.Footnote 1273

The ROTO 4 TFPM was questioned in a general sense about the nature of his involvement with the decision making process for transfers, in particular with respect to assessments of risk to detainees post transfer. He informed the Commission he was, indeed, consulted on detainee issues, but only intermittently, and never on the question of the risks post transfer to detainees.Footnote 1274 In contrast to MGen Laroche’s perception, but in keeping with BGen Juneau’s evidence, Maj Zybala said no advisory team for transfers existed in any structured sense. He said each advisor with a role in detainee affairs – the MPs, intelligence, legal - would provide their input separately. He did have occasion to meet with his Commander personally about detainee matters, such as on one occasion where it was suggested a Canadian soldier mistreated a detainee, but he said no committee meetings occurred of the nature that General Laroche’s evidence might have led one to believe.Footnote 1275

Maj Zybala agreed if he became aware of mistreatment post transfer he would have an obligation to advise the General.Footnote 1276 That said, he did not become aware of any such information. Moreover, while he knew visits were occurring, including capacity building visits, he did not have access to any actual reports:

Parce que généralement qu’est ce qui se passait, c’est que les visites étaient faites en conjonction avec ce qui s’appelait « capacity building visits », par le membre des Services correctionnels du Canada.

Alors les équipes comportaient des gens de plusieurs sources: Services correctionnels, Affaires extérieures, GRC, etc.

  • Et de quelle façon vous participiez ou vous étiez mis au courant de ce qui se passait ou des rapports?
  • Je n’avais pas accès aux rapports.
  • Vous n’aviez pas accès d’aucune façon?
  • Non.

[unofficial translation]

Because typically what happened was that visits were made in conjunction with what was called “capacity building visits”, by the member of Correctional Services of CanadA. So the teams included people from many sources: Correctional Services, Foreign Affairs, RCMP, etc.

  • And how did you participate or how were you made aware of what was happening or of the reports?
  • I didn’t have access to the reports.
  • You had no access at all?
  • No.Footnote 1277

Maj Zybala knew, to some degree, the distribution of the site visit reports. It appears he deduced this understanding from his review of the DFAIT Standard Operating Procedures. He did not meet with any of the individuals to whom the reports were distributed, such as the POLAD and the deputy commander, to specifically discuss the results. They met, instead, at the weekly “groupe d’ordres” referred to by MGen Laroche in his testimony. These meetings rarely involved discussing detainee matters, and they never appear to have involved the discussion of the particular site visit reports.Footnote 1278 Moreover, no one ever told him directly about the site visits while he was in theatre, with the exception of the November 5, 2007 site visit.

Maj Zybala did end up seeing some site visit reports, but only because he specifically sought them out on the internet, from the Complainants’ website. It is unclear whether he did this while in Afghanistan, or shortly after his return. In any event, he viewed those reports sometime in 2008, either towards the end of his rotation or immediately after his return from theatre. This was a point in time where transfers had long been stopped, and were not restarted until a series of ameliorative measures had been put in place.Footnote 1279

The article by Michèle Ouimet came out in late October 2007, reporting on allegations of abuse from Canadian-transferred detainees. Maj Zybala’s said he did not have a recollection of this article, although his evidence was somewhat confusing in this respect. The following extracts from his testimony may be indicative of the fact he knew the article existed, but for whatever reason declined to consider its contents:

[unofficial translation of responses]

  • Tab 6. This is the La Presse article that was brought to your attention by Commission Counsel, by Michele Ouimet.

    […] Now if you just look in this report, in the second and third paragraphs, there are some very serious allegations of torture.

    You testified before this was not brought to your attention, while you were in theatre?
  • Je ne crois pas que cet article a attiré mon attention, non.
  • I don’t think that this article caught my attention, no.
  • Now you are not copied on any of these documents or e mails, Major, but there was a lot of activity in theatre with the Commander and others about this newspaper article. We are aware of it.

    I think Laroche might have even testified that he had a meeting about it. You were not part of those discussions?
  • Non.
  • Given your curiosity though about the issue, Major, I gather you probably would have been curious to see this while you were in theatre, is that fair to say?
  • Pas nécessairement. Il y a certains auteurs que je ne lis pas.
  • Not necessarily. There are some authors that I don’t read.
  • But you were going -- You were checking out my client’s Website regularly to see what was new about --
  • H’m.
  • -- the prisoner litigation, the Afghan detainee litigation.

    I gather that was because you were curious a bit about what information was out there about abuse or what allegations my clients were raising about abuse of detainees?
  • La raison que j’ai été surtout sur le site Web de vos clients, c’est que c’était une affaire qui était en cour, et donc à mes yeux, plus intéressante.
  • The reason for which I went mostly to your clients’ website was that it was a case that was before the courts and, for me, more interesting.
  • So a newspaper reporter travels to Kandahar in October, 2007, while you are there, and she interviews a number of former Canadian Forces prisoners who claim that they were beaten with electrical cables, subjected to electric chocks, deprived of sleep, hit with bricks, don’t those

    Wouldn’t those allegations have caused you concern, Major?
  • La différence entre un article de journal -

    Pour répondre à la question, non. La raison que j’étais plus intéressé par qu’est ce qui se passait en Cour fédérale est que dans un processus judiciaire, il y a un échange entre deux parties qui ont tendance à se contrebalancer.

    Ça, c’est un article de journal, ce n’est pas la même chose.

    Par exemple, juste en lisant, il y a une couple de faits que je trouve un peu inusité.

    L’idée par exemple que les détenus ont passé par la base des Forces américaines spéciales, non. Ils seraient venus directement chez nous.
  • The difference between a newspaper article To answer the question, no. The reason for which I was more interested in what was happening before the Federal Court is that in a judicial process, there’s an exchange between two parties who tend to offset each other. That, that’s a newspaper article, it’s not the same thing. For example, just when reading it, there are a couple of facts that I find a little strange.

    For example, the idea that the detainees went through the Special American Forces base, no. They would have come directly to us.Footnote 1280

This exchange leaves the Commission with the impression Maj Zybala knew to some degree about this newspaper article, but either declined to look at it or placed no stock in it - it is difficult for the Commission to conclude one way or the other. In any event, it was not long after this article came out that Maj Zybala learned of the November 5 site visit and that transfers would be suspended.

The November site visit was the only site visit that Maj Zybala learned of, prior to the November 2007 suspension of transfers. He did not view the site visit report per se but was made aware verbally of the results.Footnote 1281 This was the report in which DFAIT officials documented evidence from a detainee of physical scarring and found the implements of torture under a chair in the place indicated by the detainee. In addition, the detainee provided a verbal account of his torture. As described in the following passage, Maj Zybala learned about this site visit on November 6, 2007, in a meeting convened specifically for that purpose by Col Juneau, the acting Commander at the time. At this meeting, Col Juneau informed those present that transfers would be suspended:

J’ai été mis au courant de cet incident le 6 de novembre. Spécifiquement, c’était une réunion qui a été appelée par le Colonel Juneau. Présents à cette réunion étaient en toute évidence moi même, le Colonel Juneau, l’Officier de détention le Major Boiteau, le PolAd Mr. Ed Jager, l’aviseur légal qui, à ce moment là, était le Capt(N) McKnight qui remplaçait le lieutenant Colonel Tremblay qui était en vacances et je crois que c’est tout.

  • Qu’est ce qui est survenu suite à cette rencontre là?
  • Essentiellement, le Colonel Juneau a ouvert la réunion en disant qu’une visite de la part du Ministère des Affaires extérieures avait déterminé qu’il y avait des raisons fort probables de croire qu’un détenu avait été maltraité et qu’il cherchait un avis quant à la procédure à suivre. Et en fin de compte qu’est ce qui est arrivé c’est que le Colonel Juneau a pris la décision de suspendre les transferts.

[unofficial translation]

I was apprised of this incident on November 6. Specifically, it was a meeting that was called by Colonel Juneau. In attendance at that meeting were I, obviously, Colonel Juneau, the detention officer Major Boiteau, the PolAd Mr. Ed Jager, the legal advisor who, at the time, was Capt(N) McKnight, who was replacing Lieutenant Colonel Tremblay who was on holiday, and I think that’s it.

  • What happened after that meeting?
  • Essentially, Colonel Juneau opened the meeting by saying that a visit from the Department of External Affairs had determined that there were very probable reasons to believe that a detainee had been abused and that he was looking for advice regarding the procedure to be followed. And eventually what happened is that Colonel Juneau made the decision to suspend the transfers.Footnote 1282

At that meeting with Col Juneau, Maj Zybala’s recollection was that the reasons for suspension were only discussed in the sense it was conveyed to him the allegations received on November 5, 2007 were credible. As he put it, Col Juneau had reached the decision to suspend transfers, and in his view, this was the legal and correct thing to do. It even appears Maj Zybala concurred with the opinion that stopping the transfers was the right thing to do:

Ça n’a pas été discuté avec moi autre que, à la réunion, si je me souviens bien, on avait discuté du fait que c’était -- il y avait des allégations crédibles de mauvais traitement.

Le Colonel Juneau avait décidé de suspendre et mon impression -- mon intervention c’était que c’était effectivement exactement ce qui était requis de notre part pour rencontrer nos obligations sous la loi, le Droit humanitaire international.

[unofficial translation]

It was not discussed with me except that, at the meeting, if memory serves, we had discussed the fact that it was there were credible allegations of mistreatment.

Colonel Juneau had decided to suspend and my impression my intervention was that it was effectively exactly what was required on our part to satisfy our obligations under the law, international humanitarian law.Footnote 1283

Maj Zybala was not privy to the discussions occurring prior to this meeting relating to the Commander and the Deputy Commander’s concerns that transfers might not be able to proceed. He was not privy to the draft letter dated November 4, 2007 in which those concerns were set out, where the conclusion was that the light was amber for future transfers, but that they could, for the time being, continue. He did not know there were concerns about the frequency of DFAIT visits prior to November 5, 2007. Nor was he aware of the subsequent, related correspondence.Footnote 1284

Thus, Maj Zybala did not view any of the site visit reports until he looked them up for himself on the internet, well past the point when transfers were stopped. He only heard directly about the results of the November 5, 2007 visit. He was not privy to the correspondence on the precariousness of the transfer process in October 2007, and he was not privy to discussions on this point that occurred with MGen Laroche and Col Juneau, and others. Nor did he view or hear about the details of the site visits that occurred prior to his rotation, at least not until he viewed certain site visits on the internet.Footnote 1285 He also heard nothing about any type of investigation conducted by DFAIT or others into the September allegations and the appropriateness of continued transfers.Footnote 1286

Maj Zybala explained why it did not surprise him the site visit reports were not shared with him. First, he thought the mandate to investigate any allegations received during site visits rested with DFAIT. Beyond that, he also knew of the phenomenon of compartmentalization in military affairs. From his point of view, it was to be expected these reports would be compartmentalized, and he felt he did not need to see them so long as someone was dealing with the site visits and any related follow-up activities required.

Indeed, he did not think he would have been provided the reports, even if he had asked for them:

Après quatre ans dans le renseignement, je savais que ce serait des rapports qui seraient excessivement restreints.

[unofficial translation]

After four years in that area, I knew that they would be excessively restricted reports.Footnote 1287

Returning to Maj Zybala’s involvement with the transfer decision process, he testified he either did not view the risk assessment matrix, or if he did, he saw it once at a point in time the Commission was not able to discern. Other than potentially one time, he viewed only the paper portion of the decision making process entitled the “Commander’s Review”. This portion did not contain any type of assessment of the post-transfer risk scenario.Footnote 1288 As noted, in the evidence from BGen Juneau, the Risk Assessment Matrix was only in development prior to November 5, 2007, and was not used until the start of transfers in late February/early March 2008. At that point in time, Maj Zybala was about to leave theatre. It was also a point in time where significant, new steps had been taken to improve the transfer process before starting up again.

Maj Zybala’s confidence in the transfer regime, from a legal perspective, was also buttressed for him by the conclusions of the Manley Report. He was interviewed by the Panel members but did not recall speaking to them about post-transfer concerns, except perhaps indirectly. The report reached the conclusion that Canada’s handling of detainees met international standards. Maj Zybala read the report while in theatre, and would have viewed this conclusion around January or early February 2008.Footnote 1289

Major Zybala was generally well informed of the measures put in place before transfers recommenced at the end of February 2008. He learned through classified military emails that the following measures had been implemented:

  • a more robust site visit regime, with different timing
  • RCMP involvement with mentoring for NDS interrogators
  • AIHRC training of NDS re human rights values
  • cameras installed in interview rooms
  • the dismissal of one NDS official
  • other similar measuresFootnote 1290

Once visits started up in March 2008, Maj Zybala was again not privy to the results. Indeed, by early March 2008 he was back in Canada.Footnote 1291

Maj Zybala never asked the NIS to investigate a question related to post-transfer treatment of detainees, nor did he ever hear the NIS was conducting such an inquiry. His contact with MWO (ret’d) Girard, the ROTO 4 NIS Detachment Commander, was fairly frequent, but he never discussed post-transfer treatment of detainees with him while in theatre.Footnote 1292 Nor did he ever discuss the November 2007 stoppage with MWO (ret’d) Girard, although he did recall a discussion about potential abuse by Canadians of a detainee.Footnote 1293 In terms of NIS access to information, he explained the NIS members were rarely present at the weekly meetings with the Commander (the “groupe d’ordres”). They therefore depended on the TFPM and the detainee officer for information on detainees.Footnote 1294

While he did not provide as much detail as Maj Hudson, Maj Zybala’s analysis of the legality of the Commander’s transfer decisions basically boiled down to the principle that, on a prospective basis, he saw no evidence the Commander ordered a transfer where he believed there was a substantial risk of torture.Footnote 1295 He was asked specifically about the fact it was General Laroche who ordered the transfer of the individual interviewed on November 5, 2007, who was in all likelihood tortured. Maj Zybala provided a reasoned analysis as to why his General did not need to be investigated for that transfer decision. This particular answer was based on the assumption that he knew about the September 2007 allegations of abuse which, of course, he did not:

[unofficial translation]

  • And this is a man that we know who was transferred by Commander Laroche, and that we now know - or in all likelihood he was in fact tortured.

    Do you know who inquired into whether the Commander or any potential legal liability for that transfer decision?
  • À ma connaissance, aucune personne n’a évalué le potentiel qu’il avait mal agi. Et encore une fois, quand vous évaluez le risque à la torture, c’est une évaluation prospective, non rétrospective.
  • To my knowledge, no one assessed the possibility that he acted badly. And again, when you assess the risk of torture, it’s a prospective, not a retrospective, assessment.
  • All right. But Major, the last document I took you to, even the General himself felt that at best the light was amber. That’s his own assessment. So even in his own mind he thought there was some concern. Is that fair to say?
  • Absolument. Et ça c’était de façon pour évaluer prospectivement d’autres cas de transfert dans le futur, pas dans le passé. Il se peut très bien, lisant ce que j’ai lu dans ces documents, que même sans cette allégation, le général Laroche aurait suspendu les transferts. Lisez entre les lignes.
  • Absolutely. And that was so as to assess prospectively other transfer cases in the future, not in the past. It may well be, given what I’ve read in these documents, that even without that allegation, General Laroche would have suspended the transfers. Read between the lines.
  • Right.
  • de ce qu’il dit dans ce document. Nous n’aurions eu absolument aucune allégation de torture de cet individu et le transfert a été suspendu quand même.
  • of what he says in this document. We would have had absolutely no allegation of torture of this individual and the transfer was still suspended.
  • No, but there were the two allegations of torture in September 2007. I have taken you to those; right? There were two allegations in September 2007.
  • Oui. (Yes)
  • And I appreciate you were not aware of them, no one told you about them while you were in theatre.
  • Mhmmm.
  • But presumably the commander would have been aware; right?
  • Oui. (Yes)
  • And on the basis of those allegations, if he had decided to suspend transfers, in all likelihood this man here would not have been transferred; is that fair to say? Just as a factual matter.
  • Non. Je ne suis pas d’accord. Parce qu’à ce moment là, les allégations qui étaient en septembre étaient des allégations.

    Ce que le commandant exprime de façon subséquente est:

    Je n’ai toujours pas reçu de rapport sur ces allégations quant à savoir si elles sont fondées ou non. En termes d’évaluer prospectivement des transferts futurs, je n’ai pas la confiance, alors, que je pourrais transférer et respecter le test légal.” [...]

    Je crois que c’est ça que le commandant est en train de dire.
  • No. I don’t agree. Because at that time, the allegations that were in September were allegations. What the commander says later is this: “I still haven’t received a report on these allegations as to whether they are substantiated or not. So in terms of assessing prospectively future transfers, I’m not confident that I could transfer and satisfy the legal test.” -- As read

    I think that this is what the commander is saying.Footnote 1296

Throughout his time in theatre, Maj Zybala never formulated a reasonable suspicion his Commander acted illegally. He knew the Commander had legal advice, and he had confidence in the decision making process. Since he never doubted the Commander’s integrity, in his mind, he never incurred the concomitant obligation to notify the NIS:

il n’est jamais rien arrivé pour que [je] doute de son intégrité. [...] Si j’avais formé une croyance raisonnable, oui. J’aurais été obligé d’approcher le SNE pour demander une enquête.

[unofficial translation]

nothing ever happened to make me doubt his integrity[...].If I had formed a reasonable belief, yes. I would have been obligated to approach the NIS to request an investigation.Footnote 1297

Maj Zybala’s approach to what information one would require in order to establish an unacceptable risk of torture was a bit unclear to the Commission. He seemed to suggest during cross-examination by the Complainants, that reports of mistreatment from 20% of Canadian-transferred detainees would not represent a systemic problem in the Afghan prison system requiring that transfers be halted. He suggested the allegations would need somehow to be better substantiated before reaching such a conclusion, and the ratio would need to be up around 50%. He advised the Commission he acquired his particular analysis of the law from the UN’s Committee Against Torture Reports and his legal advisor.Footnote 1298

Maj Zybala offered a possible explanation as to how his CEFCOM PM, Maj Laflamme, did not learn about the November 6, 2007 suspension of transfers until early December, by way of the Monthly SITREP. Maj Zybala’s evidence was that this was a particularly intense period of time for him, as commander of the MP company. During ROTO 4, the military police began to be involved in mentoring Afghan police at Police Sub-Stations beyond the wire and much closer to harm’s way. While outside the wire during this timeframe, one of his MP soldiers was seriously wounded, another sustained a less serious injury. His soldiers also had to deal with the trauma of the death by IED of members of the ANP. Maj Zybala also went outside the wire during the time immediately after the halt in transfers, returning only at a point in time when Maj Laflamme was on leave. Maj Zybala took his leave following Maj Laflamme’s return. He therefore does not recall ever having discussed the transfer stoppage with Maj Laflamme.Footnote 1299 He also could not recall a conversation with Maj Laflamme in November 2007 in which Maj Laflamme asked about rumours of detainee abuse, although he said it was highly probable that the conversation happened.Footnote 1300

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submitted Maj Zybala bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. They believe he bore responsibility as one of the TFPMs at the time for the failure to investigate or inquire into whether past and ongoing transfer orders were legal. The Complainants argued in their written submission that Maj Zybala had knowledge of, or had the means of knowing, the following information which should have led him to conduct an investigation:

  • Maj Zybala conducted his own research on human rights conditions in Afghanistan prior to deploying to Afghanistan.
    • Maj Zybala read the Graeme Smith article and was aware of the allegations contained therein prior to deployment.
    • Maj Zybala visited the AIHRC website and reviewed their reports prior to deployment. In so doing, he learned the AIHRC documented ongoing torture of detainees in Afghan prisons.
    • Maj Zybala read the February 2007 complaint on one of the Complainants’ websites prior to deployment.
    • Maj Zybala was informed by Maj Hudson there had been one suspension of transfers during ROTO 3, but was not informed the suspension resulted from report of post-transfer torture and abuse.
    • Maj Zybala was aware the Complainants had begun a Federal Court proceeding involving allegations of detainee abuse.
  • Maj Zybala did not have access to the DFAIT site visit reports, except for that of 5 November 2007.
    • Maj Zybala first learned of the 5 November 2007 report in a meeting with Col Juneau, after which detainee transfers were suspended.
    • Maj Zybala understood the suspension likely occurred because the 5 November 2007 report contained credible allegations of mistreatment.
  • Maj Zybala continued to monitor the Federal Court proceedings while in Afghanistan, and upon his return to Canada, out of personal curiosity.
  • Maj Zybala continued to visit the BCCLA website while in theatre, reading about new developments in the Federal Court proceedings and viewing some of the primary source documents posted there.
  • Although the Comd JTF-Afg’s detainee committee was disbanded during Maj Zybala’s time in Afghanistan, he retained custody and control over the detainee database and still had access to detainee information, and the written advice provided to the Comd JTF-Afg regarding transfer decisions, despite the creation of the position of “detainee officer” during ROTO 3.
  • Maj Zybala conducted research on the requirements imposed by international law regarding the transfers of detainees. He believed Canada was prohibited from transferring detainees to a substantial risk of torture.
  • Maj Zybala indicated he undertook his own research into international law and the state of human rights in Afghanistan because he felt there was a reasonable apprehension there may be questions about his own liability in transferring detainees. Maj Zybala believed such curiosity and prudence were part of being a military police officer.Footnote 1301

Based on this information the Complainants submit Maj Zybala should have made further inquiries or initiated an investigation into the legality of the transfer decisions. The Complainants submitted:

Yet despite [Maj Zybala’s] curiosity about his own potential liability, his awareness of allegations of detainee abuse, and general understanding of international legal obligations, Major Zybala never assessed the possibility that the [Comd JTF-Afg] may have acted illegally in ordering the transfer of detainees. Major Zybala never requested that NIS undertake an inquiry or investigation into historical or ongoing detainee transfers. He never assessed whether Brig. Gen. Laroche may have acted illegally in ordering the transfer of the individual interviewed for the November 5, 2007 report.Footnote 1302

The Complainants submit Maj Zybala’s concern regarding the treatment of detainees was focused on his own potential liability, and that “…none of this concern played a role in how he carried out his policing duties as the commander of the Military Police in Afghanistan”.Footnote 1303

Additionally, the Complainants submit Maj Zybala placed too much reliance in assuming the Comd JTF-Afg was receiving DFAIT reports and making the correct decision with respect to transfers, and he never tested the veracity of that assumption. The Complainants submitted:

There is no evidence that either Major Zybala or any MPs under his command investigated or made any inquiries into the legality of any orders to transfer detainees to Afghan custody. Nor is there any evidence that he made recommendations to the NIS to investigate the legality of the transfers. He also gave no evidence showing that while he was in theatre, he was aware that any NIS investigations – or any investigations of any sort, for that matter – were taking place. As with Major Hudson before him, Major Zybala’s failure to make basic inquiries into the legality of the transfer orders is objectively unreasonable.Footnote 1304

Submissions on Behalf of Maj M. Zybala

The submissions on behalf of Maj Zybala pointed to a number of factors which, it is said, demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards.Footnote 1305 Maj Zybala submitted, although he had read the AIHRC reports, he understood them to be generalised reports of torture and mistreatment in Afghan prisons. He argued those reports were “…useful but not determinative of the situation in Afghan prisons…”, and the situation in Afghanistan was constantly changing.Footnote 1306 Maj Zybala noted he had not read reports from DFAIT, the US State Department, or the UN High Commission for Human Rights but acknowledged having read the Graeme Smith article.

Maj Zybala told the Commission he had conducted his own independent research into international law, and knew Canada had a responsibility “… to treat detainees humanly and that Canada could not transfer a detainee if there was a belief that there is a substantial risk of torture.”Footnote 1307 He acknowledged he was aware of the Supplementary Arrangement of 3 May 2007, and it was his belief the Supplementary Arrangement satisfied Canada’s international legal obligation.

Similarly, Maj Zybala advised he was generally aware that DFAIT was conducting post-transfer monitoring visits, but he was usually not privy to these reports due to the doctrine of “compartmentalization”. Maj Zybala submitted he did become aware of allegations of mistreatment in November 2007 when transfers were suspended, and he read some redacted DFAIT reports on the Complainant’s website. Maj Zybala pointed out the DFAIT reports on the Complainant’s website had the date redacted, and said he would not know, conclusively, if they related or not to monitoring visits during his rotation.

Maj Zybala also stated, although he “[…] had some general knowledge of general conditions in Afghan prisons and was aware of generalized allegations of mistreatment[…]”, his meeting with Linda Garwood-Filbert of CSC alleviated any concerns, as the latter informed him prison conditions were improving.Footnote 1308 Similarly, it was Maj Zybala’s position his meeting with the Manley Panel and the release of its final report while he was in Afghanistan, affirmed his belief Canada was meeting its international legal obligations.Footnote 1309

Maj Zybala submitted he knew detainee transfers were suspended in November 2007 following receipt of the 5 November 2007 DFAIT site visit report. He acknowledged being present at the meeting where the decision to suspend transfers was made, but submitted he did not discuss the suspension of transfers with MWO (ret’d) Girard. As a result of attending that meeting, Maj Zybala claimed he was “[…] satisfied the [Comd JTF-Afg] was doing exactly what was required to satisfy Canada’s obligations under international law.”Footnote 1310 Maj Zybala also submitted he was aware the Comd JTF-Afg insisted upon several conditions in order to resume transfers.

In making transfer decisions, Maj Zybala was aware the Comd JTF-Afg had many sources of information and advice. Maj Zybala noted he never advised the Comd JTF-Afg on post-transfer treatment of detainees, and was confident the transfer decision process “… was a good process that worked and that the Commander was making sound decisions.”Footnote 1311

Regarding what would be required to commence an investigation into the transfer decisions of the Comd JTF-Afg, Maj Zybala said he would require “a mandate and a reasonable suspicion a crime had been committed.”Footnote 1312 The written submissions on behalf of Maj Zybala stated:

In order to have a mandate to investigate, there must be a connection between the crime and the CF and the matter must not fall within the mandate of the NIS. [Maj Zybala] never formed a reasonable suspicion that the Commander was making improper or illegal decisions; if he had, he would have requested that the NIS commence an investigation.Footnote 1313

Accordingly, Maj Zybala submitted he acted in a reasonable manner and that his actions met the professional standards expected of an MP.

Conclusions Regarding Major M. Zybala

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Zybala’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • Maj Zybala attempted to inform himself about the risks to detainees post transfer in Afghanistan and the international legal principles that were potentially applicable to the transfer of detainees, including the nature of Canadian responsibility for detainees post transfer. While the Commission may not agree with his personal assessment of the legal standard, and its potential application to the facts of this case, that is not determinative of whether he had a duty to investigate or ensure the investigation of his Commander.
  • Maj Zybala was aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, take steps to cause the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law.
  • Maj Zybala did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any particular detainee, were or could be illegal. He knew about the substance of the complaint to this Commission in February 2007, the Federal Court process, and some of the media attention the detainee question received. The information he acquired through his own research showed him to be curious about, and aware of the risks of torture in Afghan prisons, but it is reasonable the general information he acquired did not lead him to form a suspicion about the particular legality of any of his Commander’s transfer orders.
  • There was information about the post-transfer situation, such as the site visit reports from prior to his rotation and the site visits that occurred in September 2007, that Maj Zybala did not know. The fact that such information was not known to Maj Zybala is not due to personal failings on his part. Rather, it was a function of the “siloing” or “compartmentalizing” of information.
  • The first indication Maj Zybala had during his rotation that a Canadian-transferred detainee had been abused was on November 6, 2007 when, in a meeting called for that purpose, his Deputy Commander informed him that a credible allegation of abuse had been received and that transfers would be suspended. Maj Zybala provided his opinion at that meeting that stopping transfers met Canada’s international legal obligations. Therefore, it was reasonable for him not to suspect that the chain of command was behaving illegally, as his personal observations pointed to the contrary conclusion.
  • Maj Zybala was informed about the measures put in place before his Commander was willing to recommence transfers to the NDS, including the fact it took almost four months of activity and reform before the Commander was willing to transfer again. This, too, would have quelled suspicions about the legality of his Commander’s actions.
  • Maj Zybala knew or believed his Commander was getting legal advice on the propriety of transfers, something that, on these facts, could reasonably have assuaged any concerns about the legality of the transfer orders.

Finding #3: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Michel Zybala in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Zybala should have investigated his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer.

16.4 Master Warrant Officer (ret’d) Jean-Yves Girard

MWO (ret’d) Jean-Yves Girard joined the Canadian Forces as an MP in 1975. He was first posted to Chatham, New Brunswick, then to a number of places in the province of Quebec. His career path touched on most aspects of MP related work, from investigations and patrol work to security. In 2005, he was posted to the Quebec City NIS detachment. This was his first point of entry into the National Investigation Service, where he remained until his retirement in February 2010.

MWO (ret’d) Girard served overseas on four occasions, first in Cyprus in 1981, in Rwanda in 1994 and in the Golan Heights in 2001-2. His fourth deployment overseas was to Afghanistan during the timeframe of this complaint. He went over with ROTO 4, arriving on July 31, 2007, returning in early March 2008 after approximately one week of overlap with his predecessor, CWO Watson.Footnote 1314 MWO (ret’d) Girard also spent a month in Afghanistan at some point prior to his full rotation.Footnote 1315

Like CWO Watson, MWO (ret’d) Girard was the NIS detachment commander in the Afghan theatre. His detachment, including him, consisted of four NIS investigators, but given leave and vacations, his effective number was three. As NIS detachment commander, he was not under Maj Zybala’s command, and was independent of the chain of command in Afghanistan in the same sense described by CWO Watson. Like CWO Watson, MWO (ret’d) Girard had no contact whatsoever with the CEFCOM PM. His commander was the NIS commanding officer, LCol (ret’d) Garrick, but he explained his day to day contact up his chain of command was to Lt Utton and Maj Frei if he had questions about investigations. MWO (ret’d) Girard could also go to the regional military prosecutor for advice.Footnote 1316

MWO (ret’d) Girard was in contact with LCol (ret’d) Garrick before deploying, but did not receive any sort of briefing related to the time he would serve in Afghanistan. Instead, his contact with LCol (ret’d) Garrick related to his duties as NIS detachment commander for Quebec City. He had no contact whatsoever with Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore.Footnote 1317

MWO (ret’d) Girard had contact with Maj Zybala while in theatre, usually when he attended at Task Force Headquarters for investigations or administrative purposes, or to brief the Task Force Commander, MGen Laroche, on ongoing investigations. MWO (ret’d) Girard also briefed Maj Zybala on ongoing investigations where necessary. During these discussions with Maj Zybala and MGen Laroche, the discussion never turned to detainees.Footnote 1318

MWO (ret’d) Girard’s training was not identical to that received by Maj Zybala’s troops. One difference was he and his detachment spent a month in Toronto, witnessing autopsies of CF soldiers who had died in combat. This was meant to prepare them for the work they would have to do in Afghanistan, which included investigations into KIAs, escalations of force, and the resulting work in mortuary affairs:

Ma job, entre autres, en tant que commandant du détachement là-bas c’était aussi – en plus des enquêtes, c’était d’identifier les soldats qui nous sont amenés à la morgue pour qu’on puisse informer les familles par la suite.

[unofficial translation]

A part of my job as detachment commander over there was – in addition to investigations, identifying the soldiers who were brought to the morgue so that we could then notify the families.Footnote 1319

His NIS detachment also did not receive training in detainee handling and the transfer process, in general, as this was not something they would be doing while in Afghanistan.Footnote 1320

Other than this obviously difficult work, MWO (ret’d) Girard described his NIS role in Afghanistan as being similar to his role in Canada. His detachment conducted investigations into serious and sensitive matters, as judged necessary, in addition to the theatre-specific work described above.Footnote 1321 He agreed investigations into mistreatment of detainees and related violations of international law would clearly fall within the NIS mandate to investigate.Footnote 1322

MWO (ret’d) Girard was shown the technical directive that would have been applicable to him while in theatre.Footnote 1323 He did not recall seeing it at any point in time,Footnote 1324 and could offer no explanation for how it was he was on the distribution list but did not recall seeing it. He said he might have read it, but simply could not recall.Footnote 1325

MWO (ret’d) Girard was referred specifically to the paragraph 11 requirement that the appropriate component of the Canadian military police “shall” investigate allegations or instances of violations of international law, the law of armed conflict, or mistreatment of detainees “regardless of who was alleged to have carried out the mistreatment or when that mistreatment is thought to have occurred.”Footnote 1326After seeing this passage, MWO (ret’d) Girard still did not recall having seen or read the technical directive, even though he agreed it would have applied to him in theatre.Footnote 1327

MWO (ret’d) Girard said he did rely, for investigative guidance, on the Military Police Policy and Technical Procedures manual:Footnote 1328

On se fiait beaucoup avec ce qu’on a dans notre volume des techniques de la police militaire pour les enquêtes, ainsi de suite.

[unofficial translation]

We relied mainly on what was in the Military Police techniques manual for investigations, and so on.Footnote 1329

He was shown the following passage from the manual, on when the military police should initiate an investigation, and said the principles in this passage guided his decision making with respect to commencing an investigation while he was in Afghanistan:

10. Initiating an Investigation. An MP investigation may be initiated whenever:

  1. an MP observes the commission of any criminal or service offence;
  2. an MP is in receipt of a complaint originating from any other person in which a criminal or service offence is alleged;
  3. at the request of a Commander or Commanding Officer;
  4. MP learns of an incident through an informant (i.e., local police, a witness, a confidential informant, an anonymous tip, etc.);
  5. MP are tasked directly by DPM Police or CFNIS; or
  6. an authority in the MP Technical Chain so directs.Footnote 1330

MWO (ret’d) Girard also stated in testimony it would be obligatory for him to investigate allegations of breaches of international law and mistreatment of detainees while in theatre. He further understood, as set out in paragraph 14 of the Technical Directive, the TFPM’s role was to bring allegations of such breaches to his attention. However, he did not consider himself dependent on the TFPM for this type of information, and emphasized the fact the NIS was completely independent of the chain of command.Footnote 1331

MWO (ret’d) Girard did not view the TSO 321A, and, unlike CWO Watson, had no reason to come across it in his investigative work.Footnote 1332

MWO (ret’d) Girard knew little about the detainee process. He knew detainees were being held at the detention facility during his rotation given the proximity of the NIS work location to the detention facility.Footnote 1333 MWO (ret’d) Girard never discussed the detainee process with Maj Zybala or CWO Watson, and merely assumed it was MGen Laroche who decided whether to transfer.Footnote 1334 MWO (ret’d) Girard never viewed any of the transfer documents filled out by the MPs or the Task Force Commander, and never witnessed a transfer.Footnote 1335 He was not aware a detainee transfer arrangement existed between Canada and Afghanistan, and never really turned his mind to where the detainees ended up,Footnote 1336 although he knew Canada either released the detainees or sent them to someone, he presumed, within the Afghan government.Footnote 1337 He did not know transfers had been halted prior to his rotation, and did not know Canada conducted site visits to transferred detainees.Footnote 1338

MWO (ret’d) Girard was shown the November 5, 2007 site visit report, and read some of its details. Hearing those details did not jog his memory, or remind him of information he may have heard about the visit and the reasons for the November halt to transfers.Footnote 1339 He knew nothing about the lead-up to the November 5th visit, such as the CEFCOM investigation into the September 2007 allegations of abuse.Footnote 1340 While he read the papers on occasion, he had never heard of Michèle Ouimet or the October 2007 article suggesting Canada was transferring detainees to abuse.Footnote 1341

MWO (ret’d) Girard did not know transfers had been ordered stopped during his rotation, although he did notice a difference in terms of how many detainees were at the facility. Around the middle of his tour, he noticed they were staying longer at the facility. He asked no questions of others about this observation, though, and spoke of a rumour circulating about more detainees being at the facility because they liked it there, and did not want to leave.Footnote 1342 His knowledge of what was going on at the facility may also have been limited by the fact he went on leave on November 4, 2007 until the end of the month.Footnote 1343

As a result of courses he had taken early on in his career, MWO (ret’d) Girard understood detainees were to be treated as prisoners of war and in accordance with the Geneva Conventions.Footnote 1344 He never gave thought while in theatre to whether Canada was somehow still responsible for detainees post transfer:

À vrai dire, j’ai jamais pensé à cette portion là, qu’une fois transférés que c’était la responsabilité du Canada.

[unofficial translation]

To be perfectly honest, I never thought about that part, that once they had been transferred, they were under Canada’s responsibility.Footnote 1345

In this sense, he also never viewed LGen (ret’d) Gauthier’s directive to MGen Laroche, which spoke of the potential liability of the chain of command should it learn detainees were tortured or mistreated post transfer.Footnote 1346 He never turned his mind to whether the chain of command had responsibility for detainees post transfer. The idea simply never came to him while in theatre, given his focus on the investigations and work he had to do:

Ça ne m’est jamais venu à l’idée, le processus du transfert des détenus. J’étais focusé sur mes enquêtes à moi puis sur mon rôle que j’avais.

[unofficial translation]

I never gave a thought to the transfer of detainees’ procedure. I was focused on my own investigations and on my own responsibilities.Footnote 1347

MWO (ret’d) Girard’s knowledge of the human rights situation in Afghanistan was very limited, as was his knowledge of the media attention surrounding Canadian detainees. He never saw or read the February 21, 2007 complaint alleging the MPs themselves were potentially committing war crimes. He did not know the complaint existed while he was in theatre.Footnote 1348 MWO (ret’d) Girard did not read the Graeme Smith articles, nor did he know Graeme Smith had received reports of torture from former Canadian detainees.Footnote 1349 While in theatre, MWO (ret’d) Girard did occasionally view the newspaper on the internet, but he said he would have looked in particular for reports on fallen soldiers and their repatriation, as it was part of his job to ensure those fallen soldiers returned to Canada with dignity. Other than that, he looked occasionally at the sports, but little else.Footnote 1350

He never read or viewed any of the generalized reports on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, such as the reports from the UN, DFAIT, the US State Department and the AIHRC.Footnote 1351 He also did not know, while he was in Afghanistan, Federal Court proceedings related to detainees were ongoing, with the Complainants seeking a stop to transfers.Footnote 1352

MWO (ret’d) Girard did receive training on the cultural environment in Afghanistan. During this one-to-two hour session, he did not receive information about the situation in Afghan prisons, human rights issues in Afghanistan, or questions of potential torture or mistreatment within the prison population.Footnote 1353 He also appears not to have had a sense the detainee issue was drawing media attention prior to deployment. Nobody brought the detainee question to his attention, or alerted him to the possibility he might need to investigate Canada’s handling of detainees. Based on his military experience, he understood the proper treatment of detainees was important, but his awareness of the issue went no further. His pre-deployment focus was on ensuring his people were well prepared and ready to handle the six or seven months they were going to spend in theatre.Footnote 1354

At some point in time, he heard rumours of mistreatment and torture of detainees after transfer. He could not say whether he heard these rumours before going to Afghanistan, while there, or when he returned, nor could he say how he heard them. For example, he was asked whether he may have heard the rumours through informal conversations with fellow MPs in Afghanistan, but he recalled no such discussion.Footnote 1355 He was not aware that in the previous rotation, Maj Hudson’s MP soldiers had raised concerns about their personal liability relative to the detainee transfer process.Footnote 1356

MWO (ret’d) Girard was not aware of any investigations that occurred into the treatment of detainees post-transfer while he was in theatre.Footnote 1357 He did not conduct any such investigation, and never asked the Task Force Commander any questions about this topic, nor did he have any conversations about the possibility of this type of investigation with his NIS commander, LCol (ret’d) Garrick . Again, the idea of conducting such an investigation simply never came to mind while he was in Afghanistan.Footnote 1358

The Commission could surmise that while MWO (ret’d) Girard did not investigate post-transfer issues, he was involved in investigations into detainee treatment while in CF custody. It is clear he assisted Inspector Gfellner with the Operation Camel Spider investigation. He was called upon to locate three detainee medical files, which he did, without realizing it related to an investigation of alleged abuse of Afghan detainees while in CF custody.Footnote 1359 The NIS ROTO 4 detachment also investigated, while in theatre, the possibility detainees had been abused while in CF custody. This investigation flowed from a survey wherein certain respondents indicated they had witnessed detainee abuse. MWO (ret’d) Girard opened the investigation towards the end of his tour, and brought it back to Canada for completion. He did not recall, in that investigative context, any allegations or concerns about detainees being mistreated post transfer.Footnote 1360

MWO (ret’d) Girard was asked how he would have expected to learn about the need for an investigation into the legality of the transfers conducted by the Task Force Commander. He would have expected somebody, anybody, would have come to him to speak about the issue. They could also have raised the legality of the transfers with any of the MPs in theatre:

[...] mais c’est pas arrivé dans mon cas à moi. C’est pas arrivé que quelqu’un est venu me voir pour me rapporter ces telles infractions.

[unofficial translation]

[...] but it didn’t happen as far as I’m concerned. It never happened that someone came to me to report such violations.Footnote 1361

MWO (ret’d) Girard felt the NIS did have an obligation to ask questions, but only if they knew of allegations in the first place. He candidly said if he had heard allegations, he would have asked questions. He would have investigated, no matter who it was who brought him the information, and he would have done so for any type of investigation, whether related to detainees or not. He saw this as his duty.Footnote 1362

In terms of criteria for starting an investigation, MWO (ret’d) Girard first required the investigation to fall within NIS jurisdiction. Then, if the allegations were the least bit serious, he would undoubtedly initiate an investigation. He also spoke of needing a reasonable doubt an allegation had substance.Footnote 1363 Elsewhere, he spoke of needing a reasonable suspicion before starting an investigation, and agreed the more serious the alleged crime, the more carefully would he go about his decision of whether to investigate or not.Footnote 1364

Finally, MWO (ret’d) Girard was shown the details of the CEFCOM fact-check/investigation into the Globe and Mail articles.Footnote 1365 He said he did not know about this investigation by the J9, and did not know of or participate in the investigations that LGen (ret’d) Gauthier called upon the NIS to investigate.Footnote 1366 He had heard of Operation Centipede at the time of his testimony, but not during his time in theatre. Nobody came to ask him questions in relation to the Operation Centipede investigation.Footnote 1367

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submitted that MWO (ret’d) Girard bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. They submit MWO (ret’d) Girard, by virtue of his station and rank, had available to him information about post-transfer treatment of detainees. Thus, they state it would have been reasonable to expect, byvirtue of his duties as thecommander of the Afghanistan detachment responsible for major investigations into serious and sensitive matters, he would keep himself informed of publicly available information about activities taking place within the theatre of operations.

They further state, even if MWO (ret’d) Girard’s state of knowledge was as limited as he professed, he fell below thestandard one would expect of areasonably competent NIS member:

  • MWO (ret’d) Girard claimed he was unaware that transfers were suspended during his rotation for a period ofalmost three months from November 2007 through February 2008.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard’s offices were located directly next to the detainee compound, where he noticed that detainees were remaining longer than usual.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard testified that he heard rumours that detainees suffered torture and abuse post-transfer, but he could not recall if he heard those rumourswhile he was in theatre.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard’s testimony,from the Complainants’ perspective, lacked credibility, given the fact he had ample opportunities to interact with MPs and CF members who would have known the reasons for the suspension of transfers.

The Complainants took issue with MWO (ret’d) Girard’s professed ignorance on the subject of transfers during his testimony, and allege that this damaged his credibility.

In their final written submissions, the Complainants state: “MWO Girard, by virtue of his station and rank, had available to him information about post-transfer treatment of detainees. It is reasonable to expect that byvirtue of his duties as thecommander of the Afghanistan detachment responsible for major investigations into serious and sensitive matters that he would keep himself informed of publicly available information about activities taking place within the theatre of operations. Thus, even if MWO (ret’d) Girard’s state of knowledge was as limited as he professed, MWO (ret’d) Girard fell below the standard onewould expect of a reasonably competent NIS officer.”Footnote 1368

Submissions on Behalf of MWO (ret’d) J-Y. Girard

The submissions made on behalf of MWO (ret’d) Girard pointed to a number of factors which allegedly demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards.Footnote 1369

Counsel note MWO (ret’d) Girard had three other NIS members reporting to him in Afghanistan. Together, they were responsible for the conduct of serious and sensitive investigations, including Rules of Engagement compliance investigations, suicides, criminal investigations and forensic investigations with respect to CF members killed in action. MWO (ret’d) Girard supervised the investigations of the other NIS members. Counsel submitted MWO (ret’d) Girard’s main responsibility related to forensic investigations at the morgue.Footnote 1370

MWO (ret’d) Girard submitted he had a general understanding of the Geneva Conventions. MWO (ret’d) Girard understood CF detainees in Canadian Forces custody were to be treated pursuant to the Geneva Conventions and that Canada had an ongoing responsibility to ensure detainees were not mistreated after they had been transferred to the Afghan authorities. MWO (ret’d) Girard said he was unaware of LGen (ret’d) Gauthier’s directive to MGen Laroche pertaining to detainee transfers.Footnote 1371

MWO (ret’d) Girard understood detainee treatment was very important to the CF and the Government of Canada. However, counsel for MWO (ret’d) Girard noted he was unaware of important information about the detainee process and controversy, such as the complaint filed before this Commission (which he did not learn of until named as a subject), the relevant newspaper articles, and reports from international bodies regarding conditions in Afghanistan. Counsel also noted MWO (ret’d) Girard had not seen or heard about DFAIT visit reports while in Afghanistan, nor was he aware of Federal Court proceedings or the Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission.Footnote 1372

Counsel noted MWO (ret’d) Girard had no discussions with other military police with respect to Afghan detainees and the risk of torture while in Afghanistan. He had heard rumours about detainees possibly being tortured when they were transferred to Afghan authorities, but could not recall whether he became aware of the rumours while he was in theatre or following his return from the deployment. MWO (ret’d) Girard understood the Task Force Commander, MGen Laroche, made all decisions regarding the transfer of detainees. However, he never witnessed a transfer, had no involvement with detainees and did not know how the decisions to transfer were made.Footnote 1373

Counsel submitted MWO (ret’d) Girard provided limited assistance in the Op Camel Spider investigation, primarily related to locating the medical reports with respect to three previous Canadian detainees. During his rotation, he was not required to and did not leave the Canadian camp at KAF.

MWO (ret’d) Girard returned to Canada for vacation from November 4th until the 28th or 29th. He told the Commission he was unaware Canada had ceased transferring detainees to Afghanistan authorities in his absence.Footnote 1374

Despite his limited knowledge, MWO (ret’d) Girard submitted he understood the triggers to commencing an investigation were first to have a mandate to investigate and then to have sufficient resources. If an allegation was received, MWO (ret’d) Girard would review the allegation and, if it seemed serious and based on valid or reasonable grounds, would then commence an investigation.

MWO (ret’d) Girard did not rely on the TFPM to notify him about serious allegations concerning the Commander. If anyone made such allegations, MWO (ret’d) Girard would have commenced an investigation, or at least confirmed whether it was based on substance. But an investigation could not commence until he was made aware of an allegation.Footnote 1375

MWO (ret’d) Girard agreed that an investigation into the legality of the Commanders’ order would be a high profile serious investigatory matter within the NIS mandate. MWO (ret’d) Girard submitted that no such allegations were ever made to him, and that he did not conduct, direct, or recommend an investigation into the legality of the Task Force Commanders’ transfer orders and did not question a Commander with respect to detainee transfers, because he never had reason to believe they were illegal.Footnote 1376

Accordingly, MWO (ret’d) Girard submitted he was unaware of the events for which he is named as a subject in the complaint, and that he acted in a reasonable manner and his actions met the professional standards expected of an MP.

Conclusions Regarding MWO (ret’d) J-Y. Girard

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that MWO (ret’d) Girard’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police member. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • MWO (ret’d) Girard was either never provided with the Technical Directive applicable to his work while in theatre, or if it was provided to him, he apparently did not read it. The Commission believes the NIS detachment commander in theatre should have been proactive in finding and reading the Technical Directive applicable to his rotation. That said, MWO (ret’d) Girard nonetheless knew it was his obligation to investigate allegations of breaches of international law and mistreatment of detainees. Also, despite not having reviewed the Technical Directive, he used the MP Policy and Technical Procedures manual as his guidance for when to initiate an investigation.
