Despite not having read the Technical Directive, MWO (ret’d) Girard would have initiated an investigation into the Task Force Commander’s transfer decisions if he had received a complaint or if he had developed a reasonable suspicion that those decisions were illegal.
  • It is relevant to take into account the stressful and difficult nature of the work MWO (ret’d) Girard had to do while in theatre, in particular, in the area of KIAs and mortuary affairs. Given the demands of this work, and the more reactive role of the NIS, it is reasonable that his acquired knowledge of the detainee process and the treatment of detainees post-transfer was minimal. It was also reasonable for him to rely, to a great degree, on others, such as the TFPM and the MP company, to bring information or concerns to him if they existed. No such concerns were brought to his attention.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard knew Canada’s detainees were to be handled in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, although he did not turn his mind, while in theatre, to Canada’s obligations towards detainees once transferred to the Afghan authorities.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He explained, despite his heavy and stressful workload, he would have investigated a complaint that the Commander was acting illegal. He considered it his duty to do so.
  • MWO (ret’d) Girard did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports produced during his rotation. He did not even know site visits were occurring, or transfers had been halted in November 2007. His lack of knowledge about these matters was reasonable given his workload, his mandate, and his assertion that, if an allegation were brought to his attention, he would have investigated.

Finding #4: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Master Warrant Officer (ret’d) Jean-Yves Girard in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that MWO (ret’d) Girard should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstance prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police member.

16.5 Major Ron Gribble

Maj Gribble joined the CF in 1976 as a non-commissioned member. He advanced through the ranks in the Princess Patricia’s Light Infantry, performing many duties. In 1990 he entered the non-commissioned member university program, received his degree and was commissioned into the military police in 1992. He trained in all functions of the MP and worked in patrol operations, investigations, and security operations. He graduated from the MP Academy in 1994 and served as the Deputy Wing Commander – Security MP in Winnipeg for several years. During this period he was deployed to Haiti where he served as the MP commanding officer with the Airfield Security Force.

After a brief posting on his return, Maj Gribble was with Air Command Headquarters preparing the MP for operations support in such areas as the Disaster Assistance Response Team. He became the Deputy CO of an MP Platoon at CFB Edmonton and was immediately deployed to Bosnia as the Provost Marshal and CO of the MP Platoon. Upon his return he was the CO of the MP Garrison in Edmonton for approximately three years. He was then posted to the Provost Marshal’s office with 1 Area Support Group where he was mainly involved in operational planning and security oversight for various high security events such as the G8 summit in Kananaskis, where he was second in command.

Following this Maj Gribble was posted as CO to 1 MP Platoon and was soon deployed for seven months to Kabul, Afghanistan as the TFPM in Camp Julien. Upon his return he was made part of the CFPM’s staff at NDHQ where he was responsible for operational planning for deployed operations. Significantly, during this period of time he was responsible for drafting the Technical Directives which provided MPs with guidance during their earliest deployments in Kandahar.Footnote 1377

Maj Gribble returned to Edmonton as commandant of the CF Service Prison and Detention Barracks. While there, he was again deployed to Afghanistan as the TFPM and MP CO for ROTO 5.

Following his tour on ROTO 5, Maj Gribble became the CO of 1 MP Unit and also served as the JTF Land Force Western Area Provost Marshal.

In total, Maj Gribble served in seven overseas operational tours: Haiti, Bosnia, Egypt, twice in Cyprus, and his two tours in Afghanistan.Footnote 1378

Maj Gribble spent a brief period of time in Kandahar in preparation for ROTO 5 in November, 2007, after the cessation of transfers ordered by Col Juneau had occurred.Footnote 1379 He arrived in Afghanistan for the beginning of ROTO 5 on February 26, 2008 and returned on the 20th or 21st of September of that year. During his rotation he was “double-hatted”, being both the senior MP adviser to the Task Force Commander and the CO of the MP Company, with oversight of 100-plus MPs in theatre. His MP company performed a wide range of MP duties, including general policing, investigations and security, close support of dignitaries and visitors, close support outside the wire, aircraft security support, and, of course, detainee handling. He reported to the Task Force Commander and spoke to him or the deputy commander almost daily. He advised the Commission he was adequately resourced for the tasks at hand.Footnote 1380

Maj Gribble had no chain of command to the CFPM. He also had no command responsibility over the NIS detachment in Kandahar, although he was responsible for providing them with administrative and logistical support as well as referring investigations to them, and he would interact with NIS personnel on an almost daily basis. He fully understood the independent role of the NIS and indicated he would not hesitate to refer investigations which were outside his own company’s mandate to the NIS. He rejected the contention there was any conflict between his policing obligations and his command responsibilities; he was quite emphatic in stating if he thought his commander had committed an offence, he would refer the matter to the NIS.Footnote 1381

Maj Gribble reported in the technical chain to the CEFCOM Provost Marshal, initially Maj Martin Laflamme, and at the end of his tour Maj Greg Losier. According to him, any issues he referred up the technical chain would also be known to his command chain. He provided monthly SITREPs and would go through the CEFCOM PM if there were specific MP-related resource or personnel issues. The CEFCOM PM could then advise further up the technical chain to the CFPM office as well as champion those issues at CEFCOM. If he required technical direction he would normally consult with the CEFCOM PM although he could consult any MP staff member.Footnote 1382

Maj Gribble was directly involved in the detainee transfer process. If a detainee were being held, he was involved on a daily basis visiting the detention facility, reviewing daily reports, logs and information, and advising the Task Force Commander accordingly.Footnote 1383 In his capacity as adviser to the commander Maj Gribble saw his role as being a factual one – he and others passed information about the detainees on to the Task Force Commander, who then made a decision about release or transfer.

Initially during his tour this occurred in writing, independently of other parties’ input into the Task Force Commander’s decision. Later in his tour, sometime late in July 2008, a detainee “assessment board” consisting of the TFPM, Chief of Intelligence, JAG, POLAD and others met to compile information and to advise on transfer issues. It was Maj Gribble’s understanding the assessment board was implemented primarily to compile information that would assist the NDS in their further investigations and prosecutions of the detainees, not as a result of post-transfer abuse issues.Footnote 1384 While to some extent he knew what information was being provided by others to the Task Force Commander, he testified it did not include information about the risk of post-transfer abuse and this was not, to his knowledge, something discussed at the assessment meetings. Maj Gribble did not see the written record of the Commander’s risk assessment, although he saw other portions of the transfer decision forms. He agreed if he had so desired he could have accessed the form while in theatre.Footnote 1385 He said he did not know the sources of information that would enter into the Commander’s risk assessment.Footnote 1386 He was aware the Commander made that assessment with the assistance of a team of advisers, including legal advisers.Footnote 1387

Maj Gribble understood the proper handling of detainee processing was considered one of the three most important strategic imperatives for the Task Force Commander.Footnote 1388 He was physically present with some of his key staff for detainee transfers. The POLAD, Ed Jager initially, then Jennie Cheng, was present to represent Canada, the detainee officer was there to represent the Commander, and there would usually be an interpreter present. According to Maj Gribble, NDS personnel were not present during the transfer process; however, he did have significant contact with the NDS. Maj Gribble felt they exhibited a good degree of professionalism, and mentioned the close coordination with them on detainee issues in his end of tour report.Footnote 1389

Maj Gribble also understood as an MP he had independent investigative obligations in addition to his operational obligations. He was trained in the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and understood it would be unlawful for a commander to transfer a detainee to a substantial risk of torture or abuse. He had no specific training for investigating human rights abuse allegations, or allegations of unlawful orders by a commander. Maj Gribble’s view was that Canada as a power was responsible for addressing post-transfer abuse. He correctly understood it would be inappropriate to investigate his own commander, but he understood if he had suspicions about allegations of this nature or concerns about the legality of transfer orders he would be obliged to report them to the NIS.Footnote 1390

Maj Gribble indicated if an allegation of a criminal or service offence were brought to his attention which was credible and specific, he would be duty bound to initiate an investigation. If an untested allegation were encountered it would be appropriate to open a GO and conduct an assessment short of a full investigation to determine whether there was a credible basis to broaden the inquiry. He stressed he could not engage in “fishing expeditions” based on vague complaints or general discussions, nor could he investigate Afghan authorities themselves. He agreed information might come to his attention which was insufficient to cause a full investigation, but which would trigger an assessment as to whether a full investigation should occur.Footnote 1391 Maj Gribble did not feel it was within his purview to act as a monitor of the commander’s transfer orders or to assess their legality on an ongoing basis, absent a suspicion on his part that something illegal had occurred.Footnote 1392 Although he agreed a repeated pattern of transfers to abuse could lead him to question the legality of transfer orders,Footnote 1393 Maj Gribble qualified his role in investigating previous rotations as follows:

  • […] But in the rotation prior to yours, there were transfer suspensions and there were, in November 2007, some serious and apparently corroborated allegations of abuse.

    You said you had a general awareness, but did you think that there was any need to investigate the circumstances under which that could have happened, in other words, to look at what they were thinking and why they would have transferred someone who ends up getting tortured, perhaps to find that they didn’t know or couldn’t know. But did you think of looking at that issue from your previous rotation and considering whether it should be investigated?
  • The previous rotation was not my responsibility. I had plenty of work to keep me busy on the ground. I wasn’t looking at - - I actually was carrying some files from the previous roto, so I had plenty of work. So to look at something that was past post, no.Footnote 1394

Maj Gribble indicated he would have pursued such an investigation or referred it to the NIS if it had been brought to his attention. The Commission interprets this as meaning Maj Gribble would continue investigations initiated by his predecessor rotation or specifically brought to him, but he had no duty to independently examine the conduct of personnel during the previous rotation absent a specific complaint or referred file.

Maj Gribble had no specific pre-deployment training concerning the human rights situation in Afghanistan. His experience in Kabul left him with the impression the human rights situation with security authorities in Afghanistan was generally positive, although his experience was limited to police and prisons in Kabul, not in Kandahar.Footnote 1395 He had not read the various DFAIT, UN, US State Department, Amnesty International or AIHRC reports on human rights generally in Afghanistan, and unlike Maj Hudson he had no direct interaction with personnel from the AIHRC and was not their point of contact for detainee notification issues.

Maj Gribble had a working familiarity with the two Arrangements between Afghan and Canadian authorities for transfer of detaineesFootnote 1396 but played no role in their drafting. He was cognizant of the monitoring provisions for DFAIT personnel but he had not seen any DFAIT C4 site visit reports, either earlier ones from Mr. Colvin or later ones which occurred prior to and during his rotation. During his rotation MPs did not attend or accompany DFAIT personnel on these visits.Footnote 1397

Despite the fact the TFPM is mentioned in it, Maj Gribble was not aware of the June 12, 2008 complaint to this Commission by AIC/BCCLA until after he had returned from his rotation. Initially in his testimony Maj Gribble indicated he was not familiar with the February 21, 2007 complaint in which MPs were accused of knowingly transferring detainees to torture or abuse. When reminded that he had been interviewed by MPCC investigators and the RCMP concerning the Attaran complaint and the February 21, 2007 complaint, Maj Gribble agreed he was likely advised of the substance of the complaint as early as March 2007. He pointed out he had been consulted about the command role of the CFPM, not about the substance of the complaints, and he was awaiting deployment so was not in a position to review media reports concerning this complaint. The Commission accepts that the focus of his earlier interviews was not concerning the substance of the allegations but the CFPM’s role in relation to MP members in theatre. It follows that Maj Gribble would have been aware, due to this interview that the substance of the February 21, 2007 complaint was already being investigated by at least two organizations - the RCMP and the MPCC.Footnote 1398

Maj Gribble had read the April 23, 2007 Globe and Mail article by Graeme Smith outlining specific allegations of post-transfer abuse by Canadian-transferred detainees. He believes he read it around November 2007, a time which roughly coincided with his preparatory visit to Afghanistan during pre-deployment training. Maj Gribble was aware at the time he read the article there had been a suspension of detainee transfers, and he assumed it due to post-transfer abuse allegations.Footnote 1399 He had not read other newspaper articles in the Commission’s record. He expressed a general scepticism as to the reliability of media reports as in his experience they could be inaccurate or false. In his view, one would wish to verify the facts before proceeding based on such a report.Footnote 1400

Maj Gribble was unaware of the existence of the Operation Centipede investigations. He was not asked to provide assistance with this and was unaware of any other ongoing investigation into detainee abuse. Operation Centipede disclosed rumours among CF personnel concerning post-transfer abuse, but Maj Gribble was aware of no such rumours among CF members during his rotation. Nor did he hear any concerns expressed by MPs, such as had occurred during Maj Hudson’s rotation, concerning potential MP liability for such abuse.Footnote 1401 He was aware generally there had been allegations of detainee mistreatment in Afghan prisons, but he was aware of nothing specific. He was not familiar with the reasons delivered by the Federal Court in February 2008.

Transfers of detainees resumed shortly after Maj Gribble’s deployment on ROTO 5 and continued throughout his rotation. He did not discuss the reasons for the suspension of transfers or the factors leading to resumption of transfers with either Maj Zybala or MGen Laroche. He knew in a general sense there was an increased frequency of DFAIT monitoring visits, more input from Correctional Service Canada and more interaction with the NDS concerning appropriate interviewing and interrogation techniques.

Maj Gribble was asked about his understanding of the legal test for transfer of detainees. He was shown a draft letter of Col Juneau and a directive from LGen (ret’d) Gauthier to BGen Laroche (as he then was), neither of which he had seen previously. The following exchanges occurred:

  • […] In the first paragraph, the second sentence, [Col Juneau] says:

    The discretion to authorize the detainee transfer may only be exercised where there are not substantial grounds for believing that there is a real risk that a detainee would face subsequent abuse or mistreatment o[n] transfer to the NDS”

    Is that test something that you were familiar with or at least in accordance with your understanding of your legal obligations and the legal obligations of commanders who might be subject of an investigation? In other words, is that something you concur with?
  • I am not going to concur with something that wasn’t my responsibility. You would have to ask the commander. That was his responsibility.
  • […]
  • General Gauthier indicates in paragraph 24:

    The chain of command bears the potential liability should we become aware of torture or mistreatment following the transfer of detainees to Afghan authorities. For that reason, I am particularly concerned about the chain of command obligation to satisfy itself that the follow-up of transferred detainees is sufficiently robust.

    Then he outlines his expectations of a proactive engagement with DFAIT to ensure the monitoring and reporting and analysis is provided.

    My question is directed to you because as a police officer, you are a law enforcement officer, and this is a discussion, as is Colonel Juneau’s letter, about a legal obligation on the part of commanders.

    My question is: As a military police officer, what would your understanding be about the legal obligations of the commanders and the potential legal liability of the commanders for falling short on either of those two passages that we have described?

    Do you understand my question?
  • It’s a very broad question. Could you narrow it? I’m not sure what you are getting at.
  • Maybe I can draw an analogy. You are a police officer. You have to have some understanding of the law you are enforcing to effectively do your duties.
  • Very much so.
  • For instance, if you are a drug patrol officer, you have to know what drugs fall into a grey area that can be possessed, if you have a prescription, for instance. You have to have some kind of knowledge of the legal kind of framework.

    General Gauthier has described the potential for legal liability. Colonel Juneau has described his understanding of the legal obligations he has to make a transfer decision.

    I am just wondering whether you had an understanding at the time you were in theatre of those legal obligations on the part of the transferring commanders and, if you had an understanding of that, what your understanding of their obligations was, their legal obligations.
  • Their obligations are covered quite clearly under international law and Canadian law.
  • And what would they –
  • And I was very confident that they understood their responsibilities and they were acting accordingly. They had a host of advisers and people doing different things for them, a lot more knowledge and in-depth knowledge than I had. So I was satisfied that they were operating within those parameters.

Maj Gribble agreed if the Task Force Commander violated these precepts, and knowingly transferred a detainee to abuse it would be a violation of the law. He had no such concerns about the Task Force Commander’s decisions during his rotation. When asked about the previous rotations, Maj Gribble stated:

  • I wasn’t there, so I can’t speak to that.
  • My point being, you had no reason –
  • I had no reason. There was nothing that was brought to my attention, no.
  • You had no reason to suspect that they had violated the law even knowing that the transfers had ceased in November of 2007 because of a post transfer allegation of abuse.
  • No, I had no concerns.
  • I think your explanation was – and correct me if I am paraphrasing incorrectly. The measures that were put in place that you described, a number of measures, satisfied you that the transfers could be done without a risk of post transfer abuse, or without a significant risk.
  • That’s correct.
  • If you had been aware of the complaints levied, the P1 document that I showed you, the February 2007 letter from Amnesty International, or the letter from June 2008, if that had come to your attention that basically your commanders, your predecessor commander or your predecessor provost marshals were accused of unlawful activity, can you advise what your response would have been had those letters been brought to your attention in terms of your investigative duties?
  • It would depend on where I was and what my capacity was. You are asking me to hypothesize on something that you haven’t – the ground work is there, so I really – if I am in a position of responsibility, I am going to address those concerns, yes.
  • If you are the Task Force Provost Marshal, if the allegation is that your commanders have violated international law, I take it your primary responsibility would be at least to bring it to the attention of the NIS because that is within their jurisdiction.
  • Yes.Footnote 1402

Maj Gribble’s position is that he had no information which would give him cause to suspect the Task Force Commander had unlawfully transferred detainees to a substantial risk of torture or abuse. From his perspective, when problems arose the suspensions were stopped, more robust measures were put into place, and assurances were obtained from Afghan authorities. The Task Force Commander was transferring with the assistance of a team of advisers, including legal advisers, and he had no reason to question whether the process was being followed in good faith. It did not enter his mind to question the integrity of the process or the good faith of the responsible parties.

Maj Gribble reasonably noted the Commander does not have a crystal ball such that all possibility of harm could be eliminated. In his view, there were mechanisms in place to alleviate the risk, and if a credible allegation of abuse arose, Canada as a power had an obligation to respond.

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submit Maj Gribble bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint. Generally, they say he bore responsibility as one of the TFPMs during the time in question, for the failure to investigate or inquire into whether past and ongoing transfer orders were legal. The Complainants argue in their written submission that Maj Gribble had, or had the means of knowing, the following information which reasonably should have led him to conduct an investigation:

  • Maj Gribble was generally aware there were allegations of detainee abuse in Afghan prisons.
  • Maj Gribble knew transfers were suspended in November 2007 and understood the suspension of transfers occurred because there were reports of post-transfer abuse.
  • Maj Gribble read an online version of the Graeme Smith article.

The Complainants took issue with Maj Gribble’s testimony as to his lack of knowledge. In their written submissions they stated:

Unlike his predecessor TFPMs, Major Gribble testified that he had minimal awareness that there were concerns about post-transfer torture or abuse of detainees. He testified that he did not receive any background documents during his pre-deployment training that pertained to the human rights situation in Afghanistan. While in theatre, he claimed to have heard no discussion of potential post-transfer abuse, despite the fact that he started his rotation when transfers were just being resumed after the November 2007 suspension. In his conversations with the two DFAIT Political Advisors stations at KAF, he never discussed concerns about post-transfer abuse. He testified that he had no knowledge of the contents of DFAIT site visit reports; in fact, during his rotation, he was not even aware that DFAIT produced site visit reports. Despite having been interviewed by both MPCC investigators and the RCMP regarding the February 2007 Complaint, Major Gribble denied that he was aware of the substance of the Complaint.Footnote 1403

The Complainants also took issue with the fact Maj Gribble testified initially he did not know the legal test for transferring detainees to a foreign power, despite the fact he received pre-deployment training on the law of armed conflict in the “detainee package”. The Complainants submitted Maj Gribble “refused” to articulate his understanding of the Comd JTF-Afg’s legal obligations when ordering a detainee transfer when testifying.Footnote 1404 However, the Complainants noted Maj Gribble did acknowledge under cross-examination he understood it would be impermissible to transfer a detainee to a substantial risk of torture, and such an order would violate the laws of armed conflict. However, the Complainants submit Maj Gribble failed to initiate an investigation because he mistakenly believed the decisions in the previous rotations were not his responsibility.

The fact that potentially illegal conduct took place during a prior rotation was no bar to his launching an investigation, but as Major Gribble informed this Commission:

The previous rotation was not my responsibility. I had plenty of work to keep me busy on the ground. I wasn’t looking at – I actually was carrying some files from the previous roto, so I have plenty of work. So to look at something that was past post, no.

Given the seriousness of the issues at stake – violations of the law of armed conflict and the universal prohibition against torture – “being busy” is no excuse for failing to make basic inquiries.Footnote 1405

The Complainants also noted in their submissions Maj Gribble did not attempt to rely on previous investigations, such as Operation Centipede, to justify his failure to investigate, as Maj Gribble testified he was not aware of any investigations into the transfer decisions. The Complainants also submitted Maj Gribble assumed the transfer orders were legal, and took issue with the fact Maj Gribble did not attempt to verify his assumptions. The Complainants relied on these points as providing further evidence Maj Gribble was unreasonable in his responsibilities as an MP and the TFPM. The Complainants concluded:

Major Gribble never sought advice along the technical chain of command as to whether past orders to transfer required an investigation, nor did he ever express any concern up the technical chain, either. He gave no evidence that he or any MP under his command ever investigated or inquired into the legality of past orders to transfer. He never asked NIS to investigate or inquire into whether past orders to transfer detainees were unlawful. Given that Major Gribble was aware of reports of post-transfer torture and that transfers had to be halted entirely due to concerns over NDS treatment of CF-transferred detainees, his failure to investigate was also objectively unreasonable.Footnote 1406

Submissions on Behalf of Maj R. Gribble

The submissions made on behalf of Maj Gribble point to a number of factors which, it is said, demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards.Footnote 1407

Maj Gribble submitted he understood Canada was responsible to ensure detainees were not mistreated, and the Government of Canada negotiated an arrangement with the Government of Afghanistan. According to the written submissions on behalf of Maj Gribble, “post-transfer treatment of detainees was not within his area of responsibility.”Footnote 1408

Maj Gribble submitted prior to arriving in Afghanistan, he became aware detainee transfers had been suspended by the Comd JTF-Afg.  Maj Gribble also noted transfers of detainees resumed shortly after his arrival in theatre. The written submissions on behalf of Maj Gribble stated:

[h]e was aware that transfers resumed based on an increased capacity to visit detainees more frequently, support to the system through Correctional Services Canada and training provided by civilian police to NDS investigators on how to properly investigate, interrogate or interview subjects. He believed that the Government of Canada had taken action, implemented changes and received reassurances from the Government of Afghanistan before the transfers continued.Footnote 1409

Maj Gribble said he was not aware of the previous complaints relating to detainees before this Commission; nor did he read DFAIT human rights reports or other international human rights reports. Instead, Maj Gribble stated he relied upon his previous experience in Afghanistan during 2004 dealing with Afghan police and conditions in Afghan prisons, and that generally these experiences had been positive.Footnote 1410

Maj Gribble told the Commission he had read the Graeme Smith newspaper article in late 2007, but did not believe the newspaper articles alleging mistreatment of detainees contained allegations a CF member had done something unlawful. As such, Maj Gribble submitted he lacked sufficient basis to initiate an investigation.

Maj Gribble also said it was “… not possible for [him] to investigate allegations regarding previous rotations given that none of the people who would be allegedly involved in a crime were in theatre.” Similarly, Maj Gribble believed it was beyond his jurisdiction to investigate allegations of abuse of Canadian-transferred detainees at the hands of Afghan authorities. Moreover, Maj Gribble stated allegations of detainee abuse by Afghan authorities “… would not be a sufficient basis to investigate the Task Force Commander.” Similarly, Maj Gribble submitted he never received a complaint or allegation the Comd JTF-Afg had violated the laws of armed conflict or international law; but if he had, he said he would have referred the matter to the NIS to investigate.Footnote 1411

Maj Gribble noted he attended every transfer of detainees that occurred during his rotation, and emphasized NDS demonstrated professionalism and concern for the condition of detainees.Footnote 1412 He also said, during his tenure as TFPM, the decision to transfer detainees was an informal paper process and he was responsible for advising the Comd JTF-Afg on whether to transfer, release or hold detainees. Maj Gribble stated he was not privy to information relating to treatment of detainees post-transfer, such as the DFAIT site visit reports,Footnote 1413 nor did he receive a copy of the Commander’s risk assessment.Footnote 1414

Maj Gribble also submitted it was not his role to verify the Comd JTF-Afg was giving orders that were in accordance with the law, and said this would properly be the role of the JAG officer providing the Commander with legal advice. Counsel for Maj Gribble submitted:

It was not Maj Gribble’s role to ensure that the Commanders’ orders were in accordance with the law; the Commander had a legal advisor who filled that role. Maj Gribble had full confidence in the propriety of the decisions the Commander was making and believed that he was receiving relevant information and advice to enable him to make those decisions.Footnote 1415

[...]

Major Gribble was confident that the Commanders understood their responsibilities and that they had a host of advisors, including legal advisors, to assist them in making the decision to transfer. He had no reason to suspect that the Commanders had violated the law. Maj Gribble would have no issue or concern with laying a complaint about anyone in his chain of command, where warranted.Footnote 1416

Accordingly, Maj Gribble submitted, in all the circumstances, he acted in a reasonable manner and his actions met all professional standards expected of an MP.

Conclusions Regarding Maj R. Gribble

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Gribble’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • Maj Gribble demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles that were potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees, including the nature of Canadian responsibility for detainees post transfer.
  • Maj Gribble was also aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law.
  • Maj Gribble did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He only had some knowledge of the substance of the complaint to this Commission in February 2007, the Federal Court injunction process, and the media attention the detainee question received. He reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he observed his Commander and the Government taking to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer, such as the suspension of transfers until a more robust monitoring regime was in place.
  • The Commission concludes Maj Gribble took his duties as TFPM seriously. However, the Commission did have concerns with Maj Gribble’s comments that previous rotations were not his responsibility, as such comments may suggest he construed his duties too narrowly. In the Commission’s view, MPs have a broader obligation as police officers to be alert to potential commission of offences regardless of their timing and how the information of a potential offence is obtained. MPs should be open to the prospect of having to examine or inform themselves about events from previous rotations whether or not they have been specifically assigned this task.
  • That being said, there was insufficient information available to Maj Gribble to obligate him to investigate conduct from the previous rotation. However, had sufficient information of any offence committed on the previous rotations come to his attention, he would have been obligated to respond to it by initiating an assessment or for full investigation by either his own company or the NIS, depending on circumstances.
  • It was reasonable that Maj Gribble did not form a suspicion whether his Task Force Commander was transferring to a known and unacceptable risk of torture. It was reasonable for Maj Gribble to consider that his Commander’s behaviour demonstrated a willingness to stop transfers where necessary, despite the operational obstacles this created.
  • Maj Gribble was generally aware of information indicating torture was a serious concern in Afghanistan, from sources such as his general understanding of the February 21, 2007 complaint to this Commission, the fact transfers had been suspended during the previous rotation, and the media attention given to the detainee transfer question, particularly Graeme Smith’s Globe and Mail article from April 2007. Maj Gribble had, on the other hand, information that transfers had been suspended when the Commander thought the risk warranted it, he was aware that DFAIT was monitoring detainees post transfer, and he was of the belief remedial measures were put into place prior to the resumption of transfers in early 2008. These factors would reasonably have militated against the development of a suspicion that transfers were being made illegally.
  • Maj Gribble did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports from May onwards, other C4 traffic, the legal opinions the Commander was receiving, and any discussions his Commander may have been having with respect to post-transfer risk assessment. The fact that Maj Gribble did not have access to this information is not due to personal failings on his part, but rather to factors discussed previously.
  • Maj Gribble reasonably assumed his Commander was getting legal advice on the propriety of transfers. In the absence of any information to the contrary, and given his knowledge of CF operations and command resources, it was not unreasonable for him to expect that his Commander would be receiving appropriate advice as to the Commander’s own liabilities in regards to detainee transfers.

Finding #5: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major Ron Gribble in the June 12, 2008 complaint to be unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Gribble should have investigated the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or should have caused such an investigation to occur. The Commission finds his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standards of a reasonable police officer.

16.6 Major John Kirschner

Maj Kirschner joined the CF on January 4, 1983 as an electronics technician, and in 1986 changed occupations to become an MP. On completing basic MP training Maj Kirschner was posted to 1 MP Platoon in Calgary serving as a field MP and a patrolman on base. In 1989 he was posted to Lahr, Germany as a patrolman, criminal investigator, and shift commander for a patrol crew. In 1991 while on his German deployment he was deployed to support Canada’s contribution to the first Gulf War, Operation SCIMITAR.

In 1994 Maj Kirschner was posted to the Militia Training and Support Centre in Meaford for 11 months. He was promoted to sergeant and transferred to Ottawa where he was employed in surveillance with the Special Investigations Unit, and later employed by the NIS. In 1998 Maj Kirschner was deployed to Bosnia as the NIS detachment commander in Coralici. On return he was posted to the NIS Sensitive Investigation Unit as a sergeant, investigating allegations concerning senior public servants and higher ranking officers.

In 2000 Maj Kirschner was selected for commissioning from the non-commissioned ranks and was appointed lieutenant. After language training he was posted to the NIS as the officer in charge of the Criminal Intelligence Program. In 2002 he was posted to CFB Halifax as the deputy naval provost marshal of the MP detachment. Three years later he was placed in command of the Halifax NIS detachment, where he remained until his pre-deployment training and deployment as NIS detachment commander in Kandahar.Footnote 1417

Maj Kirschner was the Commanding Officer of the CFNIS detachment in Kandahar for ROTO 5, from 15 February to August 2008. This followed approximately 8.5 months of pre-deployment training. He reported to the Deputy CO of the NIS, who at the time was Maj Frei, with LCol (ret’d) Garrick being next up his chain of command. Maj Kirschner had no formal command relationship with non-MP personnel in Kandahar, but had a briefing protocol wherein commanders were kept apprised of investigations in a perfunctory manner insofar as they might impact operations. Maj Kirschner thus had met with MGen Laroche and his successor, but was not under their command. Maj Kirschner had regular contact with the ROTO 5 TFPM, Maj Gribble and received administrative support from the MP Company commanded by him. Maj Gribble and Maj Kirschner did not have a mutual reporting or command relationship, but they shared activities and daily happenings since Maj Gribble was the senior technical adviser to the commander. In Maj Kirschner’s words, he did not report to Maj Gribble, but kept him apprised of what the NIS were doing.Footnote 1418

Other than some brief contact during a Site Inspection Visit, Maj Kirschner had no contact with the CFPM Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore. He neither reported to nor received direction from Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore during his rotation, and his contact with the CEFCOM PM was limited to discussions unrelated to detainee issues. Maj Kirschner said none of the TFPM, CEFCOM PM or any other party impeded the independent investigative duties of the NIS during his rotation, and he in fact described his communications and relationship with the TFPM as “stellar”.Footnote 1419 Maj Kirschner expressed confidence in the guidance he was receiving from his chain of command and felt clear and confident about what his duties and responsibilities were.Footnote 1420

Under Maj Kirschner the NIS detachment consisted of a total of four MP personnel. With leave entitlements, for the better part of his rotation the detachment consisted of three MPs including himself, and he said they were “overwhelmed”, with a workload including 36 conducted and completed major crime investigations during his deployment. The NIS in theatre was not only responsible for investigating escalations of force and KIAs but also dealt with the undoubtedly difficult and “thankless” tasks of mortuary affairs and repatriation of fallen CF soldiers that flowed from these incidents.Footnote 1421 Maj Kirschner did not determine the number of personnel he commanded, but did request additional support through CEFCOM with the assistance of LCol (ret’d) Garrick. Logistically, it is difficult to deploy additional personnel because of the length of pre-deployment training although in exceptional situations untrained MPs can be deployed. Unfortunately, with the ceiling on the total number of CF members deployed to Afghanistan and the logistic impediments to increasing the allotment with the NIS, Maj Kirschner’s requests for more personnel were unfulfilled.Footnote 1422

Maj Kirschner was not familiar with the February, 2007 AIC/BCCLA complaint against the military police, nor had he seen the June 12, 2008 complaint underlying this hearing despite the fact it was an allegation against MPs and the NIS in Afghanistan filed during his tenure there. He agreed this would be subject matter for the NIS to investigate. The Commission notes that as a potential subject of the complaint, Maj Kirschner would not be in a position to investigate the issues in the complaint after it had been filed because, in essence, he would have been placed in a clear position of conflict investigating his own conduct.Footnote 1423

Maj Kirschner indicated the detainee issue was “omnipresent” during his tour. His pre-deployment training dealt with detainee handling, but not with assessing detainee transfer risks; his NIS commanders did advise him to remain alert to detainee abuse issues. Maj Kirschner was not familiar with general reports from DFAIT, or public reports from the UN, the AIHRC or other organizations, concerning the human rights situation in Afghanistan and he was not exposed to this information in pre-deployment training.Footnote 1424

Maj Kirschner had not specifically read the newspaper accounts of alleged abuse, but was aware through the media of complaints about detainee abuse which included allegations of post-transfer torture. Because the allegations dealt with post-transfer abuse, they did not hold much interest for him since investigating them would be, in his view, outside his jurisdiction unless there was a joint venture with Afghan authorities. Moreover, his office was not tasked with undertaking any such investigation. Maj Kirschner was aware, through the media, implements of torture had been found in the NDS detention facility and advised his troops to be alert to signs of abuse when they had occasion to visit the facility in March, 2008. Since allegations of CF abuse of detainees were also known to him through the media, he encouraged his NIS members to distance themselves from the KAF detention facility in case they were called upon to investigate any issues with detainees arising from it.Footnote 1425

Maj Kirschner was aware transfers were suspended when he arrived in theatre and inferred this was due to post-transfer abuse allegations arising in November 2007. He was unaware of the previous transfer suspensions. Maj Kirschner had no specific discussions with MWO (ret’d) Girard about detainee transfer suspensions because detainee transfers were not the NIS’s responsibility. Maj Kirschner was not aware there were Federal Court proceedings concerning detainee transfers until the Commission’s investigation into this matter began, and he was unaware of the reports from DFAIT either prior to or during his rotation, although he assumed they would be making reports of their site visits. Maj Kirschner was aware of, but not involved in, the investigations collected into Operation Centipede – they were classified investigations and the details were only shared on a “need to know” basis. Similarly, he was aware of Insp Gfellner’s investigation into Professor Attaran’s complaint about possible CF abuse of detainees and failure to investigate by MPs (Operation Camel Spider) but was not informed of its subject matter.Footnote 1426

Maj Kirschner’s detachment was involved in investigations concerning detainee abuse, but it was alleged abuse by CF members, and not post-transfer abuse. When his subordinates were sent to the NDS detention facility to interview the detainees in question, Maj Kirschner asked them to look out for signs of post-transfer abuse simply because detainee abuse issues were of international significance. They saw no such signs of abuse. Maj Kirschner never heard negative rumours about the NDS; to the contrary, at the end of the moratorium on transfers there was a confidence conveyed about the NDS. Maj Kirschner had no concerns about their conduct based on what he heard from his subordinates who had met with the NDS.Footnote 1427

Maj Kirschner was aware that CF personnel had obligations towards detainees under international law and under the applicable TSO which included treatment in accordance with the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. While he did not know Canada had certain post-transfer legal obligations with respect to humane post-transfer treatment, he understood Canada did have a monitoring regime in place to ensure this was the case, and he was satisfied this was in fact occurring. His CF training included some measure of understanding of the laws of armed conflict and the Conventions, and he believed all CF members must have knowledge of and adhere to these legal precepts. He, as a member of the NIS, had access to regional military prosecutors to answer any questions concerning international law principles if he had required such guidance, but he did not feel any need to consult while he was in theatre. Maj Kirschner was never given legal instruction on the test for lawful transfer of detainees, but noted if an investigation had been initiated one of the steps in planning was to outline the essential elements to be investigated, and legal counsel could be consulted on this. He believed Canada’s agreements with Afghan authorities mandated that the latter, not CF members, were obliged to investigate abuse at the hands of Afghans. Maj Kirschner noted he could only investigate persons who fell under MP jurisdiction. He believed he had no peace officer power to compel information from DFAIT personnel and indicated legal counsel might be sought if a writ or warrant was required for an investigation.Footnote 1428

Maj Kirschner agreed he would have jurisdiction to investigate a commander if he suspected the commander had committed an offence with respect to a transfer decision. The test for self-initiating an investigation would be a “reasonable suspicion” of wrongdoing, less than reasonable and probable grounds. He noted that for suspicion of illegal transfer orders, this would entail having some knowledge of the commander’s state of mind, and given what he saw in theatre, he believed there was no cause to investigate.

From Maj Kirschner’s perspective, when detainee abuse allegations had arisen, the Commander had suspended transfers. He was not informed of the conditions which had changed to permit the resumption of transfers, but he assumed something significant had been done to satisfy the Commander and Government of Canada that they could be safely resumed. Even if he had seen the site visit reports outlining torture or abuse, they would speak to the conditions after transfer but not directly to the commander’s state of mind when making the transfer. Maj Kirschner was in theatre during the latter portion of MGen Laroche’s tenure as Commander and thus in principle could have inquired directly as to his state of mind, but at no time was Maj Kirschner asked to review or investigate the legality of MGen Laroche’s transfer orders, nor did he believe he independently had cause to do so.Footnote 1429

Maj Kirschner agreed investigation of allegations of this nature would be mandatory under the Technical Directives and MP policy. In the Commission’s view, Maj Kirschner is not the kind of MP to shy away from his investigative duties. His approach to policing could fairly be described as proactive or, as he described it, tenacious – in appropriate circumstances he would consider it appropriate to investigate or take steps such as initiating surveillance based on rumours or newspaper accounts of uncertain veracity in order to substantiate or discount the need for further investigation or prosecution. Maj Kirschner simply did not feel that even such a minimal degree of suspicion existed with respect to the legality of the Commanders’ orders; to the contrary, the Commander’s conduct suggested to Maj Kirschner that appropriate precautions were being taken. He did not feel his obligations as an investigator went so far as to require him to play an ongoing oversight role with respect to Commanders’ decisions.Footnote 1430

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submit Maj Kirschner bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attributed to him during the time period of this complaint.

Maj Kirschner served under BGen Laroche and BGen Thompson.During this rotation, Maj Gribble was the JTF-A TFPM.

During his pre-deployment training, Maj Kirschner was not briefed about the human rights situation in Afghanistan or the post-transfer risk of abuse. The Complainants submit Maj Kirschner stated he had not been aware of theFebruary 2007 Complaint while he was in theatre.Footnote 1431 The Globe and Mail, but did read or hear other media reports about detainee mistreatment treatment byAfghan authorities post-transfer. They submit in his testimony before the Commission, Maj Kirschner could not recall who authored, published or transmitted those media reports. Maj Kirschner was also unaware of a proceeding in Federal Court seeking to halt detainee transfers or human rights reports from theAIHRC, UNHCR, Amnesty International and the U.S. Department of State.Footnote 1432

Maj Kirschner was aware Canada had an agreement in place with Afghanistan forvisitation rights to their detention facilities. When he arrived in theatre, he understood DFAIT was conducting site visits in order to interview prisoners who had been transferred from Canadian custody. The Complainants submitted he was aware at least one DFAIT site visit uncovering an allegation of torture. They submit Maj Kirschner never sought to obtain copies of the reports and never questioned any DFAIT officials about the reports.Footnote 1433

The Complainants note that Maj Kirschner testified he was aware of general and specific allegations of post-transfer torture and mistreatment. He told the Commission the detainee issue was “omnipresent” during his deployment and it was something of which he was “very cognizant.”Footnote 1434 He was also aware of specific allegations of post-transfer torture and was aware that during the previous rotation someone had observed a chair with instruments of torture under it. Maj Kirschner told the Commission he believed this discovery is what prompted the suspension of the transfers.Footnote 1435

Independently of any other investigation, Maj Kirschner deployed investigators around March 2008 to an Afghan prison to collect evidence for an investigation into complaints he had received about MPs who purportedly had mistreated detainees in their custody. According to the Complainants, this suggests he perceived a genuine risk of torture or abuse which they believe should have spurred him to look at the legality of the transfer orders.

The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschner gave mixed messages about his understanding of the CF’s obligations regarding detainee post-transfer abuse under international and domestic law. At one point, Maj Kirschner told the Commission he would be required to investigate pursuant to the technical directive if detainees were knowingly transferred to a risk of torture. However, at a later point, Maj Kirschnerindicated a lack of understanding when questioned by counsel for the Complainants about post-transfer obligations under the Geneva Conventions.Footnote 1436

The Complainants alleged Maj Kirschner’s understanding of the law could not be ascertained with certainty. As well, they were left with “a troubling impression” Maj Kirschner did not have a correct understanding of theJTF-A Commander’s legal obligations.Footnote 1437

Counsel for the Complainants submitted:

  • Maj Kirschner did not investigate thelegality of the Commander’s transfer orders and the matter of post-transfer torture.
  • Maj Kirschner did not collect any evidence.
  • Maj Kirschner did not interviewany witnesses.

The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschner offered several reasons for his failure to investigate. First, Maj Kirschner testified he was extremely busy and had a limited ability to be curious about such matters. Second, Maj Kirschner believed only the Afghans had jurisdiction to investigate incidents that occurred outside Canadian custody. They stated Maj Kirschner said it was not part of his job to conduct investigations of any abuse suffered by a detainee under Afghan custody.

The Complainants submitted Maj Kirschnersimply had confidence in the JTF-A Commander and trusted his judgment when he himself believed there to be a risk of post-transfer abuse.Footnote 1438

For these reasons, the Complainants alleged that Maj Kirschner breached a duty to investigate his Task Force Commander while in theatre. Accordingly, it was their view he breached the professional standard expected of an MP in his position.

Submissions on Behalf of Maj J. KirschnerFootnote 1439

The submissions made on behalf of Maj Kirschner point to a number of factors which are said to demonstrate his actions were reasonable and he met all professional standards.

Maj Kirschner worked in an office of four people responsible for major criminal investigation and mortuary affairs, which involved the processing and repatriation of human remains of Canadian soldiers. During his rotation, the detachment conducted 36 major crimes investigations. It was not his duty or responsibility to act as a “watchdog for the Commander’s transfer orders”.Footnote 1440

Maj Kirschner’s position is that he was very aware of the detainee issue when he deployed. The moratorium on transfers was in place when he arrived in theatre, which suggested to him the process was working and the Commander was exercising due diligence to ensure he was protecting those persons who earlier fell under his responsibility.Footnote 1441

In the course of an ongoing investigation involving CF personnel, Maj Kirschner dispatched two investigators to interview detainees in Afghan prisons. Maj Kirschner instructed the investigators to check for signs of mistreatment. Following a private interview with no NDS personnel present, Maj Kirschner was told the detainees said they were being well treated. This led him to conclude Canadian-transferred detainees were being treated satisfactorily.

Maj Kirschner testified investigators were sent outside the wire normally only in cases where there was substantial and significant cause. Most often, this involved investigating a fatality. The risk to CF personnel in going outside the wire to investigate was so great it could not be undertaken unless there were clear grounds to do so.

The NIS detachment and Maj Kirschner had no involvement in the detainee transfer process and received no information regarding that process or post-transfer monitoring reports. In fact, Maj Kirschner submitted he explicitly directed MPs under his command to distance themselves from anything to do with the detention facility because it would be their responsibility to investigate MPs for any allegations of mistreatment of detainees.Footnote 1442

The NIS detachment had no involvement with ongoing detainee investigations such as Operation Centipede. Maj Kirschner submitted he was unaware of specific newspaper reports or generalized human rights reports, but was generally aware of allegations of abuse regarding detainees transferred to Afghan authorities. He received no specific complaints or allegations which would spur an investigation.

Maj Kirschner noted he was not provided copies of the DFAIT monitoring reports nor was he briefed on their contents. He had no occasion to meet anybody from the NDS. He was aware of some of the content of the reports through open source media reports and did not see a need to request the reports. In fact, there were no reports of allegations of mistreatment by Canadian-transferred detainees following the resumption of transfers during Maj Kirschner’s rotation.

In order to self-initiate an investigation into the Commander’s decision to transfer detainees, Maj Kirschner submitted he would have needed some reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing. Maj Kirschner understood dedicated NIS legal counsel could advise him if he had any questions about legal issues related to the transfer of detainees.Footnote 1443 Maj Kirschner speculated he might, in some cases, undertake further inquiries as a result of a newspaper article or rumour, but would not necessarily commence an investigation on that basis alone.

Maj Kirschner did not believe it was his responsibility to conduct investigations into the treatment of Afghan detainees under Afghan custody, based on his understanding of his mandate, which was limited to investigating Canadians, and the agreements negotiated between Canada and the Government of Afghanistan.

Maj Kirschner testified he never formed a reasonable suspicion during his time in Afghanistan the Task Force Commander had breached the law of armed conflict or international law.

On the basis of his understanding of the mandate and the information available to him, it was submitted that Maj Kirschner acted reasonably and appropriately in carrying out his policing mandate. No complaints or allegations were ever received by him regarding the legality of the command decisions to transfer detainees. Based on his experience as an MP and member of the CF deployed in operations, it was reasonable he had full confidence in the command decision-making process. Maj Kirschner had no reason to doubt the appropriateness of decisions made by senior commanders. In conclusion, Maj Kirschner’s position was that he had not failed to investigate any allegation or set of facts which required investigation.

Conclusions Regarding Maj J. Kirschner

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Maj Kirschner’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • Maj Kirschner demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees. His awareness of post-transfer international legal obligations was sufficient to lead him, without prompting or guidance, to direct MPs under his command to watch out for signs of post-transfer abuse at the NDS facility.
  • Maj Kirschner was also aware of his obligations pursuant to the Technical Directive in place during his rotation, and the TSO 321. In particular, he understood it was his duty to either investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law.
  • Maj Kirschner did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal. He had some understanding of the substance of the reasons for the moratorium on transfers in November 2007 and an awareness of the international attention the detainee question received. He reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he observed his Commander and the Government taking to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer, such as the suspension of transfers until a more robust monitoring regime was in place and the bolstering of the monitoring regime.
  • Maj Kirschner took his duties as NIS detachment commander seriously, and undertook his extremely demanding and resource-challenged role in a professional manner. It is relevant to take into account the stressful and difficult nature of the work Maj Kirschner had to do while in theatre, in particular, in the area of KIAs and mortuary affairs. Given the demands of this work, and the more reactive role of the NIS, it is reasonable that his acquired knowledge of the detainee process and the treatment of detainees post-transfer was minimal. It was also reasonable for him to rely, to a great degree, on others, such as the TFPM and the MP company, to bring information or concerns to him if they existed. No such concerns were brought to his attention.
  • Maj Kirschner reasonably considered his Commander’s behaviour to have demonstrated a willingness to stop transfers where necessary.
  • Maj Kirschner did not have access to important information about the post-transfer process, such as the site visit reports from May onwards, other C4 traffic, the legal opinions the Commander was receiving, and any discussions his Commander may have been having with respect to post-transfer risk assessment. The Commission does not find Maj Kirschner personally blameworthy for the fact that he did not have access to this information. In the absence of access to information about the post-transfer process, and combined with the Commander’s demonstrated willingness to stop transfers in the face of allegations of mistreatment, it was reasonable that Maj Kirschner did not harbour suspicions whether his Commander was illegally ordering detainee transfers.
  • Maj Kirschner was never asked to review or investigate the legality of the transfer orders. The Commission is satisfied that had he been tasked with this, Maj Kirschner would have initiated a proper investigation.

Finding #6: The Commission finds that the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against Major John Kirschner in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude Maj Kirschner breached a duty to investigate his Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer.

16.7 Lieutenant-Colonel (ret’d) William H. Garrick

LCol (ret’d) Garrick joined the military police in 1981 as a Private. Following basic military police training, he was posted to Edmonton and Cold Lake, Alberta, spending five years in each primarily in the areas of patrols and criminal investigations.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was accepted into the university training program for NCO’s and went to the University of Manitoba, completing a degree in criminology. On completion of his military police commissioned officers’ course he was appointed as the section commander with the Special Investigation Unit in Winnipeg.

In 1997 on the creation of the NIS LCol (ret’d) Garrick was posted as the Operations Officer for NIS central region. He was subsequently posted as the operations officer for the Sensitive Investigations Detachment. During that time LCol (ret’d) Garrick was posted to Sarajevo, Bosnia on a tour as a team lead on a multinational investigation.

Upon return to Canada, LCol (ret’d) Garrick was tasked with standing up the investigation support detachment for the NIS which was the surveillance team, criminal intelligence unit, polygraph unit, and computer crime unit. He was appointed to the rank of Major and stayed as the CO of that unit. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was then transferred to the position of Deputy Provost Marshal - Police for a year. He was next posted to Greenwood, Nova Scotia as the main Provost Marshal for the base, overseeing MP operations.

In 2005 LCol (ret’d) Garrick was transferred back to Ottawa as the Senior Operations Officer, Deputy Commanding Officer of the National Investigation Service. Upon his promotion to Lieutenant Colonel in 2006 he was appointed as Commanding Officer of the National Investigation Service, a position held until he retired in July, 2008.Footnote 1444

LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s chain of command was straightforward – he reported exclusively to the CFPM, both on the command and the technical chain. LCol (ret’d) Garrick had almost daily contact with the CFPM about NIS matters and on strategic planning as a senior MP branch specialist. Below him in the MP chain were a deputy CO and a staff officer, and his detachment commanders. He had contact with the NIS detachment commanders in theatre two or more times per week by email.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick told the Commission the purpose of the NIS was to conduct independent investigations of major crimes – large-scale financial crimes, sexual assaults, homicides – as well as investigations potentially implicating senior members of the CF. LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed the type of investigation described in the AIC/BCCLA complaints to the Commission would fall within the NIS mandate and would not be left for investigation by individual MP detachments or units.

The independence of the NIS from the military chain of command was “of paramount importance”, and was to ensure there could be no direction of or interference with investigations by non-MP members. Consistent with this independence, LCol (ret’d) Garrick had no contact with the Task Force Commander, infrequent contact with the CEFCOM commander and received “absolutely” no direction from CEFCOM on how to conduct investigations even when they were being conducted parallel to a commander’s BOI investigation. LCol (ret’d) Garrick had an information reporting relationship with the CEFCOM PM since the chain of command had to be kept informed of NIS investigations in order to address their operational impact, but the manner of conduct of investigations was left to the NIS.Footnote 1445

LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed there was a general sense that MPs in general and the NIS in particular were not always “welcomed with open arms” by the chain of command, but did not feel there was genuine resistance to MPs performing their investigative functions once the parameters and needs of investigations were explained. At times the logistics of supporting investigations could put CF members at great risk. Thus, it is understandable the chain of command would wish to be informed of the significance of the investigation prior to offering the support. By and large LCol (ret’d) Garrick found commanders and others in the chain of command to be helpful when called upon to provide support to the NIS while balancing this with the operational needs of their mission.Footnote 1446

Asked whether he agreed with the statement from army doctrine that the “purpose of the NIS is to support chain of command in the execution of the assigned mission” LCol (ret’d) Garrick indicated this was not stated in language he would have chosen since it does not convey the notion the independent investigative mandate of the NIS might sometimes be at odds with the immediate imperatives of the chain of command. Some NIS duties, such as forensic investigations when CF members were killed by IED’s, directly and clearly supported the mission, but at times investigations might be somewhat disruptive to a mission. Overall, however, the independent investigations of the NIS supported the chain of command by ensuring lawful conduct within the military.Footnote 1447

In LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s view, it was not the role of the NIS to ensure ongoing compliance with military orders, and it was not their role to investigate the general risk of detainee torture in Afghanistan. Their primary role is to respond to complaints raised when there is a potential offence to be investigated. Others, such as the chain of command, were responsible for maintaining ongoing compliance with orders. NIS members are not patrol officers whose job is to continuously maintain law and order; they respond to complaints and follow up leads. LCol (ret’d) Garrick did expect a degree of situational or background awareness such that investigations might arise tangentially out of an existing investigation, or might be self-initiated in appropriate circumstances. He spoke positively about Maj Kirschner’s initiative to have his personnel take note of prison conditions when they were visiting the NDS facility and expected his personnel to look outside the immediate parameters of their investigations. He did not expect proactive efforts to continually monitor legal compliance by commanders – this kind of ongoing “virtue testing” as his counsel termed it is beyond the scope of their mandate, and in fact might go beyond their legal authority to gather information.Footnote 1448

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was aware the CF were transferring detainees to Afghan authorities including the NDS, and he understood it was always the Task Force Commander who made the decision to transfer and MPs who carried out the transfers. He was aware of the transfer agreements from December 2005 and May 2007 and believed it was DFAIT and CSC who were responsible for post-transfer monitoring. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was familiar with TSO 321 as signed by MGen (ret’d) Grant on May 27, 2007 and was familiar with MGen (ret’d) Grant’s transfer decision form, although LCol (ret’d) Garrick was not certain when he became aware of it and he did not know whether it contained a record of the commander’s transfer risk assessment. LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed there was a legal obligation on CF members, including the commander, to ensure detainees were not transferred to a known risk of torture or abuse, although he was not familiar with the particular language of the legal test for transfer articulated by the CEFCOM commander in his directives to the Task Force commander.Footnote 1449

LCol (ret’d) Garrick had read reports from the U.S. State Department, UN and Amnesty International outlining general concerns about the human rights situation in Afghanistan. He viewed these human rights and Rule of Law issues as the reason the CF was deployed to assist the Afghan government. He had not read the AIHRC reports although he was familiar with the organization. He had never seen any reports from DFAIT, whether produced by Mr. Colvin et al prior to the monitoring arrangement or by Messrs Gosselin and Davison afterward, but he assumed DFAIT was producing a record of their site visits. He did not personally request such information from CEFCOM but he understood the NIS obtained some such information in the course of Operation Camel Spider. LCol (ret’d) Garrick had read reports at a strategic level concerning the Rule of Law issues that would relate to the NDS but had never personally been in contact with members of the NDS to assess their professionalism.Footnote 1450

LCol (ret’d) Garrick had received training in the Geneva Conventions and Laws of Armed Combat during his MP training, and he tried to ensure his members attended a legal course prior to deployment. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was surprised to hear MWO (ret’d) Girard had testified he had no such training since his early days in the CF. However, in his view, advanced training in these areas of law was not necessary, since the basic concepts were “relatively straightforward” and legal advisers were available on short notice for any areas of uncertainty.Footnote 1451

Responsibility for training NIS personnel for deployment was held jointly by the CFPM, LCol (ret’d) Garrick and the CF chain of command. There were clear combat readiness requirements which were non-negotiable, but one week of training was dedicated specifically to NIS duties. Investigation of detainee issues as a whole were the top priority and “they all knew it was our number one priority”.Footnote 1452

LCol (ret’d) Garrick felt there was sufficient opportunity for information to be conveyed from one rotation to the next. Each deployed NIS detachment commander was sent on a pre-deployment visit, although it was usually when the incumbent was on leave. Returning detachment commanders were brought into training to speak about issues and expectations when deployed. There was a one-week overlap period between deployments, and in any event, most detainee investigations were occurring from detachments in Canada.Footnote 1453

In terms of specific allegations, LCol (ret’d) Garrick was aware of the first AIC/BCCLA complaint to this Commission, and promptly arranged for the RCMP to investigate these allegations since they involved his direct commander, the CFPM. This resulted in a thorough and detailed investigative report by Inspectors Rideout and BlizardFootnote 1454 with which LCol (ret’d) Garrick was also familiar. He was also familiar with the facts underlying Professor Attaran’s allegations from the March 2007 Globe and Mail article since it was the subject of one of the NIS investigations arising out of Col Noonan’s Federal Court affidavit. He read the Graeme Smith articles from the Globe and Mail and launched investigations (canvassed in Operation Centipede) into some of the allegations contained in them.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was not familiar with the allegations outlined in DFAIT site visit reports from June 2007 or September 2007 although he was aware there had been at least one cessation of transfers in May or June 2007 due to the investigation surrounding conditions one detainee was held in during the hiatus in transfers. LCol (ret’d) Garrick became aware of the November 2007 suspension of transfers when the CFPM Site Inspection Visit report became available; he did not see the DFAIT site visit reports from November 2007 but assumed the reason for the cessation was post-transfer abuse issues. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was also not aware of the factors which led to the resumption of transfers.Footnote 1455

LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed information such as was contained in the site visit reports, summary of allegations, commander’s letters and DFAIT letters would potentially be relevant to investigators if an investigation were undertaken into the legality of the commander’s transfer decisions. He agreed information concerning the pattern of transfers, visits and abuse allegations would also be worth looking at in assessing allegations of abuse and allegations of unlawful transfer orders. In LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s view, the fact transfers were suspended from time to time as a response to abuse allegations, and the fact more robust monitoring measures were implemented, both suggested the commander was “taking the correct actions that I would have expected to take place.”Footnote 1456

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was aware of the Federal Court application brought by Amnesty International Canada and BCCLA for an injunction prohibiting detainee transfers He had read the decision of the Federal CourtFootnote 1457 wherein the safety of detainee transfers was questioned, but LCol (ret’d) Garrick was satisfied, based on his own knowledge of the general human rights situation in Afghanistan, as well as information on the checks and balances in place (learned through the Camel Spider investigation), sufficient safeguards had been put into place by CanadA. Had problems with the legality arisen, he noted there were many personnel who would be in a position to detect it and inform the NIS - the TF Commander’s staff and legal advisers, CF personnel conducting the transfer, CEFCOM personnel who reviewed the orders, CSC, DFAIT and RCMP personnel on the ground in the prisons. LCol (ret’d) Garrick felt if there was any legal concern about the transfer decisions or process leading to it, he would be made aware of it.Footnote 1458

LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not request any information from DFAIT, CSC, RCMP or other CF personnel about prison site visits or prison conditions. LCol (ret’d) Garrick felt the general information they could provide would be similar to what he already knew from his review of human rights reports, and he did not feel it would be appropriate to request information without an investigation having been initiated:

And they just generally are not going to wander through National Defence Headquarters asking if anybody has information relating to an issue so they may then form something to investigate.Footnote 1459

LCol (ret’d) Garrick said he had shared the Federal Court decision with the investigators on Operation Camel Spider and this resulted in a conversation with Inspector Gfellner about keeping his eyes open for detainee issues beyond the specific complaints Camel Spider was investigating. LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not provide it to the investigators on Operation Centipede looking into the allegations from the Globe and Mail articles because he originally conceived these would be “Camel Spider 2”, a spin-off investigation, rather than a separate operation. LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed that the Federal Court opinion raised some concerns, and felt the ongoing investigations would sufficiently cover the appropriate areas if there were any question about the legality of transfer orders.Footnote 1460

In addition to Operation Camel Spider and other NIS investigations, LCol (ret’d) Garrick was aware there was a chain of command Board of Inquiry (BOI) into detainee issues, although he was not privy to the particulars of that investigation.
