LCol (ret’d) Garrick was aware as well of the MPCC investigation into both Professor Attaran’s complaint matter and the February, 2007 AIC/BCCLA complaint concerning the CFPM. To his knowledge, the NIS was not provided with LCol Boot’s CEFCOM fact-check arising out of the allegations in Graeme Smith’s article, despite the fact that CEFCOM requested an NIS investigation into the allegation CF members encouraged a detainee to provide information to avoid abuse. LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed information from the CEFCOM investigations and DFAIT reports would be potentially helpful to the NIS investigations both in terms of verification of facts and prioritizing those investigations.Footnote 1461

Detainee investigations constituted a major proportion, approximately 75%, of the NIS workload during the period covered in this complaint, and were their number one priority. LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s MPs were also tasked with many other duties, including between 400 and 500 ongoing major investigations, investigation of every instance of escalation of force in theatre, investigation of IED attacks on CF personnel, forensic investigations when CF members were wounded or killed in action, retrieval and identification of fallen CF service members, mortuary duty and repatriation of remains. The workload could fairly be described as overwhelming, and in theatre it took a physical and psychological toll on NIS personnel. LCol (ret’d) Garrick said no NIS member came back from theatre the same person, and for some rotations three of four returning members would take their leave from the CF.Footnote 1462

Operation Centipede was created to address a backlog of potential investigations stemming from the Camel Spider investigation. LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s original plan was to direct each incident to an appropriate regional NIS office for assessment and, if warranted, full investigation. The reasoning was the regional offices would be proximate to the returning deployed troops (for example, ROTO 3 consisted of troops based in Edmonton, ROTO 4 were from Valcartier) and thus would be in the best position to conduct interviews. It quickly became apparent to LCol (ret’d) Garrick that this plan would not work for various logistic reasons, including the prioritization of Operation Camel Spider. After a period of dormancy, Maj Bolduc’s Central Region NIS detachment was directed to halt or wrap up every investigation save an ongoing major fraud investigation and to proceed with the outstanding detainee investigations under the umbrella of Operation Centipede. Operation Centipede was formally initiated on March 19, 2008.Footnote 1463

LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed that the NIS investigations including Operation Camel Spider, Operation Centipede and other detainee-related investigations dealt with allegations both of CF abuse and post-transfer abuse, and did not explicitly deal with the legality of transfer orders. Maj Kirschner testified he was advised by LCol (ret’d) Garrick to be alert to detainee issues generally, but had not been asked specifically to look at the legality of the commanders’ transfer orders.Footnote 1464 LCol (ret’d) Garrick testified he believed the documentary evidence collected during the Operation Camel Spider investigation “involved the entire holistic detainee process” even though its specific mandate was an allegation of CF abuse of detainees.Footnote 1465 Overall, LCol (ret’d) Garrick expected any detainee related issues, including the legality of the commander’s transfer orders, would be picked up in the course of one of the several ongoing investigations, particularly Operation Camel Spider, Operation Centipede, and the Rideout-Blizard investigation.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s comments on particular investigations shed some insight into his reasoning. LCol (ret’d) Garrick pointed out that GO 2008–6918 dealt with the allegation in Col Noonan’s affidavit of CF members becoming aware of post-transfer abuse and doing nothing, but also in its synopsis posed the question why the chain of command did not report this to MPs. LCol (ret’d) Garrick said this meant his investigators would look at:

[…] if in fact there were any legal issues with respect to the transfer process. And then as a follow on to that, would there have been any issues that would have given rise to the chain of command reporting this to the military police.Footnote 1466

In other words, the conduct of the chain of command was to be examined, albeit not their transfer orders in this particular investigation.

Regarding the investigation of Graeme Smith’s Globe and Mail article containing a similar allegation, covered under GO 2008–6920, LCol (ret’d) Garrick described his expectations:

I mean, there’s some obvious things; actions of the CF members if in fact they were in the area and did not take any action. Then, you know, following to that is again looking at the whole transfer process.Footnote 1467

LCol (ret’d) Garrick said he would have expected some factual follow up to this article based on more than simply reading the article – attempts to independently verify the information such as were conducted by CEFCOM, for example. The exclusive focus in this GO on whether CF members had actually abused the detainee and the refusal to consider such allegations as they were “based on hearsay” fell short of LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s expectations. While LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed with the general proposition expressed in the GO summary that only offences within NIS jurisdiction would merit consideration he disagreed with the investigator’s conclusion that nothing in the article merited NIS consideration.Footnote 1468 In fairness, LCol (ret’d) Garrick had retired as NIS commander when Operation Centipede was completed. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was not ultimately responsible for the fact that the concluded investigations fell well short of his expectations.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed the entirety of Operation Centipede took far longer to complete than would be ideal for a police investigation. LCol (ret’d) Garrick had difficult decisions to make with the resources at his disposal. Management of NIS priorities was one of his major challenges. At any given time, LCol (ret’d) Garrick would have available approximately half of a full-strength contingent of 120-124 personnel. Specific factors which played a role in setting priorities when there were detainee investigations were the degree to which the CF were implicated in the allegations, the time sensitivity of the case, the solvability of the case, attentiveness to victims of sexual assault or other serious violent crimes, attentiveness to the families of murder victims and fallen soldiers, and an assessment of the risks faced by investigators and in fact by the potential victims in conducting investigations.Footnote 1469

During the period May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008, Operation Camel Spider (the investigation into allegations of detainee abuse raised in January 2007 by Professor Attaran) was given top priority and required a tremendous proportion of NIS resources.Footnote 1470 Further allegations arising from Camel Spider were placed on hold until the primary investigation could be completed. As noted, these allegations were for the most part eventually compiled into Operation Centipede and were not investigated until a year or more after they arose.

Another resource challenge was the shut-down of entire detachments for pre-deployment training, deployment to theatre, and post-deployment recovery from such issues as physical or psychological trauma. Transfers into and out of the NIS resulted in loss of personnel for training, and the need for a period of mentorship for some inexperienced officers. In addition, particular task forces (some unrelated to detainees) occupied personnel for extended periods.Footnote 1471

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was not responsible for determining the level of resources allocated to the NIS. He could, and did, request resources from the CFPM when appropriate, and the CFPM was responsive to the degree possible, but there were limits to the human resources that could be allocated to his purposes. LCol (ret’d) Garrick indicated it was a problem of human, and not financial, resources that presented him with difficulty.Footnote 1472

LCol (ret’d) Garrick described the test for launching an investigation:

  • You referred in your testimony to conducting investigations [mis-transcribed “information”] based on police evidentiary standards. Can you explain what you mean by that?
  • Yeah, I mean every time we conduct an investigation, we’re conducting it either in support of a potential service offence prosecution, or a Canadian criminal court prosecution. Therefore, all the investigations are held to the same standard we hold in Canadian criminal prosecution for evidentiary purposes.
  • Okay, and what would be the standard to commence such an investigation?
  • We would have to have more than a suspicion. We have to have reasonable grounds to enter into the investigation.
  • […]
  • And once the threshold – I might have asked you this with respect to the duty to investigate. What’s the threshold for commencing a criminal investigation?
  • It would be reasonable grounds to believe that an offence [within the NIS mandate] has taken place […]Footnote 1473

Asked how investigations unfold in practice, LCol (ret’d) Garrick described a process involving an assessment of the initial facts or complaint in order to determine whether some sort of more comprehensive or formal investigation ought to be initiated. This assessment phase would potentially involve preliminary interviews, follow-up on leads, and possibly seeking legal advice to determine the merits of conducting a full-fledged investigation with a view to pursuing prosecution for an offence. LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed it would be appropriate to consider all facts, both supportive of and counter-indicative of the commission of an offence, in order to properly consider the extent to which an investigation would proceed. The investigative assessment could be undertaken on as little basis as a rumour or an account from a newspaper, depending on the facts and circumstances of the case, but ideally would look at “all the factors”. This investigative assessment phase, prior to forming reasonable grounds to investigate, is “absolutely” part of the policing function.Footnote 1474

LCol (ret’d) Garrick also agreed MPs could self-initiate investigations or investigative assessments where appropriate, noting the Operation Centipede investigations, including the investigations into the March and April 2007 Globe and Mail articles, were examples of MP self-initiated investigations. Based on observations or facts which came to their attention during Operation Camel Spider, new investigations were initiated into other detainee-related matters despite the fact nobody had levied a complaint or requested an investigation;Footnote 1475 it goes without saying the initial evidence in some of those investigations fell well short of “reasonable grounds to believe an offence had taken place”, yet the matters were appropriately flagged to be further examined. LCol (ret’d) Garrick said self-initiation of an investigation could come from “a variety of triggers” – in essence, if the facts suggest it is appropriate to take a further look into something, an MP could do so. The Commission is satisfied with LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s understanding of the appropriate method of determining whether to conduct investigative assessments, full investigations, and self-initiation of investigations.

Based on all this testimony, the Commission understands LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s position essentially to be that an initial assessment can occur to determine if there are reasonable grounds to pursue a more extensive investigation with a focused end of criminal or service offence prosecution. Care must be exercised when examining LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s position to distinguish the right to conduct an assessment or investigation, versus the duty to do so. LCol (ret’d) Garrick was entirely clear in stating that if an MP formed the reasonable suspicion a commander had committed an offence such as unlawful transfer of a detainee, the MP was under a positive duty to investigate.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was equally clear and consistent in stating that at no time did he form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Afghanistan Commander had issued such an illegal order. LCol (ret’d) Garrick cited the evidence in support of the contrary view, that commanders were taking their transfer decisions quite seriously and were continually taking steps to mitigate the risk of transfer to torture, ceasing to transfer at times when it appeared to be unsafe to do so. He also noted the more broadly based initiatives by the Government of Canada with DFAIT and CSC personnel in place, as well as the fact the Commander had a team of advisers including legal advisers to assist him in making transfer decisions. LCol (ret’d) Garrick felt, if an unlawful transfer order had been issued, he would have been notified.Footnote 1476

LCol (ret’d) Garrick noted the NIS was never asked by the Chain of Command during the period May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008, to examine whether the commander fulfilled his obligation to ensure that monitoring safeguards were in place. As well, there was never a request by any member of the public to investigate the legality of the transfer orders.Footnote 1477 LCol (ret’d) Garrick agreed if an MP had been provided all of the information contained in the DFAIT site visit reports and summaries, had been aware that DFAIT visits were not occurring for substantial periods of time, and had seen the correspondence from the Commander in November 2007 describing the situation as “amber” and expressing concerns about the lack of monitoring information being received, “it might trigger some further inquiry” to determine what factors had entered into the transfer decisions leading to the abuse allegation disclosed in Mr. Gosselin’s report of November 5, 2007.Footnote 1478

During a conversation with the CFPM on June 12, 2008, LCol (ret’d) Garrick and Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore discussed the fact the AIC/BCCLA complaint to this Commission of June 12, 2008 was about the legality of the commander’s transfer decisions. They felt any illegality with respect to transfer orders would be uncovered by the existing NIS investigations, the BOI and other checks and balances.Footnote 1479 Their approach was to see what information would be derived from the other investigations and then consider whether there was anything about the transfer orders to investigate. Thus, despite the strategic importance of detainee abuse issues and LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s view that the legality of transfer orders was implicitly covered by the first AIC/BCCLA complaint, this issue was not directly addressed by LCol (ret’d) Garrick or the NIS at any time between May 3, 2007 and June 12, 2008.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified he had previously discussed this issue with LCol (ret’d) Garrick sometime after the February 21, 2007 AIC/BCCLA complaint:

At the same time I had asked him to have a look at the NIS investigations that were ongoing to see if there was anything in there that may suggest a Commander had committed an offence by transferring these detainees; to ask questions or raise the issue with his investigators. And at the same point in time, I told him that I would be taking opportunities in regular conversation with Commanders just to raise the issue to see what they said and would also followup with the Task Force Provost Marshals at the time.Footnote 1480

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was examined by Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s counsel one day prior to Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s testimony and was not asked to confirm this conversation. LCol (ret’d) Garrick otherwise made no mention of such a conversation in his testimony. LCol (ret’d) Garrick had indicated everyone knew detainee issues in general were a top priority and they were to be aware of detainee issues in general, but direct focus on the legality of the transfer decisions is absent from his testimony and from the NIS records prior to June 12, 2008.

It appears to the Commission the commanders’ transfer decisions came into sharp focus for LCol (ret’d) Garrick only when the Complainants in this matter issued their second complaint on June 12, 2008. To the degree the issue was being implicitly addressed in the other ongoing investigations, it occurred during the course of investigations which proceeded during his tenure at an unacceptably slow pace as a result of the extreme caseload, resource pressure and prioritization that had to occur.Footnote 1481

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submit LCol (ret’d) Garrick bore responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they attribute to him during the time period of this complaint.Footnote 1482

It was submitted LCol (ret’d) Garrick, as the CO of the NIS reporting directly to the CFPM, was responsible for overseeing all serious and/or sensitive criminal investigations by the CF military police. Further, the NIS is vested with independence from the normal CF chain of command and is the branch responsible for investigating allegations related to harm to detainees. The Complainants’ submission points to LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s testimony that issues concerning detainees were his top priority and occupied 75% of his time,Footnote 1483 and he was aware of international reports about torture in Afghanistan and had read Graeme Smith’s articles in the Globe and Mail.Footnote 1484

LCol (ret’d) Garrick testified he was aware Canadian officials were monitoring detainees in Afghan custody. Although LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not specifically ask his NIS officers to seek out this information, he believed it appropriate for the MPs to make occasional inquiries into detainee treatment post-transfer. LCol (ret’d) Garrick indicated this kind of inquisitiveness was part of their job, and he would expect MPs to look outside their general parameters when they’re doing their business.Footnote 1485

It was submitted LCol (ret’d) Garrick believed he did not have to look into the DFAIT monitoring visits himself, and said there was no reason to follow up on these reports. The Complainants submit LCol (ret’d) Garrick later acknowledged such information would have been useful to his investigators.Footnote 1486

The Complainants submitted that LCol (ret’d) Garrick acknowledged a discussion of the February 2007 complaint with the CFPM Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, where they decided that an outside police force should investigate given that the allegations were directed partly against the CFPM. The RCMP was approached and asked to look into the allegations. Supt. Wayne Rideout and Supt. Wade Blizard were the senior RCMP officers tasked with the investigation.Footnote 1487

Following a three-month investigation of the scope of the CFPM’s role in detainee transfers (commencing March 13, 2007) and numerous interviews, the RCMP submitted a final report. The investigators stated in the report they would consider “the existence of any knowledge, information or intelligence of actual detainee abuse, post-handover, known by the Military Police, or indeed DND” to be significant.Footnote 1488 According to counsel for the Complainants, the RCMP sought any kind of information about post-handover abuse which was known by, or ought to have been known by, the CFPM. The June 2007 final RCMP report concluded there was no evidence of an offence, in part based on their understanding there was no “knowledge, information or intelligence” indicating post-transfer torture and abuse by Afghan authorities.Footnote 1489

Counsel for the Complainants submitted it was “unfortunate” the RCMP investigators had concluded their investigation in the absence of critical information: namely, the graphic first-hand accounts of torture heard by DFAIT officials in Kabul and Kandahar only a few weeks earlier. Counsel submitted that it appeared all of the RCMP’s interviews were carried out before the DFAIT visits elicited the disturbing allegations on June 4 and 5, 2007 and it is not known why this information was not shared with the RCMP before they submitted their report.Footnote 1490

The Complainants submit LCol (ret’d) Garrick said he could not share the DFAIT reports or discuss the suspension of transfers in June 2007 when he met with the RCMP investigators after reading their conclusions because he did not have such information. They questioned why LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not take further action after he learned about the allegations in the DFAIT reports.Footnote 1491

When Operation Centipede commenced to address numerous allegations that CF personnel had illegally or improperly carried out their duties in the handling of Afghan detainees, the Complainants submit LCol (ret’d) Garrick, as the CO of the NIS, had overall responsibility for these investigations. They included the following allegations:Footnote 1492

  • a detainee was executed by Afghan authorities post handover and tossed in a ditch;
  • a soldier reported witnessing a detainee being beaten in the head by Afghan soldiers;
  • a detainee transferred to an Afghan authority was subsequently taken behind a building and executed;
  • CF personnel witnessed a detainee being abused post-handover; and
  • a CF captain alluded in an email that Afghan authorities abused detainees in their custody.

Although LCol (ret’d) Garrick testified significant resource constraints forced him to prioritize investigations as necessary, the Complainants submitted such “evidence is troubling given the weight that LCol (ret’d) Garrick appeared to place on the investigations in other contexts”.Footnote 1493 In his testimony, LCol (ret’d) Garrick said repeatedly one of the main reasons why he did not look into the subsequent allegations of detainee abuse was the fact the Operation Centipede investigations were underway. The Complainants pointed in particular to LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s testimony that he believed the Globe and Mail investigations would look into those issues, and submit this explanation is “wholly insufficient”.Footnote 1494

Submissions on Behalf of LCol (ret’d) W. Garrick

The submissions made on behalf of LCol (ret’d) Garrick identified a number of factors which it was said demonstrated his actions were reasonable and that he met all professional standards.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was Commanding officer of the CFNIS during the period of this complaint. He was not notified he was a subject in this proceeding until after he had retired from the CF.Footnote 1495

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he was satisfied the NIS detachment in Afghanistan was fulfilling investigative functions which related to operational issues, including the use of force by CF members, and conducting post mortem forensic investigations of CF members killed or injured in the line of duty. He was satisfied all of the subject NIS investigators were trained adequately. He was also satisfied that if NIS investigators encountered a complicated investigative issue or one outside their normal mandate, independent legal advice was available.Footnote 1496

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he had read some high level strategic material pertaining to the Rule of Law in Afghanistan which discussed the NDS, as well as UN Human Rights Reports, US State Department Reports and some Amnesty International reports. Although familiar with the AIHRC, LCol (ret’d) Garrick had not read its reports. LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he believed the CF was in Afghanistan due to the overall atmosphere relating to human rights in that country.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick acknowledged being aware of the transfer of Afghan detainees by the CF to Afghan authorities during the relevant time period and understood the decision to transfer was always made by the Task Force Commander. He submitted he knew there was a process in place for determining whether a detainee would be transferred or released, but he was unaware of the particulars of the decision making process. He was aware of both Canada-Afghanistan detainee transfer arrangements and understood DFAIT and Correctional Service Canada personnel were monitoring detainees post-transfer.Footnote 1497

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he did not receive any DFAIT site visit reports and was unaware of their contents or their existence.Footnote 1498 He acknowledged being factually aware of how the detainees were handled and stated he was comfortable in knowing that a process was put in place by the Canadian Government to ensure Canada would be aware of any problems.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he was aware of the February 2007 Amnesty International Canada and British Columbia Civil Liberties Association complaint, and responded by requesting an RCMP investigation into the allegations against the CFPM.

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted that allegations of detainee mistreatment would not be sufficient on their own for him to form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commander had committed an offence. Information being uncovered by the NIS through other investigations was leading LCol (ret’d) Garrick to a different understanding about detainee abuse allegations than was being portrayed in the newspapers.Footnote 1499 LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted that he expressed concern at the time to the CFPM about personnel constraints impeding progress of the ongoing detainee investigations in OP CENTIPEDE. The CFPM agreed to give OP CENTIPEDE investigations low priority.Footnote 1500 LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he had been aware of pauses in detainee transfers during in June and November 2007, although he was unsure of when he became aware of the latter. LCol (ret’d) Garrick said he assumed an incident had taken place which caused the Commander sufficient concern to cease the transfers.Footnote 1501

LCol (ret’d) Garrick was confident the situation in the Afghan prison system was monitored by a wide range of government departments and military officials all the way up to the CDS, and any of them could have brought forward a complaint for investigation. On the basis of additional information he had not seen previously, LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he was satisfied in hindsight that the CF and the whole-of-government were taking appropriate action.Footnote 1502 LCol (ret’d) Garrick stated he agreed any allegation of detainee mistreatment by CF members would result in a mandatory investigation.

During the relevant period, LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he received no complaint or allegation the Task Force Commander had knowingly ordered the transfer of a detainee to a risk of torture by Afghan authorities. He submitted, if such an allegation had come forth, the NIS would have investigated.Footnote 1503 LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he did not expect the MPs under his command to be collecting information on detainee transfers in the absence of a specific ongoing investigation. He did not expect them to go into Afghanistan prisons to investigate alleged complaints made by detainees about their post-transfer treatment.Footnote 1504

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted there were many other investigations looking at the legality of the Commander’s detainee transfer order, including Boards of Inquiry and this Commission, and any discovery of wrongdoing would have been detected and he would have been informed.Footnote 1505 LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he would have been aware if the Task Force Commander had given an unlawful order because there were ample checks and balances in place.Footnote 1506

LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted that at no time did he form a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commander had transferred detainees to a real risk of torture. Nor did LCol (ret’d) Garrick ever feel any of his subordinates failed in their duties with respect to assessing whether or not an investigation was required.Footnote 1507

In conclusion, LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted he acted reasonably and appropriately in carrying out his policing mandate. No complaints or allegations were ever received by him regarding the legality of the Commander’s decisions to transfer detainees. Based on his experience as an MP and member of the CF deployed in operations, LCol (ret’d) Garrick submitted it was reasonable for him to have full confidence in the command decision making process and to have no reason to doubt the appropriateness of the decisions made by senior commanders.

Conclusions Regarding LCol (Ret’d) W. Garrick

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • LCol (ret’d) Garrick demonstrated knowledge and awareness of the international legal principles potentially applicable to the illegal transfer of detainees, and he understood it was his duty either to investigate, or more likely, ensure the investigation of any allegations of breaches of international law.
  • LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not receive any direct allegations or complaints that the orders to transfer detainees generally, or to transfer any detainee in particular, were or could be illegal until the Complainants submitted their letter to this Commission on June 12, 2008. He then believed that the existing investigations, particularly Operation Camel Spider and Operation Centipede, would uncover any evidence of illegal transfer orders if it existed.
  • Just prior to the period of this complaint LCol (ret’d) Garrick had exhibited an awareness of the necessity of investigating any allegations concerning detainees by ensuring that investigations into the allegations made in the Globe and Mail articles were included in the NIS investigations which became Operation Centipede.
  • LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s tenure as CO of CFNIS ended shortly after receipt of the June 12, 2008 complaint letter and at that time, there were ongoing investigations which he expected would be thoroughly conducted.
  • The Commission does not find that LCol (ret’d) Garrick is at fault for the fact that the NIS investigations were not pursued promptly and thoroughly between May 3, 2007 and June 12, 2008. The NIS does not have infinite resources, and he adequately explained to the Commission the profoundly strained resources of the NIS during this period of time. He also adequately explained the manner in which discretion was exercised to prioritize NIS investigations as he did. It was ultimately within his discretion as CO of the CFNIS to consider the disposition of his force and the concentration of his resources on any particular investigation area, so long as this was reasonably done.
  • Based on what he knew, including particularly his reliance on the fact that other Government agencies and components of the CF were involved in detainee monitoring, it was reasonable that LCol (ret’d) Garrick did not harbour any suspicions whether Commanders had issued unlawful transfer orders. He was aware of the human rights background, the media attention to the issue, and ongoing investigations of complaints into related issues, and reasonably balanced these concerns against the measures he understood were being taken to guard against potential mistreatment following transfer.

Finding #7: The Commission finds the allegations made by AIC and BCCLA against LCol (ret’d) William Garrick in the June 12, 2008 complaint are unsubstantiated. Viewing the evidence as a whole, the Commission finds no grounds to conclude that LCol William (ret’d) Garrick breached a duty to investigate the Task Force Commander while in theatre, or to cause such an investigation to occur. The Commission concludes his actions under the circumstances prevailing at the time met the standard of a reasonable police officer.

16.8 Captain (N) (ret’d) Steven Moore

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was appointed CFPM in June 2005 and served in that capacity until June 15, 2009, a year after the end date of this complaint. Shortly thereafter, he took full retirement from the Canadian Forces. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was the CFPM for the entire period of the Amnesty/BCCLA complaint, being May 3, 2007 to June 12, 2008. In this capacity, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore reported directly to the Vice Chief of the Defence Staff.Footnote 1508

In November 2007, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore took command, in his capacity as CFPM, of a formation called the Canadian Forces Military Police Group. This group consisted of the National Investigation Service, the Military Police Security Service, the Canadian Forces Prison and Detention Barracks and the Canadian Forces Military Police Academy.Footnote 1509 Except for members of the NIS, at no point during the timeframe of this complaint did Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore have command responsibilities for the MPs involved in or with the Afghanistan deployment, such as the TFPM and other members of the MP company in theatre, and the CEFCOM PM.Footnote 1510

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s evidence can be divided into three subject areas within the context of this failure to investigate complaint. First, as with all subjects, the Commission has looked at the extent to which Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had access to information about the detainee transfer process, the risks post transfer in Afghanistan, and the Task Force Commanders’ decisions to transfer, and whether the information he had access to should have caused him to investigate the transfer decisions. Second, the Commission will address the evidence as it relates to Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s command responsibility for the NIS, in particular, the nature of his involvement with Operation Centipede. The third subject area relates to concerns raised by the CFPM about the MP command and control structure, and the impact this may have had on the ability of the military police to carry out its policing work. Of note, as of April 1, 2011, the MP command structure changed. As the Commission understands it, the CFPM now has a command relationship with MPs in theatre when they are carrying out their policing functions.

16.8.1 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s Access to Information about the Detainee Process and Detainee Treatment

During the time relevant to this complaint, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore held the most senior position within the MP organization, but testified he was not kept in the loop on basic detainee information coming to Ottawa from in-theatre. For example, he was unaware of early information about the detainee process, such as the fact the ROTO 1 TFPM had been designated as the national point of contact for detainee issues in-theatre. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had no access to the C4 reports generated in 2006 and 2007 by Richard Colvin, on topics such as ICRC cooperation concerns and the conditions in Afghan prisons.Footnote 1511 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said the CEFCOM Provost Marshals and the TFPMs did not generally come to him to discuss issues related to the post-transfer treatment of detainees, or raise such issues in meetings.Footnote 1512

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not aware of the high-level discussions occurring in early 2007 between DND, DFAIT and others about changes to the detainee transfer process. He was aware of the more major media reports coming out about the detainee process, including the Globe and Mail articles from Graeme Smith so often discussed in these proceedings.Footnote 1513

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not informed of the April 2007 suspension of transfers until well after the fact.Footnote 1514 He was aware the original transfer arrangement was revised, but could not say exactly when he acquired this knowledge, agreeing he may have learned of the new arrangement through the media.Footnote 1515 The fact a new monitoring regime was being implemented, though, did not cause him to question whether a particular individual, such as the Task Force Commander, had committed a criminal offence. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore felt, instead, the need to implement a new regime spoke to a need to improve government policy: “I felt that the improvements or previous insufficiencies, if you want to call them that, spoke to government policy rather than [an] offence by any particular individual.”Footnote 1516

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not aware around this time certain MPs under Maj Hudson’s command had concerns about their own personal liability in actually doing the handovers. This was something he would have liked to have known.Footnote 1517

When the new site visit regime was put in place, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not see any of the site visit reports until seeing them as a result of disclosure from this Commission.Footnote 1518 He knew site visits were occurring, but felt, if individuals within the process saw what they felt constituted negligence or an offence, it would be reported to the military police. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not feel so curious about the process that he needed to ask to see the results of those visits, and, as discussed below, he felt this would have been seen as an “intrusion”.Footnote 1519

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not learn about the November 2007 suspension of detainee transfers until January 2008, as a result of an in-theatre MP Staff Inspection Visit. As noted in the Commission’s discussion about CEFCOM, the fact he learned so late was likely due to a snag in information flow somewhere along the technical chain between the CEFCOM PM, Maj Laflamme, the CANOSCOM PM, LCol Taylor, and the CFPM.Footnote 1520 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore lamented the convoluted nature of the technical chain flowing from the TFPM in Afghanistan to himself, suggesting it was something he tried regularly to improve during his tenure.Footnote 1521

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was unaware of the November 25, 2007 letter from MGen Laroche (then BGen) setting out his decision to suspend transfers and the reasons for doing so, until he was shown it during his appearance before the Commission on December 1, 2010. Similarly, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not view any of the correspondence drafted by BGen Juneau (then Col) and MGen Laroche, in which they set out their concerns about the transfer process, and the lack of visits in October 2007.Footnote 1522

When Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore learned of the suspension of transfers in January 2008, he was not advised of the reasons behind the suspension. He did recall a discussion around Christmas 2007 with the Vice Chief of the Defence Staff about the possibility of MPs conducting inspections of Afghan prisons, which he advised the VCDS the military police had the expertise to conduct. In fact, he noted the TFPM at the time, Maj Zybala, was a former Commandant of the CF Service Prison and Detention Barracks. Nothing seems to have developed from this discussion, and the military police were never tasked with this role. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore inquired with the VCDS as to whether he should begin to work on the possibility of the military police doing the visits, but was told by the VCDS the military was stretched too thin, and he was negotiating with other branches of the government, to have them do the monitoring: “… if that failed, then he would come back to me.”Footnote 1523

While Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified he did not learn of the specific reasons for suspension, in the context of his conversations with the VCDS, he learned some of the site visits to transferred detainees had created some concern, and so they were dealing with this by exploring more ways to look at the monitoring program. The VCDS was not more specific about the reports, and did not mention allegations of abuse. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s perception was the military police were potentially being sought out for background and experience “that could potentially be complementary to that process.”Footnote 1524

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified that around the same time, he also had a conversation with Maj Zybala about how the TFPM felt the detainee process was working, and if there were any issues to be examined. Maj Zybala told the Commission he spoke twice with the CFPM while in theatre, but Maj Zybala did not expand, nor was he asked to expand, on the nature of those conversations.Footnote 1525 It seems likely one of the conversations to which Maj Zybala was referring was this one, mentioned by Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore described the nature of the conversation as follows:

Well, I did have a conversation as well with Major Zybala who’s Task Force Provost Marshal at the time. Talked to him about the process itself, if he had confidence in the process, if he saw issues that we should be investigating and also make him alive to the fact that it was being discussed now that we may need some of his people to do these visits.Footnote 1526

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore recalled specifically he contacted Maj Zybala at home around Christmas time, i.e., while Maj Zybala was on leave in Canada, to have the particular conversation about MPs assisting with the site visit process.Footnote 1527

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said he followed the proceedings launched by Amnesty/BCCLA in Federal Court, but did not read the 2008 judgments at any point prior to the end date of this complaint.Footnote 1528

Despite the limited nature of his information, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said he asked questions of a number of people about the detainee process, including detainee treatment post-transfer. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had concerns about this issue from the time it began to attract scrutiny, which, for him, started with the first Amnesty/BCCLA complaint dated February 21, 2007.Footnote 1529 The Complainants cited what they called “highly credible reports on Afghanistan” from bodies such as the AIHRC, the UN, and the US State Department. These reports described a risk of torture and abuse in the Afghan prison system. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said he had actually heard general reports about torture in Afghanistan even before reading the first Amnesty/BCCLA complaint, although he did not read the reports first hand.Footnote 1530 The particular reports cited within this complaint letter did not cause Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore particular concern because it was his assumption the Government of Canada, in crafting its detainee policy, would have taken all of this information into account:

What I felt was that the government, when they craft their policy would take, they would have access to all of these and much more … my assumption was that they would be taking specific measures and negotiations with the government of Afghanistan to develop a process and get reassurances that where Canadian Forces were transferring detainees that they would be free of risk of torture.Footnote 1531

Nevertheless, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore took several steps after seeing the first complaint. He viewed it as a criminal allegation against himself personally, so he ordered LCol (ret’d) Garrick to report it to the NIS, and to request they investigate it, if they felt appropriate. Ultimately, this task would be taken on by RCMP investigators. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore intentionally asked not to be briefed on the matter. At the same time, he asked LCol (ret’d) Garrick to have a look at any of the existing NIS investigations to see if they revealed information suggesting a need to investigate post-transfer abuse. At the same point in time, he advised LCol (ret’d) Garrick he would take the opportunity in regular conversation with Commanders to raise the issue, and would likewise talk to the Task Force Provost Marshals to see if they had concerns about the detainee process, or saw things which needed to be investigated. As such, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified, by the time the Graeme Smith Globe and Mail articles had come out, he had already set certain things in motion:

So at the time the article came out, I was aware that the RCMP investigation was underway as well and had also felt that should any of these questions or inquiries turn something up at that point to indicate that there may in fact be an offence that we would in all likelihood have to turn it over to the RCMP as long as I was the subject of their investigation.Footnote 1532

On June 29, 2007, Superintendents Rideout and Blizard of the RCMP concluded (N) (ret’d) Moore had done no wrong. They found, at the time of their investigation, no information or intelligence existing within DND to substantiate any allegations of abuse post handover, and, as such, the CFPM could also not have possessed such knowledge.Footnote 1533 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was verbally briefed on the results of this investigation, but did not read the actual report himself.Footnote 1534

Even after the completion of the RCMP investigation, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore continued to have questions about the detainee process. The RCMP investigators advised him they had found nothing to incriminate him, and reiterated what he felt he was hearing from other sources, namely, the detainee process was solid. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said this raised his confidence level, but he kept on asking questions: “I did carry on listening, you know, talking to commanders about the issue, asking questions of Task Force Provost Marshals after that time.” Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore spoke to the operations officer at CEFCOM at some point, the TFPM at various points, and to MGen (ret’d) Grant when he was at CEFCOM shortly after his return from theatre:

So essentially, if I was dealing with somebody or happened to run into somebody that I felt might be knowledgeable about the process, then I would try and work that into the conversation.

And to be clear here, I wasn’t going around accusing people of things here, but working in questions about, you know, how was your tour and what were the big issues and we’ve seen a lot about the detainee issues in the paper, what were your thoughts on that and, you know, listening for somebody to perhaps say, well, you know, actually that caused me some concern or something, which they did not.Footnote 1535

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified that to his knowledge the JAG was involved in monitoring some of the ongoing court cases. He expected them to report any criminal offences they thought might have occurred in relation to the detainee process. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore referred, as well, to the ongoing processes before this Commission (both the Attaran and the Amnesty/BCCLA complaints), and expected the MPCC would document and report any criminal offence thought to have occurred.Footnote 1536 Finally, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore knew other investigations into the detainee issue were ongoing, including Camel Spider and internal boards of inquiry on the detainee topic within the Canadian Forces.Footnote 1537

Throughout the course of his testimony, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was shown documents, such as the correspondence from MGen Laroche and BGen Juneau, the site visit reports alleging abuse from June 2007 to November 2007, and the DFAIT chart indicating almost 30 percent of detainees interviewed from May 2007 to February 2008 had alleged abuse. This was information Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had not viewed during the timeframe covered by this complaint, and he agreed some of it was troubling. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said if he had seen this information during the timeframe of the complaint, it would have given him a different perspective on the detainee transfer question, and could have caused him to make more inquiries than he did.Footnote 1538

With respect to the MP role in enforcing international law, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore agreed MPs handling detainees had a responsibility to be familiar with the Geneva Conventions.Footnote 1539 Furthermore, he expected MPs engaged in operational functions, such as detainee handling, to nonetheless investigate, or report for investigation, suspected offences of any stripe:

Does that mean that, again, any member of the military police regardless of their rank or the position they happen to be posted to have a duty to investigate possible offences?

  • Generally, yes. I’d say within that, I know if someone, if a military police person comes across an offence and is not employed at that time during an investigations section will probably report that offence and cause it to be investigated by somebody else within that unit. But generally, yes.
  • Without talking about any of the subjects or any person in particular, just put it in the abstract.

    Supposing you’re a Master Corporal MP, and you get some concerns about something you see or you may have read about or somehow you get some information that you think maybe should be looked at a little further, see if there’s any reason for concern there or not. Would that Master Corporal MP be expected to just go about and start asking questions or would there be some protocol they should follow within the MP technical chain to raise that matter to an appropriate level?
  • It would depend on what their specific functions were at the time.

    Some functions that they would be providing may not allow them time to properly go out and conduct an investigation wholly on their own.

    I would say that they would be expected, if they came across information that they believed may be an offence, then they need to either investigate that or pass it to somebody in the military police to be investigated.Footnote 1540

What, for Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, would have constituted an allegation he would have expected his military police to investigate? He was asked whether allegations of possible breaches of international law, found in newspapers, court actions, written reports from diplomats, court judgments, and site visit reports, would invoke a duty to investigate the transfer decisions. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said it depended on the circumstances, and required some evidence of the Task Force Commander’s state of mind:

It would wholly depend on what was in those documents, but if you had allegations that caused you to form a belief that a Canadian detainee was transferred by Commander X, was subsequently tortured post transfer, and Commander X had information that he knew that this person was going to be tortured or would face a substantial risk of torture and transferred him anyway, then that would constitute an offence and require an investigation.

  • So what I think what I seem to be hearing you say is that in your opinion, one of the elements that there would have to be some information about is the knowledge of the Commander at the pertinent time?
  • The Commander’s state of knowledge would be crucial at the pertinent time.Footnote 1541

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore expected, if any MPs had issues with how to carry out their duties, they would consult the Military Police Policies and Technical Procedures manual.Footnote 1542

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was asked about the notion of a pre-investigation investigation, i.e., an initial duty to ask questions before commencing an actual investigation. He thought it was “fair to say there are situations that you come across that you’re not ready yet to say there’s an offence associated with this, but it prompts you to start asking more questions.”Footnote 1543

Based on everything he knew and everything he was hearing during the timeframe of this complaint, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore never developed the suspicion the Commander had a culpable state of mind at the time of transfer. He saw nothing to “suggest that the Commander’s state of knowledge at the time he did a specific transfer was such that he should have halted the transfer and he carried on anyway.”Footnote 1544 Had he received a direct accusation against a commander, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore would have caused an investigation to take place. He never did.Footnote 1545

To the extent Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was aware there were reports of torture, such as reports in the media and possibly through the court process, he also had information the transfers were halted on two occasions. This indicated to him people were keeping an eye on the process and doing what they were supposed to do.Footnote 1546 All told, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore never formed a reasonable suspicion the Task Force Commanders in Afghanistan had committed an offence.Footnote 1547 He would not have expected his military police to self-initiate an investigation if they themselves had not formulated a reasonable suspicion of criminal behaviour. In the same vein, given he personally did not have such a suspicion, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore felt he had not incurred a professional responsibility to conduct an investigation. He made inquiries in a general sense about the detainee process, but did not feel, for example, he had a professional obligation to seek out the site visit reports or additional information on the detainee process.Footnote 1548

On a final note, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore received copies of some type of legal advice on the detainee question, which seems to have come via CEFCOM and JAG. In this respect, then, he appears to have been privy to some of the legal advice the Canadian Forces were receiving on the detainee issue.Footnote 1549

16.8.2 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s Responsibility for the NIS

The Commission heard evidence from Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore he met with the Commanding Officer of the NIS, LCol (ret’d) Garrick, to discuss the allegations in the Amnesty/BCCLA complaint after it was filed on June 12, 2008. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified the purpose of this meeting was to consider whether, given the allegations in the Amnesty/BCCLA complaint, there should be some police investigative action specifically into the issue whether Commanders had acted illegally by ordering the transfer of detainees. It was concluded at this meeting, in light of ongoing NIS investigations, if there was evidence or allegations against a Commander and his state of knowledge when he ordered the transfer of a detainee, this would come to light and prompt further investigation into that issue.Footnote 1550 This, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore said, was a reference to everything under the OP CENTIPEDE umbrella, as well as the work done by Inspector Gfellner in Camel Spider, which, at the time, was wrapping up.Footnote 1551 Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore stated the following:

I do remember discussing this with Lieutenant Colonel Garrick and he felt that a number of the allegations that were referred to in the Amnesty complaint were already under investigation.

I believe we also at that time discussed with respect to CAMEL SPIDER that inspector George Gfellner was being sent into theatre as well and that Lieutenant Colonel Garrick had asked him specifically to have a look, as we had asked others, ask questions about the transfer process and see what people say.Footnote 1552

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore does not appear to have had the notion of an investigation into the Globe and Mail articles in mind during this conversation with LCol (ret’d) Garrick. It appears from LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s evidence that it was under LCol (ret’d) Garrick’s supervision in late April 2007 that these articles were added to the collection of investigations which eventually became Operation Centipede.Footnote 1553 By all indications, therefore, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not personally even aware of this at the time the articles were released, or at any point during the timeframe of this complaint. This is confirmed by the fact Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not recall the Globe and Mail investigation was one of the investigations discussed on June 12, 2008 as being part of the Op Centipede fold.Footnote 1554

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore expected, as of June 12, 2008 and, indeed, prior to then, the ongoing NIS investigations would answer the question of the legality of the transfers, even though he understood post-transfer abuse was not the specific subject of those investigations: “… we had a number of investigations now that were focusing on issues around that, enough so that if there were allegations against a specific Commander and his state of knowledge when he transferred a detainee, that those would come to light and then prompt an investigation into that very issue.”Footnote 1555

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s expectation was seemingly based on certain assumptions about the quality of the ensuing NIS investigative effort. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified he was not satisfied with the pace of the NIS’ Op Centipede investigation. He ascribed this in part to a resourcing issue, which meant some investigations were just taking longer than anyone would have liked.Footnote 1556

With particular reference to the “investigation” into the Graeme Smith articles contained within Op Centipede, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was even hesitant to call it an investigation. As described in the earlier NIS section, the closing comments of the Globe and Mail investigation would seem to suggest the investigator(s) never considered the possibility the transfer decisions themselves may have been illegal. The following is a passage from what Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore referred to as a decision not to investigate, as opposed to an actual investigation into the Globe and Mail articles:Footnote 1557

2. Although these newspaper journalists are reporting that they have interviewed former Afghan captives or at least received information concerning their treatment at the hands of the Afghan authorities, considering the general rules of evidence, the inadmissibility of statements as they pertain to hearsay information, and the lack of any other credible evidence, there is no satisfactory justification to continue to investigate. Likewise, if these reports were some how deemed to be credible, the allegations of ill-treatment are directed against the Afghan authorities. This alone excludes our jurisdictional interests and the mandate of the CFNIS …

3. To that end, any pending media reports/articles concerning the treatment of Afghan prisoners by Afghan authorities which are void of any direct accusations of criminal wrongdoings of CF members, will not be investigated by this office. This file is concluded.Footnote 1558

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not sure whether he read these closing comments about the Globe and Mail articles before his term ended as CFPM. Moreover, Op Centipede came to a close after the timeframe of this complaint. During the timeframe of this complaint, it appears Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not even aware LCol (ret’d) Garrick had asked to have these articles added to the Op Centipede fold.Footnote 1559

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore agreed, ultimately, during his tenure, no investigation was ever completed which answered the question whether the detainee transfers were legal. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore specified an NIS investigation would not have looked broadly at the legality of the detainee regime as a whole. Rather, this would be more in the nature of an investigation against the Government of Canada as a whole, and would have been within the RCMP purview. An NIS investigation, he explained, would have looked at whether a particular Commander, who transferred a particular detainee to torture, had prior knowledge to indicate the detainee would be tortured, but did it anyway.Footnote 1560

16.8.3 Issues Related to Command and Control

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore suggested his lack of command capacity over non-NIS MPs left him with no control over critical decisions being made by and about MPs.Footnote 1561 The CFPM’s lack of command authority over MPs in theatre and at CEFCOM is a structural feature of the chain of command in the CF, and a significant consideration within the context of this complaint. The Commission notes this appears to have been addressed by a change implemented as of April 1, 2011, whereby the CFPM now has command of MPs in theatre when performing their policing duties.

However, the command structure during the timeframe of this complaint seemed to dictate the flow of information (or lack of it) to the CFPM and to MPs generally. For another, it created a concern for the CFPM about the mindset of members of the MP and the perceived independence of MPs to carry out policing tasks. In particular, the CFPM expressed concern about the fact the TFPM in theatre was under the operational command of the Task Force Commander, and yet, could be called upon to question the actions of that Commander, the same individual who would later prepare his performance evaluation reports.Footnote 1562 While the Commission heard no evidence during these hearings indicating MPs felt constrained in their policing decisions by the influence the Task Force Commander could exert over him, this remained a point of concern for Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore throughout his tenure as CFPM:

The major issue in my view is having the military police officers cut off from the senior MP chain of command … the sole decision maker within a different chain of command responding to a commander that then writes their evaluation. So the incentive for them is to please that Commander before anybody else. […] And then when it comes to them seeking advice from senior police officers in their chain of command, because there is no formal command link, that seeking advice is at their discretion.Footnote 1563

The reason for the lack of information flow for the military police, on the detainee question, according to Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, was that information relating to “operational matters” took place within a closed circle, of which the MPs, and the CFPM, were not a part. The chain of command viewed detainees as an operational issue, not a policing issue, and therefore believed the CFPM (and by extension other MPs) need not be involved in that process. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified he pushed for a different command structure during his tenure, which would see all MPs under his direct command. He felt this would have enhanced information flow among MPs and increased the chances the military police would be invited to the table for operational matters like detainees. Without this type of command and control, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore felt left out of a lot of important operational discussions, and indicated to the Commission that requesting documents on detainees would have been seen as an intrusion into the operational field: “… I believe, my requesting any documents without the authority of an investigation behind me would have been seen as an intrusion and I would have been pushed off.”Footnote 1564

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore also had no involvement or input into the role the Afghanistan Task Force Provost Marshals, and the MPs in theatre, would play in the detainee process. He was seen as a policing entity by the operational chain of command, who therefore felt he did not need to be part of the process of determining the proper role for MPs in theatre.Footnote 1565 The CFPM also had no direct input into the number of MPs to be deployed to Afghanistan, although it could be assumed his input would come through the influence he could exert on the CEFCOM PM:

  • So you have no input into the number of MP’s deployed?
  • No. CEFCOM had their own military police adviser, Provost Marshal assigned to them.

    Typically, the way the many people within the chain of command viewed it is they wanted their MP advice from the MP that worked for them. They didn’t want to take their MP advice from somebody that was outside their system, including myself.

    So the result was you got the training, the experience, and the opinion of one military police person, in this case, at the Major level injected into that operation.

    I could try to influence that Major, but I was working against quite an information deficit.Footnote 1566

The chain of command and reporting structure was a serious concern for Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore for a considerable period of time, with senior MPs in theatre not reporting to him, and information not being forwarded to him for action he, as CFPM, may have considered necessary to take. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore referred in his testimony to the chain of command for MPs being “siloed”, resulting in the command structure itself having a detrimental effect on the system of policing in the CF:

I’ve, well, I’ve written numerous letters, papers, conducted many presentations on the topic. But from the time I took over as Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, I think this was probably the issue that took up the majority of my time.

I tried to focus on, tried to stay away from chasing symptoms of problems and go after the problem itself. And in my view, the chain of command for the military police was siloed in such a way that you did not have one formed unit, you had a whole bunch of series, pockets of them across the country.

So you had military police men and women, some of them senior, some of them not terribly senior that are reporting directly to a Commander. And that Commander writes their evaluation at the end of the year and that Commander has, in many cases, a limited knowledge of policing and you know, let’s face it, a police investigation is never a convenient thing. So it could often be perceived as an inhibitor in certain situations when operations are moving very, very fast.

So in my view, having the military police siloed off in many different chains of command, it effected a number of issues. All that I’ve outlined in the documents that I’ve referred to the Vice, to the Chief of Defence Staff. But the overall result was that in my view, the policing system in the Canadian Forces was not was below that of Canada and not because of the men and women in the military police. It was because of the system that we were working under.Footnote 1567

Finally, the Commission heard evidence, throughout the hearings, about the MP technical chain of command and the MP ‘technet’. The MP technical net is a set of vertical and lateral channels of communication between MPs at all levels. It is designed to facilitate the resolution of MP matters related to law enforcement and security inquiries. The technet is comprised of the CFPM and staff, Formation Senior MP Advisors and MP organizations. The responsibility of the MP technical chain is oversight, audit and review of MP functions.Footnote 1568 It is the only formally recognized channel of communications which allows for influencing policing across different chains of command. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore described it as an essential, but sometimes awkward, way of influencing MP decision making on policing matters. He viewed technical control as “[...] a loose association connected by subject matter expertise. [...] But there is no, there is no command associated with technical control. You are essentially trying to influence people that are getting their taskings and directions from somebody else.”Footnote 1569

In short, he felt the technical chain was an unwieldy way in which to run a police force for the Canadian Forces. It depended on the day-to-day discretion of each and every MP as to whether each particular piece of information coming their way should also go up the technical chain, as opposed to, or in addition to the regular CF chain of command: “[...] we had a lot of very intelligent, responsive and dedicated people within the military police as well that would make every effort to advise us if something important was going on, but that was at their discretion.”Footnote 1570

As described earlier, the Commission heard evidence from individuals at CEFCOM, such as LGen (ret’d) Gauthier, LGen Deschamps, and Ms. Duschner. These witnesses described a debate or discussions occurring in the first half of 2007 about the extent to which MPs should be the repository of information about the detainee process, and about disciplining the MP technet.

At first, it appeared to the Commission the CEFCOM hierarchy wished somehow to limit or entirely shut down the flow of information through the MP technical net, at least on the detainee issue. LGen Deschamps and LGen (ret’d) Gauthier made it clear this was not the case. The intent was merely to ensure all information relevant to operations made its way up the operational chain of command, and did not somehow remain exclusively within the MP ranks where operations personnel would have no access to it. This was what MGen Deschamps and LGen (ret’d) Gauthier suggested had occurred in relation to the Attaran complaint, and the information about those detainees. Nevertheless, in hearing this evidence, it was clear to the Commission discussion had occurred, at senior levels within the CEFCOM chain of command, about the role MPs would play in the detainee information retention process, and about disciplining the technical chain in order to ensure operationally important information made its way up the operational chain of command. These discussions related to the mission-critical question of detainees, and the role MPs would play in the process. The CFPM was not a participant in this process,Footnote 1571 nor was the CEFCOM PM. Clearly, this was an important decision-making stage not only in relation to the role of the military police in the new site visit regime, but also in relation to the role they would play in assisting with the investigation and retention of information about detainees who might, one day, be prosecuted within the Afghan system. Key decisions about the MP function, and the information they would retain, were made in the absence of input from key figures in the MP hierarchy.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s efforts to improve the flow of information and the command structure for the military police culminated with his address to the Commander’s Council on October 17, 2008.Footnote 1572 Indeed, LGen (ret’d) Gauthier recalled Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had raised these concerns in the meeting.Footnote 1573 These very fundamental issues emerged as major concerns in Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s testimony, and he evidently struggled with them throughout his tenure as CFPM. Throughout his tenure, he worked diligently within the CF command structure to bring about meaningful changes for the MP branch and the improvement of CF policing. Accordingly, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore did not believe the command and control structure as it existed during the timeframe of this complaint purposefully prevented him or the other subjects of this complaint from investigating the Task Force Commanders and their decisions to transfer. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s concerns in this respect spoke mainly to the system in a general sense and the overall flow of information, which may have been different if his efforts to reform the command structure had succeeded during the timeframe of this complaint. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not implying, however, the Task Force Commanders, such as MGen Laroche and MGen (ret’d) Grant, in any way purposefully prevented the TFPMs in theatre from investigating the transfer decisions.Footnote 1574

The Complainants’ Submissions

The Complainants submit Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore bears responsibility for a number of acts or omissions which they ascribe to him during the time period of this complaint. Generally, they say he bore ultimate responsibility as the CFPM, and as the most senior member of the military police, for a lack of investigative activity and for failures of MP education and training. In general, their written submissions state the failings for which Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was responsible include the following, which the Complainants consider tantamount to a leadership failure:

  • None of the allegations of detainee abuse documented throughout 2007 resulted in any review of the transfer orders.
  • There was no MP inquiry following the allegations of torture leading to the November 2007 suspension of transfers, despite the fact the detainee interviewed for the November 5, 2007 DFAIT report was very likely tortured by the NDS.
  • Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was aware of reports of NDS torture and testified as to his concern, but this concern amounted to a cursory and inadequate investigation. When further reports of post-transfer abuse emerged, he declined to devote any resources for further inquiry and failed to take the necessary steps to ensure Canadian commanders were fulfilling their legal obligations.
  • During his command there was virtually no activity on the Globe and Mail investigations for a significant period of time, a problem for which Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was ultimately responsible.
  • He failed to provide adequate training and education for MPs, and briefings for NIS commanders, on reports of post-transfer abuse and the potential legal issues concerning the post-transfer treatment of detainees.
Submissions on Behalf of Capt(N) (ret’d) S. Moore

The submissions of Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore point to a number of factors which, he submits, demonstrate his actions were reasonable in the circumstances.

In those submissions, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore referred throughout his evidence to what he saw as a problem with the chain of command structure. Under that structure, although he was CFPM he had no command authority over the majority of the military police in the Canadian Forces. This significant impediment was noted by the Commission in the Attaran complaint, where the Commission recommended a new and more complete command and control structure which allowed the CFPM to fulfill the important responsibilities of that office (Recommendation 1(a)). Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had made considerable efforts to try to change the status quo.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore submitted, because detainee handling was seen as an operational and not a policing matter, the CFPM had very little, if any, input. He lobbied for a role to be played by the CFPM in decisions with respect to processes involving detainees similar to that played by the Royal Provost Marshal in Great Britain.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore submits that the view detainee handling was an operational matter drove the flow of information concerning detainees post-transfer. The military police were not provided with post-transfer information. The C4 communications which would have included site visit reports and the concerns of Richard Colvin were not distributed to the CEFCOM PM, and therefore could not be forwarded by them to the CFPM.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore testified he was not consulted on the arrangement for the transfer of detainees between the Canadian Forces and Afghanistan signed on December 18, 2005. However, he submits it was reasonable for him to assume the Government had done its due diligence in crafting the agreement and it was legal. The subsequent arrangement of May 3, 2007 strengthened the original agreement in a number of ways.

Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore submits the evidence shows a commitment to the human rights of detainees by all concerned with the transfer policy and process. When problems were identified, they were not ignored but assessed and responded to with thought and care. This is evidenced by monitoring, suspending transfers when there were concerns, improving agreements and monitoring procedures. The process was taken seriously, overseen at very high levels, and subject to extensive legal review.

Around the time of the first AIC/BCCLA complaint, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore started to think about the issue of post-transfer treatment of detainees. He assumed in formulating its transfer policy, the Government had crafted a legal regime and it would develop a process where detainees would not face a risk of torture. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore submits these were reasonable assumptions.

According to Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore, the legality of a transfer order depends on the Task Force Commander’s state of knowledge with respect to the risk of torture associated with that particular transfer. The fact an allegation of torture is subsequently made does not reveal the Task Force Commander’s knowledge at the time of transfer. This information would be necessary to cause an investigation since, without it, there would be nothing on which to base a reasonable suspicion a crime had been committed.

The factors influencing the CFPM’s thinking an investigation was not required are said to include the following:

  • The Rideout/Blizard Report dated June 27, 2007.
  • Following the original AIC/BCCLA complaint, he directed the CO/NIS to examine current and past investigations to see if there was any link between them and the issue of post-transfer abuse. He was told there was no need for an investigation.
  • No concerns were brought to the attention of Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore by the TFPMs. He knew the TFPMs and had confidence in their integrity and commitment to duty.
  • The MPCC did not refer any evidence of an offence to him during its investigation of the original AIC/BCCLA complaint.
  • Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore reasonably expected existing investigations, including Camel Spider and Centipede (which was actually a collection of investigations), would uncover any allegations around transfer orders and the Task Force Commander’s state of knowledge, although this was not their actual subject matter. The broadening of the Camel Spider mandate showed an effort on the part of the CFPM to become aware of the situation. He acknowledges in his submissions it appears Centipede “was lacking in vigour”, and the shape of the investigation envisaged by the CO/NIS did not square with what appeared to have actually been done. However, there was at the time an expectation these investigations would uncover any issue around the transfer orders.
  • It was reasonable for Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore to believe, with respect to the Federal Court litigation, the cases were being monitored by JAG lawyers who knew more about the issue than he did.
  • Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had a level of confidence in the Task Force Commanders and a belief they would follow the law. He knew decisions were being made with the advice of lawyers and other advisors. Because the process involved a number of people, if something were wrong it would be brought to the attention of the MPs.
  • No complaint or allegation was ever made to the military police about Task Force Commanders “illegally” ordering transfers.
  • In the absence of a complaint, there was no cause to launch a formal investigation. Simply requesting documents short of a formal investigation would have been seen as an “intrusion”.
Conclusions Regarding Captain (N) (ret’d) S. Moore

Having considered the totality of the evidence and submissions, the Commission is not persuaded that Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore’s conduct failed to meet the standards expected of a police officer. We note in particular the following points in reaching this conclusion:

  • Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore knew Canada’s detainees were to be handled in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, and from the outset of the timeframe of this complaint was attuned to the legal issues surrounding the transfer of detainees to a potential risk of torture.
  • For various reasons for which the Commission concludes he is not personally responsible, Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore had a limited degree of information about the detainee process and the potential risks of mistreatment of detainees post transfer. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was not provided the site visit reports from DFAIT visits, nor was he privy to core correspondence and the high-level decision-making process with respect to detainee policy. Capt(N) (ret’d) Moore was conscious of the February 21, 2007 Amnesty/BCCLA complaint, and from then forward, he took several steps to monitor the detainee process and address the allegations against him personally. These steps included the following:
    • Requesting, via LCol (ret’d) Garrick, his NIS Commander, an independent body investigate his role in the detainee transfer decisions
    • Directing LCol (ret’d) Garrick to review existing NIS investigations to see whether they raised concerns about post-transfer abuse
